paragraphs: Water has driven the biggest local fight over a Google data center. In Botetourt County, Virginia, an agreement between Helios Botetourt, the entity developing Google's campus, and the Western Virginia Water Authority allows the site to draw 2 million to 8 million gallons a day from Carvins Cove Reservoir, the main drinking water source for Botetourt County and much of the Roanoke Valley. A Cardinal News analysis found that at the contracted 2 million gallons a day, Botetourt would be Google's eighth-largest campus in the world by water use.

Google has lost fights elsewhere. In Indianapolis, its attorney withdrew a rezoning petition for about 468 acres of Franklin Township farmland at a City-County Council hearing on September 22, 2025, after hundreds of opponents packed the room. "The equation is to mount a large opposition as soon as you can," said Meredith Sharp of Protect Franklin Township. In Chile, a court ruled in February 2024 that Google must revise its application for a $200 million data center in Cerrillos, Santiago, to account for climate change, after locals cited a proposed 7.6 million liters of potable water a day.

Where Google has won approval, opposition has sometimes continued after the vote. Sand Springs, a Tulsa suburb of about 20,000, rezoned 827 acres for Google's Project Spring on a 6-1 council vote in February 2026. Residents who said they were kept in the dark formed the Protect Sand Springs Alliance and petitioned to recall two council members, but the city clerk's office found too many of the more than 1,600 signatures were invalid, the Tulsa Flyer reported on May 1, 2026.

One of the sharpest fights over a Vantage campus has been in Port Washington, Wisconsin. Vantage's Lighthouse campus there is a $15 billion project for OpenAI and Oracle under the Stargate program. Its four data center buildings are expected to need 1.3 gigawatts of electricity, and a Clean Wisconsin analysis said the campus could need as much as 3.5 gigawatts once fully built. The Common Council approved the development agreement in August 2025, and in November 2025 unanimously created a tax increment district under which Vantage pays upfront for an estimated $175 million of infrastructure and is repaid from the tax increment. "Vantage is putting all the capital up front for all of the infrastructure," Mayor Ted Neitzke IV said. Residents were less sure. Christine Le Jeune of Great Lakes Neighbors United called it "a gigantic complex". The power it needs has brought with it a proposed $1.4 billion transmission line from American Transmission Co.

Great Lakes Neighbors United, a residents' group formed after the Vantage announcement, drew up a ballot measure, and more than 1,000 residents signed the petition that put it on the ballot. On April 7, 2026, 66 percent of Port Washington voters approved the measure, which requires voter approval for any tax incentive above $10 million; Fox News reported that this made it the first city in the nation to pass a referendum restricting AI data center development. It does not affect the existing Vantage deal. "We are not against development," said Carri Prom, the group's co-founder. "We are for development that the community understands, supports and has chosen together."

Vantage's largest project is Frontier, a 1,200-acre, 1.4 gigawatt campus in Shackelford County, Texas, near Abilene, planned as ten single-story buildings at a cost the company puts at more than $25 billion. Vantage said in December 2025 that it had broken ground as part of the Oracle and OpenAI Stargate expansion.

In Wyoming, the Laramie County commissioners unanimously approved a zone change in September 2026 for Project Latigo, a 1,835-acre, 480 megawatt campus on Terry Ranch Road about 12 miles south of Cheyenne. Vantage says it would run on Wyoming natural gas and use a closed-loop cooling system, with water drawn from on-site wells; its permit application says it will restore 110 gallons of water for every 100 it uses, through projects such as floodplain and wetland restoration, and it puts the investment at up to $20 billion. Vantage hopes to begin construction in 2027 and continue into 2030.

STACK Infrastructure's largest proposal is the Southern Virginia Megasite at Berry Hill in Pittsylvania County, less than 10 miles west of Danville. In May 2026 the Danville-Pittsylvania Regional Industrial Facilities Authority approved a performance agreement that had grown from an initial $73 billion and 2,050 jobs to $100 billion and 2,500 jobs paying at least $80,500 over 30 years. STACK bought nearly 3,000 acres there in April 2026. Three residents spoke against it at the meeting over water use and transparency, and one spoke in favor.

The deal depends on Virginia's sales tax exemption for data center equipment, which the General Assembly nearly cut short before extending it to 2035 at the end of June 2026, though data centers will now pay a separate tax on the electricity they use. Matt Rowe, Pittsylvania County's economic development director, said losing the exemption "would severely cause the project to be at a disadvantage." The Berry Hill project is separately exempt from state retail taxes until at least 2040 under a deal requiring at least $35 billion of investment and 1,000 new jobs. Its first phase is due to close by June 2027 and the rest by June 2031.

Closer to Washington, STACK has been turned down. In September 2025 the Prince William County Board of Supervisors voted 4-2 to reject its request to rezone about 58 acres along Nokesville Road in Bristow, an expansion of its NVA02 campus, after residents objected over its closeness to homes and effect on property values. The vote came with the Gainesville seat empty after the death of Supervisor Bob Weir, an opponent of data centers in western Prince William. "We have no voice in these votes that impact every single community member in Prince William County," said Elena Schlossberg of the Coalition to Protect Prince William County.

CoreWeave sells AI cloud computing and is expanding fast. On its second-quarter earnings call in August 2026 it reported 4.2 gigawatts of contracted power, and aims to have more than 3 gigawatts running by the end of 2027 and more than 8 gigawatts by 2030. Asked if growing local opposition could slow those plans, chief executive Mike Intrator said moratoriums "are not going to impact the demand for this infrastructure. They are going to impact where this infrastructure gets built." His comment followed New York's yearlong statewide pause on environmental permits for new large data centers.

Its most contested site is in Kenilworth, New Jersey, where a $1.8 billion, roughly 400,000-square-foot data center is under construction on the former Merck site on Galloping Hill Road; the mayor expects it finished by the end of 2027. The borough council approved it with little notice, and by spring 2026, with building underway, residents were rallying against it and a petition to stop construction gathered more than 1,500 signatures. "We're going to have major issues with the water in the future, with so many data centers being built," resident Rosa Joseph said. Mayor Linda Karlovitch said CoreWeave would pay sales tax on its power and fund required transmission upgrades.

In Lancaster, Pennsylvania, CoreWeave is the sole tenant of a $6 billion data center at 216 Greenfield Road, a former printing plant site, starting at 100 megawatts with room to grow to 300. The city said existing zoning already covered the use, so no council approval was needed; about 20 residents objected at a July 2025 meeting. Resident Emma Burgess said the first 100 megawatts would use as much power as at least 85,000 homes, in a city of about 21,000 homes. "We all know these are not wholesale trade and storage facilities," resident Amy Ernst said.

QTS gave up in July on what would have been the largest data center campus in the world. On July 2, 2026 it withdrew its Virginia Supreme Court appeal over the Prince William Digital Gateway, planned across 2,000 acres beside Manassas National Battlefield Park, saying it had decided "to terminate the Digital Gateway project" after courts voided the county's 2023 rezoning over improper public notice.

Its Fayetteville, Georgia campus, one of the largest in the country, became a story about water. A May 2025 county letter showed the site had used nearly 30 million gallons without paying, through a connection installed without the utility's knowledge. QTS called any suggestion of improper use "categorically false," blamed a billing error, and paid a retroactive $147,000 bill. The company says about 8,000 workers are on site at peak on a campus planned for up to 13 buildings.

In York County, South Carolina, residents near a $1 billion QTS campus under construction have petitioned against it over traffic, blasting and constant construction noise. "If I had known that and all that would follow with it, we could've gone somewhere else," resident Melanie Cody said. QTS doubled its footprint there in December 2025 by buying another 400 acres.

In Wisconsin, QTS moved a 1,600-acre Dane County proposal from the Town of Vienna, which had voted it down, to the village of DeForest. Emails obtained by a local group show the village president discussed the move with QTS before the public was notified. Residents in DeForest have organized to stop it.

Lackawanna County, around Scranton, has faced a wave of data center proposals: thirteen campuses, about 90 buildings in all, by the count of Resilience in June 2026, with Archbald, a borough of about 7,500, carrying five or six of them on its own. Among the largest is Wildcat Ridge, a $2.1 billion plan for 14 three-story buildings on nearly 400 acres of mountainside. Others have been proposed in Dickson City, Clifton and Covington townships and Ransom Township. In Newton Township, landowner Popca LLC applied in January 2026 to build two buildings on the 90-acre Ira Tripp Tract on Newton Road; the zoning officer turned the application down that February, and the zoning hearing board heard Popca's appeal on April 27, 2026, with no result published since.

Archbald has become the center of the fight. On November 24, 2025 its borough council voted 4-2, with one abstention, for a data center overlay that opened land near Business Route 6 zoned for conservation and residential use to data centers, over the objections of a packed and angry room. "Zoning is supposed to protect borough residents, not data park developers," resident Sheri Skrutski told them. By March 18, 2026 the balance had turned: four council members removed the president, Dave Moran, the vice president, Richard Guman, and the president pro tem, Marie Andreoli, from their leadership posts. "This gives me no pleasure, and a lot has been lost," said Erin Owen, who moved the removal. Nine days later, with state law set to approve the application by default if council failed to act by close of business, the council voted 5-0 against Provident Realty Advisors' Project Scott, 18 buildings filed under the name Archbald I LLC, in front of about 200 residents, many in yellow shirts. The developer appealed to county court on April 24.

Neighboring boroughs have written rules rather than wait. Dickson City council unanimously passed an ordinance in February 2026 zoning an area of the borough for data centers as a manufacturing use, with a 60-foot height limit and noise restrictions. Many speakers there asked for a moratorium, but Mayor Robert MacCallum said Pennsylvania law does not currently allow one at the municipal level. County Commissioner Bill Gaughan has called for a three-year statewide moratorium on new data center approvals. "Is this development or is this exploitation?" he asked at the Archbald vote.

The power is already being planned. PPL plans a new high-voltage substation on Archbald Mountain, three new switching stations, and about eight miles of new power lines through Archbald, Jessup, Olyphant and Jefferson Township, part of it on a newly cleared 250-foot-wide corridor, to be built between 2027 and 2030 if the state Public Utility Commission approves it. The substation would sit near the quarry where Green Mountain 6 LLC has proposed a 272-acre data center campus. PPL would not say whether its new customers are data centers. One Archbald campus alone may need up to 3.3 million gallons of water a day from Lake Scranton, according to Resilience.

Caroline County sits on Interstate 95 between Fredericksburg and Richmond, and with space in Northern Virginia at a premium it has begun to attract data center developers. On August 12, 2025 the Board of Supervisors approved a performance agreement with a CleanArc Data Centers subsidiary for a 650-acre campus on the old Virginia Bazaar flea market grounds just east of I-95 off Exit 110: three buildings of 490,000 square feet each, with the possibility of two more. Bowling Green District Supervisor Jeff Sili cast the only vote against. The county expects more than $13 million a year in tax from it, about 17 percent of its general fund, which it said would be needed for schools, fire engines, ambulances, deputies and water and sewer upgrades. CleanArc puts the campus at 900 megawatts in three 300-megawatt phases running from 2027 into the mid-2030s, and no potable water is to be used for cooling.

The county has also turned one down: a 900-acre campus proposed by VALCO on land along Mount Airy Drive beside the North Anna River, west of the interstate. It had been defeated twice by the planning commission and once by the board, then brought back at the request of Madison District Supervisor Clay Forehand, who argued a single campus would bring the tax of eight to ten distribution centers without the trucks. "I call it the zombie project," said resident Kevin Collins, "because it keeps popping up out of the grave on us." On June 18, 2024 supervisors rejected the plan amendment 5-1, saying there was plenty of land already zoned industrial; the county's planning director noted 1,848 acres of undeveloped industrial land east of the interstate in the Carmel Church Growth Area. "We have rezoned a number of parcels for industrial use that still have not produced any development," Sili said. VALCO withdrew its rezoning request.

Amazon's Mattameade campus, planned as eleven two-story buildings on about 1,143 acres southeast of the I-95 and Mudd Tavern Road intersection, straddles the line with Spotsylvania County. Its federal wetlands permit application proposes buying wetland and stream credits to offset the damage, and includes three substation pads; a consultant's letter attached to it says the project allows for at least roughly 770 megawatts of capacity by 2027. Six more filings sit around Ruther Glen and Ladysmith: ADP's Ladysmith Data Hub and its approved Carmel Church Data Hub, the Caroline Center for Innovation, Thornberry Data Center Campus, Bull Church Data Center and Ladysmith Technology Park, all still proposed with no power figures made public.

Water has already shaped the county's own plans. In November 2024 the Board of Supervisors dropped industrial cooling water from its application to the state Department of Environmental Quality to withdraw water from the Rappahannock River. Friends of the Rappahannock has warned that data centers can use millions of gallons of water a day for cooling.

Ireland's planning appeals body, An Coimisiún Pleanála, overturned permission in September 2026 for a 30,000-square-meter data center in Killala, County Mayo, proposed by Mayo Data Hub Ltd, part of the US firm Avaio Digital. It found the developer had not shown enough local electricity or any deal to buy renewable power, and ruled that it "has failed to demonstrate that the proposed development would be in accordance with the overarching objectives of the Climate Action Plan 2025." Mayo County Council had approved the 1.5 billion euro project despite objections including one from the novelist Sally Rooney.

Most of Ireland's data centers are around Dublin, where new grid connections were effectively frozen for years. The energy regulator, the CRU, ended that freeze in December 2025 with rules requiring each new data center to bring its own generation or storage and to get at least 80 percent of its yearly power from new Irish renewable projects, with six years to get there.

On April 27, 2026, Friends of the Irish Environment, Friends of the Earth Ireland and ClientEarth took the CRU to the High Court, arguing the rules let data centers run on fossil gas for six years and leave backup generation out of the 80 percent test. Outside Dublin, Amazon plans data centers at Bord na Móna's Eco Energy Park in County Offaly and Microsoft at Naas.

Apple's €850 million data center at Derrydonnell Woods near Athenry, County Galway, first announced in 2015, was never built. Apple won planning permission in 2016 but dropped the project in 2018 after legal challenges delayed it. Galway County Council granted a five-year extension in 2021; a resident and the group Eco-Advocacy challenged it, and in June 2022 the High Court quashed the extension, so Apple would now need an entirely new application to build there.

In Denmark, Apple bought a 285-hectare site at Aabenraa in 2017 for a planned $921 million data center, then cancelled it in June 2019, put the land up for sale, and said it would instead grow its nearby Viborg data center. Aabenraa's mayor, Thomas Andresen, called the cancellation "an undesirable bump" in the town's efforts to build jobs around data centers.

In the United States, Apple's $1.3 billion Waukee, Iowa data center, announced in 2017 with about $214 million in incentives, did not open its first building until October 2024; Apple has not applied to build the additional buildings once planned for its 2,000 acres there. In Maiden, North Carolina, where its campus already spans about a million square feet, Apple is adding a 237,600-square-foot building, a $175 million investment. Nevada approved $62.2 million in tax abatements in August 2024 for Apple to expand its Reno-area data center. Apple has also begun shipping AI servers from a Houston factory that a source told the Houston Business Journal will supply sites including Mesa, Arizona and Maiden.

France's biggest data center fight is over Campus IA at Fouju, near Melun in Seine-et-Marne: eleven data centers on about 90 hectares, 70 of them mostly cereal fields, eventually drawing up to 1,400 megawatts of power, about as much as one nuclear reactor. The Seine-et-Marne prefect authorized the first buildings on July 29, 2026, after a public inquiry held from April 30 to May 30. Opponents, led by France Nature Environnement and the farmers' union Confédération paysanne, are weighing a court appeal.

They object to the loss of farmland, the heat, more than 600 backup generators running on fuel oil, and refrigerants classed as PFAS chemicals. A petition against the project has more than 50,000 signatures. The grid operator RTE plans to connect the site in steps, 240 megawatts by the end of 2027 and 700 by the end of 2029. The prefect's order bans drawing local water for cooling.

Residents have won twice this summer. In Le Bourget, north of Paris, the newly elected mayor, Mehdi Nezzar, withdrew Segro's building permit for a data center on the former H&M site on June 12, 2026; on July 28 the Montreuil administrative court refused to suspend his decision. On July 10, a judge in Grenoble suspended Sesterce's permit for an AI computing center of more than 60 megawatts at the Rovaltain business park in Alixan, near Valence, because no environmental impact study had been done.
The largest plans are in the north. SoftBank has committed up to 75 billion euros for AI data centers in France, starting with 3.1 gigawatts by 2031 at Loon-Plage near Dunkirk, Bosquel and Bouchain.

Williamson County's sharpest fight is over a project the city of Taylor says it cannot stop. Project Mustang, from South Dakota's Big Watt Digital and Virginia's PowerHouse Data Centers, would put at least two data centers and a 477-megawatt gas-fired power plant on 665 acres east of Taylor, between FM 112 and U.S. 79. Taylor had negotiated a voluntary annexation to hold the developer to rules on water, noise, air quality and drainage, but in August 2026 the city's planning and zoning commission paused approval for 90 days.

On September 3 the developers withdrew the annexation application and said they would build anyway: the site sits in Taylor's extraterritorial jurisdiction, where state law imposes no zoning. "Taylor currently has no authority to stop this project or regulate how it's developed," the city said, adding it also cannot collect property or sales tax from it.

Residents had already tried to force a vote. Halt Taylor Data Centers collected the 1,400 signatures needed for a petition seeking a moratorium, but the city council ruled that state law barred the measure from the initiative process or the ballot; the group has asked the Third Court of Appeals to order a vote. "Everything happens behind closed doors, then we're told to just trust" the city, organizer Carrie D'Anna told the Austin Free Press.

In Round Rock, Gary Oldham's group Protect Round Rock gathered 3,500 signatures against an AI data center planned near Old Settlers Park, but the city council signaled unanimous preliminary approval. In Jarrell, Prominent Property Group's Mesone Data Center, proposed on about 150 acres with access to 200 megawatts of gas and grid power, drew resident concern in September 2025; the planning and zoning commission recommended the rezoning for a city council vote on October 14, 2025, and no result has been published since.

Williamson County, in the Austin area, had 30 data centers operating or planned across nine campuses by June 2026, the Austin Free Press reported. The eight already running have a combined capacity of about 500 megawatts; at full build the county's total would be 1.6 to 1.9 gigawatts. Developers include Sabey, Switch, Skybox Datacenters, Iron Mountain, which plans seven buildings, and Blueprint Data Centers.

In the Columbus area, one of the country's top data center markets, a Licking County town has turned one down. On August 25, 2026 Pataskala City Council unanimously rejected a site plan from Aligned Data Centers for a 200-megawatt, three-building campus on about 89 acres at Broad and Mink streets in the city's industrial park, following the planning and zoning commission's 5-2 recommendation on June 3. That hearing ran four hours before a standing-room crowd. Aligned said the land was already zoned for the use, that it sat beside American Electric Power facilities, and that it would not seek or accept local property tax abatements. Maritza Motino, who lives across Broad Street, sat through it holding a "No Data Center" sign listing noise, environmental impact and the cost of electricity. Council President Brandon Galik, who moved to accept the commission's recommendation, said the "plan is incomplete" and he was not comfortable voting for it.

Licking County already hosts one of the country's biggest data center clusters, mostly in New Albany: Meta's 562-megawatt Prometheus campus, Google's 453-megawatt site, and Amazon Web Services' 213-megawatt campus are all operating, with Vantage building a fourth. Microsoft has two projects under construction in the county, in Heath and at New Albany's Beech Road site, alongside more capacity Meta arranged in November 2025 to draw from AEP's Green Chapel substation, built for an Intel chip plant that Intel has since delayed.

The state has pulled back its own incentives at the same time. On June 1, 2026 the Ohio Tax Credit Authority approved a $42.3 million sales tax exemption for Cologix, part of it for a 150-acre site in Johnstown drawing 75 megawatts at first and up to 176, which also has a 15-year, 100 percent property tax abatement from the city. It was the last such exemption for the indefinite future: days earlier Governor Mike DeWine had announced a pause on them, exempting the Cologix project, after reporting that the 2025 breaks had come to $1.568 billion, eleven times what the state had estimated.
What comes next in Pataskala is the ballot: council has agreed to put a proposed data center ban before voters on November 3, 2026, after residents gathered more than 500 signatures.

Nscale is a British AI infrastructure start-up backed by Nvidia, with large contracts from Microsoft. In March 2026 it agreed to buy the company that owns the 2,250-acre Monarch Compute Campus in West Virginia, expected to reach 2 gigawatts of power by early 2028 and 8 gigawatts by 2031. Microsoft has agreed to rent 1.35 gigawatts of servers there starting in 2027.

Nscale's UK flagship site, at Loughton in Essex, tests how far the government will lean on local planning. Loughton Town Council's planning officers said Nscale's proposed changes made the approved site 50 percent bigger, with 50 percent more internal capacity, and called for a new application in March 2026. Epping Forest District Council, the actual decision maker, approved it anyway in June 2026 over objections from the town council and residents; a government minister had written to the council's chief executive the previous November backing the project. Completion has slipped from the end of 2026 to 2027.

In Norway, Nscale's campus at Narvik, above the Arctic Circle, draws on the region's cheap surplus hydropower; its first phase will use about 230 megawatts. The site was originally meant to be the first European stop for OpenAI's Stargate project, but in April 2026 Nscale dropped the Stargate name and said Microsoft, not OpenAI, would be the direct customer there; OpenAI says it will still use the site's capacity through Microsoft.

Nscale's other UK project has stalled. OpenAI said in September 2025 it would build Stargate UK with Nvidia and Nscale at Cobalt Park in North Tyneside, then halted it in April 2026, saying it was waiting for the right "regulation and cost of energy." No construction has started at the site, which already holds about 35 megawatts of older data center capacity.

In Fulton County the zoning decisions belong to its fifteen cities, so the county commission has used the one lever it holds: money. On August 5, 2026 the Board of Commissioners passed a resolution opposing tax abatements or any other incentive for data centers from development authorities in the county, and urging the Development Authority of Fulton County to decline to consider them. That authority has granted $150 million in data center tax breaks since 2020, and the county says the state's own incentives are estimated to cost county and city governments $1.1 billion in sales tax revenue in 2026. "This resolution is about fiscal responsibility, protecting our tax digest, and respecting our municipal partners," said District 1 Commissioner Bridget Thorne, who sponsored it with District 2 Commissioner Bob Ellis.

The county's north end has been pausing. Milton's city council voted unanimously in June 2026 for a 30-day moratorium, open to extension, on every kind of data center application from rezonings to business licenses, and Roswell has adopted a moratorium too. Atlanta went earlier, and further: on September 3, 2024 the city council banned data centers along and near the BeltLine and within half a mile of MARTA stations. "Atlanta's data center market is one of the fastest growing in the nation," said Councilmember Jason Dozier, and it "raises serious concerns about the impact on our urban environment and essential infrastructure."

The south end is where the buildings are going. At least 20 data centers are being planned in southern Fulton County, an area of majority-Black cities including South Fulton, Union City and Fairburn, among them Vantage's 105-megawatt College Park Data Center Campus, Edged's 100-megawatt ATL01-2 building in Atlanta and xAI's site at QTS in Atlanta. South Fulton adopted rules in June 2025 on noise and distance from homes, then that August approved another project that the city had said could generate $7 million to $10 million in revenue. Water for Fairburn, Palmetto and Union City comes through a decades-old regional water and sewer authority that Chris Manganiello of Chattahoochee Riverkeeper said is struggling to find direction, identify partners and address funding needs. "They're noisy … they use a tremendous amount of water and electricity," said resident Yvonne Cole Boone. "We don't want our tree canopy to be knocked down."

Niagara County's largest data center is TeraWulf's Lake Mariner campus in Somerset, near Barker, on the site of a former coal-fired power plant, where AI buildings leased to Core42 and Fluidstack are going up beside five crypto-mining buildings. In October 2025 the Somerset planning board and town board unanimously approved two more AI buildings on 61 acres, after two on 30 acres were approved that September. In Niagara Falls, Niagara Falls Redevelopment's planned $1.5 billion digital campus cleared a legal hurdle in June 2026, though no start date for work has been set.

Lake Mariner has 750 megawatts of power allocated from NYSEG and the New York Power Authority, 90 percent of it from hydropower. The cooling fans on the AI buildings are rated at 45 decibels, quieter than the crypto buildings, and Town Supervisor Jeffrey Dewart said staffing could grow from 52 full-time workers to 150. There would be no room for further expansion once these buildings are finished.

The Niagara Falls deal settled eminent domain litigation over land on Falls Street near the Seneca Niagara Casino and gave the city 10 acres for Centennial Park and an event center. The council meeting was heated. "These machines require and contaminate a lot of water, and once it's gone, we don't get it back," one speaker said. Mayor Rob Restaino said: "Last night wasn't the approval of a data center, last night was the approval of an agreement between two parties in litigation."

Towns are writing their own rules. North Tonawanda's moratorium has stopped DigiPower X from turning its Erie Avenue crypto mine into an AI data center with a new 80,000-square-foot building. In July 2026 the Niagara County Planning Board backed proposed moratoriums in the Town of Lockport, for 18 months, and Cambria, for nine months; the Town of Lewiston adopted an 18-month moratorium earlier in 2026. The Lockport and Cambria town boards make the final decision.

Data centers have clustered on San Antonio's far West Side around Westover Hills, where the city gave Microsoft a 10-year property tax break in 2007. Vantage Data Centers held its first public hearing, on May 28, 2026, on an air permit for a three-story building at 5207 Rogers Road; company officials told the crowd it is already built and partly operating, backed by 65 diesel generators, while a separate Vantage site on Omicron Drive has 86. Neighbors packed the hearing over noise and light.

San Antonio is writing rules that would confine data centers to industrial and commercial zones, keep them at least 500 feet from homes, schools and hospitals, and ban them from the Edwards Aquifer Recharge Zone; a project that doesn't fit would need a council vote. The city's Zoning Commission was set to finish the rules by the end of September, with a possible council vote in October, while members also weighed a separate 180-day moratorium. "Data centers are one of the largest, fastest-growing threats to our communities," said Councilman Jalen McKee-Rodriguez.

Water is a sharp worry in a region facing long-term drought. A San Antonio Water System analysis found the city's Microsoft and Army Corps data centers used a combined 463 million gallons of water in 2023 and 2024, while residents were held to once-a-week lawn watering. CPS Energy has told its board these large customers already draw about 324 megawatts and could need roughly 2,700 more by 2028, against a total portfolio of about 7,246 megawatts.

CloudHQ, founded in 2016 by former DuPont Fabros chief executive Hossein Fateh, builds large data centers it leases to hyperscale tenants including Meta, Google and Microsoft. The company has 56 data centers operating or in development worldwide, totaling about 1.1 gigawatts, and as of November 2024 had leased 11 of them, with more than 970 megawatts of contracted capacity, more than half still under construction. Its largest US buildings are in Ashburn and Manassas, Virginia.

In Chaska, Minnesota, the city council voted 4-1 in October 2024 for preliminary approval of a 1.4 million square foot, roughly $1 billion building in the West Creek Corporate Center, with a new 200-megawatt substation. Neighbors in the adjacent Clover Ridge neighborhood objected for three hours. "It will impact my quality of life," said Susan Nelson. "This is going to decrease our property values." CloudHQ agreed to build a 30-foot screening berm. The project still needs final site plan approval, and the substation cannot proceed until a system impact study is finished.

In Mount Prospect, Illinois, CloudHQ broke ground on a $2.5 billion, 1.5 million square foot campus on the former United Airlines site, with three data center buildings of more than 80 megawatts each planned and a dedicated ComEd substation. Mayor Paul Hoefer welcomed the project. In Loudoun County, Virginia, a company connected to CloudHQ has asked to raise the allowed data center space on its 96.8-acre Dulles Berry site in Ashburn from about 1.67 million to about 4.05 million square feet.

In France, CloudHQ opened the first phase of its CDG campus in Lisses, south of Paris, whose waste heat is meant to warm up to 7,000 homes in nearby Corbeil-Essonnes. In Germany it is building a 112-megawatt campus in Offenbach, next to Frankfurt, which has drawn criticism over energy use, backup generators and noise, and it plans a separate 276-megawatt campus in the Frankfurt-Hochst industrial park.

About 15 data centers are planned or being built in Brandenburg, the state around Berlin, according to project data compiled by Entwicklungsstadt in September 2026. Under construction are the Schwarz Group's "Home of STACKIT" in Lübbenau, about 200 megawatts of power on a former power plant site and due in 2027; Maincubes' BER02 campus in Nauen, also due in 2027; Vantage's BER2 in Mittenwalde; Yondr's campus at Ragow; and Amazon's European Sovereign Cloud data center at Massen. Amazon also plans one at Baruth/Mark, and NTT Data and Virtus plan campuses in Brieselang and Wustermark.

Three projects, at Heidemühle in Hoppegarten, in Neuenhagen and in Trebbin, are paused. In Hoppegarten, the local SPD opposed the Heidemühle site, inside a protected landscape about 100 meters from a nature reserve, where plans called for four to eight backup-power chimneys 30 to 38 meters tall, run for an hour once a month. In Baruth, where Amazon plans its second site, a citizens' group is already fighting Red Bull's right to pump up to 2.35 billion liters of groundwater a year for a can plant, which campaigners say is 92 percent of the town's water allowance.

Google has walked away from its site. In July 2025 it confirmed it would not build its planned data center in Mittenwalde, about 30 kilometers south of Berlin, after "thorough examination of feasibility, general market developments and our business priorities."

The grid is already stretched: as early as 2025 the regional grid could not serve every connection request quickly. In June 2026 the state Greens demanded a statewide plan for where data centers may go, saying Brandenburg must not become "a mere supplier of electricity and land for large digital corporations."

Norway's cheap hydropower has drawn close to 90 data centers, and the biggest projects are still being built. Nscale is building a campus at Narvik, above the Arctic Circle, for Microsoft, whose customer OpenAI will rent space; its first phase will use about 230 megawatts of power. Google is building a data center of up to 240 megawatts at Gromstul in Skien, with the first phase due to go live in 2026. TikTok runs a 90-megawatt data center built by Green Mountain and plans to grow it to 150.

The fight is over who gets the power. In 2023 the ammunition maker Nammo said electricity it needed for an expansion had gone to TikTok. On March 12, 2026, Parliament rejected a national licensing system for data centers, leaving siting decisions to municipalities, but asked the government for a bill banning data centers used for cryptocurrency mining. Another 53 data centers are registered with grid operator Statnett, which has reserved 3.4 gigawatts for them, more than 8% of the country's installed capacity.

In 2026 the government reclassified data centers as industry, which cuts them off from the cheap "concession power" that hydropower towns receive for their dammed rivers and had been selling on to data centers. Energy Minister Terje Aasland said the change was needed because data center power use is growing fast. Mayors in Sogn were furious: Luster's mayor, Andreas Wollnick Wiese, said the town's power deal with a local data center was now worthless. Rødt, which won 5% at the 2025 election, wants no new data centers until there is a national strategy.

Lake County's biggest data center projects are Amazon's campus in Hobart, near 61st Avenue and Colorado Street, and Sentinel Data Centers' Project Shirley in Eagle Creek Township between Lowell and Hebron. The Hobart City Council approved Amazon's $11 billion plan in January 2026, and Amazon has paid the city $47 million. The Lake County Council voted 6-0 to rezone Sentinel's 162-acre site on State Road 2, east of Clay Street; Sentinel still needs a special exception and site plan approval under the county's data center rules.

Amazon says the Hobart campus will bring more than 400 permanent jobs, but there is still no site plan; the mayor has said there could be up to 25 buildings. Residents led by Angelita Soriano have sued the city over the rezonings and tax break, and in February 2026 asked a Lake County judge to block a fill permit that lets Amazon dig and test the soil. A hearing was set for that month; no ruling has been published. "We want transparency before approvals happen not after," Soriano said.

Project Shirley is a $5 billion, four-building campus that would use about 500 megawatts of power, with about 250 permanent jobs. The county Plan Commission sent it to the council with no recommendation after a 4-4 tie. Hebron resident Dylan Ricard, who lives less than a mile away, says he has had trouble with water from his well in recent years.

Merrillville has paused new data center approvals from June 1, 2026, to May 31, 2027, after four developers approached the town, including Karis Critical, whose nine-building campus on 101st Avenue won zoning approval in 2024, Province Group and Wylie Capital. Council President Rick Bella said the town wants to watch Hobart's campus being built first.

Morrow County, a farming county in northeastern Oregon, has become a hub for Amazon data centers around Boardman, and the county has courted them. In May 2023 the Port of Morrow approved tax breaks worth an estimated $1 billion for six more Amazon data centers, adding to four already there. "If you want to have people move to your county, if you want your young people to come back... you have to give them jobs," said county commission chair David Sykes. In March 2026 Amazon confirmed it had bought 1,300 acres near Boardman, formerly grazing land; a filing describes 16 to 20 buildings of 250,000 square feet each, about 1,000 megawatts of power and $8 billion to $12 billion of investment.

A seventh company, Rowan Digital Infrastructure, is separately proposing a 300-megawatt data center near Boardman called Project Percheron. The county's data centers have been drawn into its worst environmental problem: at least 634 domestic wells nearby have unsafe levels of nitrate, some at nearly ten times the federal limit, and many of the affected families are low-income and Latino. Nitrogen-rich wastewater the Port of Morrow collects from food processors and data centers, including water used to cool Amazon's servers, is spread on farm fields and adds to the pollution, according to the Oregon Capital Chronicle.

On March 31, 2026 Amazon agreed to pay $20.5 million to settle its part of a lawsuit brought by residents who cannot drink their well water, without admitting fault. "These billion-dollar companies pollute with impunity, without regard for the human cost," said Nella Parks of Oregon Rural Action, which has urged Amazon to slow its expansion and treat its wastewater. The case continues against the Port of Morrow and other defendants.

Cloverleaf Infrastructure, based in Houston, is a powered land developer: it does not run data centers itself, but readies sites with grid access and sells them to companies that do. It says it has sold projects able to support more than 7 gigawatts, including sites in Wisconsin for Oracle and OpenAI, and Nvidia took a minority stake in the company in 2026. Its sites have repeatedly drawn local opposition, most recently in Wisconsin, Oklahoma and Kansas.

In Brown County, Wisconsin, Cloverleaf offered landowners in the village of Greenleaf $50,000 to $120,000 an acre for a data center site, then dropped the plan after residents and a local winery objected; LedgeStone Vineyards called it an "attack" on the community by a "nameless, faceless, megacorporation." On August 11, 2026, voters in the nearby Village of Wrightstown were asked in an advisory referendum whether the village should support public improvements tied to a large data center project; 87 percent voted no. "They definitely came out at our meetings," village administrator Travis Coenen said.

Cloverleaf's current fight is in Piedmont, Oklahoma, where it wants about 630 acres north of the city rezoned for Project Open Sky, a campus with 1,000 megawatts of planned IT capacity that the company says would need about 1.5 gigawatts of total power once cooling and other systems are counted. In June 2026 the Piedmont Planning Commission recommended the city council deny the rezoning after a meeting packed with residents. Chief development officer Aaron Bilyeu told the commission the cooling system "circulates water like the radiator in your car" and said data centers "are not noisy." "It's coming to Piedmont. And it's frustrating," resident Rodney Jones said. The council was scheduled to decide on September 28, 2026; no result has been published.

Cloverleaf has also pulled back elsewhere. In Dundee Township, Michigan, it withdrew its agreement for a 750-acre site in October 2025 after resident protests. In Leavenworth County, Kansas, it has discussed Project Bluestem, a nearly 1,000-acre campus near Tonganoxie, with county commissioners, though no official filings have been made and many residents raised concerns in public comment.

Victoria announced new rules for data centres on September 22, 2026. Under the strategy unveiled by Premier Ben Carroll, new data centres will have to provide their own renewable energy and storage, will be banned from using drinking water for cooling, must sit at least 150 metres from homes, will not be permitted near schools and childcare centres, and must pay into a local investment fund to help build TAFEs and parks. "Data centres must power themselves, protect homes and pay their way," Carroll said. Belinda Dennett, chief executive of the industry body Data Centres Australia, called the changes "disappointing", arguing that the 150-metre setback "singles data centres out" for a restriction that comparable industrial uses do not face. Greens MP Sarah Mansfield called the announcement a "huge win for communities" but said the government should provide "acoustic modelling and health and environmental advice" behind the 150-metre buffer. The rules will not apply to projects already approved or to eight applications currently before the planning minister.

Before the change, the state had been fast-tracking projects. Its Development Facilitation Program lets developers bypass the local council and VCAT appeals and apply directly to the planning minister; NextDC had a $1 billion data centre in Port Melbourne approved by the minister within 75 days. In Campbellfield, on the site of a former Ford car factory in the state's north, Singapore-headquartered Zerra DC applied through the same program for a 210,000 square metre, 336 megawatt campus. A petition against it started by local resident Sophie Hopkins passed 1,000 signatures, and even the local Labor MP, Kathleen Matthews-Ward, said the site "would be best used for productive and advanced manufacturing."

The water ban follows documents released under freedom of information in 2025 showing that the water company Greater Western Water was reviewing 19 data centre applications requesting a combined 19,714 megalitres of drinking water a year, enough to supply about 330,000 residents. One proposal at Mt Cottrell alone could consume up to 3,926 megalitres. "We really are at a crossroads," said Professor Tim Fletcher of the University of Melbourne.

The power side is tighter still. Data centres in Victoria are permitted to draw up to 840 megawatts but, according to market operator data, currently consume about a quarter of that; their consumption is set to quadruple by 2030, and the Yallourn coal plant is scheduled to close in 2028. That demand has revived the fight over two proposed transmission lines, the Western Renewables Link and the VNI West interconnector, which face opposition from landholders in western Victoria.

Google wants to build a US$200 million data center on about 23 hectares in Cerrillos, on Santiago's southern edge, and is waiting for the Environmental Assessment Service (SEA) to decide whether the project needs a full environmental review. Google filed on June 17, 2026, calling it a new, air-cooled project. On September 3 the community groups OLCA and Mosacat asked the SEA to require a full assessment with public participation. Google has told the press it has not yet decided to build.

Google's first design, approved in 2020, could draw up to 169 liters of water a second from the Santiago Central aquifer. In February 2024 the Second Environmental Court partly annulled that approval for failing to rule out harm to the aquifer, and Google later gave it up. The new filing keeps the same land, budget and substation plans but uses air cooling and 44 backup generators totaling about 120 megawatts. "Google is trying to override a ruling of the Second Environmental Court," said OLCA director Lucio Cuenca.

Most of the region's existing data centers are north of the city in Quilicura, including Google's and Microsoft's, around a wetland that activists say is drying out; a 2022 estimate put their water draw at about 1.5 billion liters a year. TECfusions plans a campus of up to 100 megawatts in Puente Alto. The jobs are few: permit filings show Google's Quilicura project would employ no more than 223 full-time operations staff. "Those jobs are very specialized, they can't be filled locally," Quilicura councilwoman Alexandra Arancibia told Rest of World.

Most of Italy's data centers, built and planned, are around Milan in Lombardy. The fight there started this summer in Lacchiarella, a town of about 9,000 between Milan and Pavia, where residents held Lombardy's first street protest against data centers on July 12, 2026. They oppose a planned campus of 230,000 square meters and more than 3.5 billion euros that its opponents say would be the biggest in Italy.

Enrico Duranti, a founder of the local Ciarlasco committee, said the campus would use as much energy as 500,000 families and called it colonization. Residents say they, not their town halls, worked out what the projects meant. In late July more than 150 people met in Rho to call for an immediate moratorium on new data centers across Lombardy, and organizers are planning a regional march.

In Travagliato, near Brescia, the town came out against a 120-megawatt data center this summer after 450 residents signed a letter against it; Mayor Renato Pasinetti said the developer, a new company with 10,000 euros of capital, had given only vague answers. The developer, East Gate, has since withdrawn its application. Lombardy's new regional law, in force since June 20, 2026, steers data centers toward old industrial land and charges more to build on farmland.

Aragón, around Zaragoza, has about 30 data center projects in the approval process, ten of them already backed by the regional government, with more than €47 billion committed and about 2,500 megawatts of power projected, Hoy Aragón reported in August 2026. Amazon Web Services accounts for €33.7 billion: it already runs data centers in the region and has waited since 2024 for a 300-megawatt grid connection for a new complex at La Cartuja in Zaragoza. Microsoft plans campuses beside Puerto Venecia in Zaragoza, in La Muela and in Villamayor de Gállego.

Blackstone's Campus Rhodes at Calatorao is planned for up to eight data centers and 650 megawatts, its budget grown from €7.5 billion in 2024 to €11.8 billion. In August 2026 it emerged that INAGA, the regional environmental agency, had given it a simplified review, which takes about three months instead of a year. Noisy work must happen between July 15 and February 15, outside the lesser kestrel's breeding season. Carlos López of Ecologistas en Acción said he believes the developers are trying to speed up construction because opposition keeps growing.

Microsoft's Puerto Venecia project faces 349 objections from the group Salvemos los Pinares de Venecia over a plan to dump almost two million cubic meters of excavated earth at a closed landfill beside the pine woods. In Villamayor de Gállego, Microsoft's 81-hectare site has power approved only for a first 50-megawatt phase. In January 2026 Tu Nube Seca Mi Río and Ecologistas en Acción challenged the fast-track "general interest" approval of Amazon's expansion, and the Superior Court of Justice of Aragón admitted the case weeks later.

A draft Spanish royal decree put out for comment in late August 2026 would require 80% of a data center's power to come from newly built renewable plants, with six months for projects already in process to adapt. Aragón's government prepared objections before the consultation closed on September 4; its energy director, Yolanda Vallés, said the combined conditions would make installing almost any data center unviable.

Cobb County, northwest of Atlanta, has banned new data centers in its unincorporated areas while it writes rules for them. Commissioners passed the moratorium on February 24, 2026, extended it in August, and it now runs to early February 2027. The county's cities are not covered: Marietta has approved a 108-megawatt data center at 1751 Bells Ferry Road for Grind Capital Group and, in August 2026, an 18-megawatt conversion at 1155 Powers Ferry Place.

Neighbors near Bells Ferry Road organized as Not For Us, Cobb County, disputing the developer's estimate of 40 permanent jobs; public records they gathered put the number at five to twenty. At the Powers Ferry Place hearing, residents raised noise and runoff into Rottenwood Creek, and the city's own review found its zoning code has no data center standards and that part of the site sits in the floodplain. "Are you kidding me? You represent us, not them," someone shouted from the crowd after Councilman Daniel Gaddis asked for order. The Cobb Chamber of Commerce backed the project anyway.

St. Louis has just finished a year of writing rules for data centers, after word broke in September 2025 that a developer wanted to build one at the Armory in Midtown. On September 11, 2026, the Board of Aldermen passed Board Bill 49, and Mayor Cara Spencer signed it Sept. 17. It sorts data centers by size, sets setbacks of 150 to 600 feet from homes, bans water-heavy evaporative cooling, and requires the largest projects to hold public meetings and sign community impact agreements; most facilities must start on at least 25% renewable power, rising to 100% by year ten.

The project that set off the debate is exempt from the new rules. On April 21, 2026, the city approved a conditional use permit for a 120-megawatt data center beside the Armory, part of a $3 billion Armory Innovation District expected to generate about $423 million in tax revenue over ten years, roughly half of it for St. Louis Public Schools. Fox Park resident Kat Logan Smith said there was "a serious lack of transparency, not exactly adequate public notice, and a shortage of public engagement."

A companion bill bars the city from giving data centers tax incentives, and it took effect the same day. An earlier attempt at a moratorium failed 7-8 in February when it needed ten votes; Alderman Michael Browning, who sponsored it, said data centers come with "serious risks."

Hillsboro has more data centers than any other city in Oregon: at least 35, according to the Data Center Maps website, with seven more under construction or moving through permitting. On July 27, 2026, the Hillsboro City Council voted unanimously for a 120-day moratorium on new data center and battery-storage applications while it rewrites its development rules; existing data centers and already-filed applications are unaffected. The county's largest operators include QTS, STACK Infrastructure, Digital Realty and Aligned Data Centers in Hillsboro, and Crane Data Centers, which is building two sites in Forest Grove.

Mayor Beach Pace said the city gave only a day's notice of the vote to stop companies from rushing in applications first. "Taking a pause to study, reflect and gather all the facts is both prudent and ethical leadership," one commenter told the council. The Washington County Chamber of Commerce's Jen Little argued a moratorium "should only be considered after the established planning processes have been completed."

The industry has also been stopped at the city's edge: in March 2026 state Senator Janeen Sollman dropped a bill that would have brought 373 acres along U.S. 26 into Hillsboro for data centers, after developer Dirk Knudsen's campaign filed more than 1,000 pieces of opposition. "We fought Janeen every way we could," he said.

Power costs are rising too. Under a new state law that separates out very large electricity customers, regulators in July 2026 approved a 29.7% rate increase for Portland General Electric's data center customers, while residential rates fell 1.3%, about $1.91 a month for a typical home. "These changes ensure that costs created by data centers in PGE's territory are more accurately reflected in their rates," said commission chair Letha Tawney. The moratorium runs until November 24, 2026, when the council can extend it another 120 days or let it expire.

Lehigh County, around Allentown, has one large data center already operating and expanding, Tierpoint's TekPark site in Breinigsville, and several more proposed. The biggest is Project Atlas, Edged's plan for three buildings of about 1.5 million square feet and 725 megawatts on 410 acres at 2493 N. Cedar Crest Boulevard in South Whitehall Township, across from Parkland High School; more than 3,000 people have signed a petition against it. Smaller proposals include J.G. Petrucci's 100-megawatt project and Quantm Group's 80-megawatt project, both in Allentown. Air Products, by contrast, has abandoned its plan for three buildings on its 194-acre former Upper Macungie headquarters: the township zoning hearing board ruled against it in July 2026, and the company let its August 5 appeal deadline pass without appealing, after neighbors like Carol Kuhns raised concerns about water use during a drought and Paul Heintzelman said simply, "We don't want it. I grew up around here."

Municipalities are writing rules first. Upper Macungie's supervisors adopted a zoning amendment in December 2025 restricting data centers to its general industrial and rural technology districts, with standards for setbacks, noise, water, power and emergency planning; the rules apply only to future applications, not the Air Products site. In Allentown, a city council committee recommended Bill 20 in May 2026, which would restrict data centers to the city's most intense industrial zones and require facilities over 50,000 square feet to sit on properties of at least five acres; only 36 parcels in the city qualify, according to its Environmental Advisory Council. "If something is 'strongly encouraged,' it won't be done," said Councilwoman Ce-Ce Gerlach, who wanted water-efficient cooling made mandatory.

State Senator Jarrett Coleman has proposed letting municipalities pause data center projects to review their rules, and ending the state's data center tax breaks. "There's also a false premise that's kind of spreading that oh, these data centers are coming, and there's nothing that can be done to stop them. That's untrue," he said. On power, state regulators approved a PPL rate settlement in June 2026 that raises typical household bills by about $6.48 a month while creating a separate rate class for large loads such as data centers, with ten-year service commitments and, from 2027, $11 million a year toward low-income assistance.

Louisa County has taken two Amazon Web Services data center campuses under a 2023 technology overlay district, and is fighting off a third. AWS's Lake Anna Technology Campus, on 153 acres next to Dominion's North Anna nuclear plant, and a second campus near the Northeast Creek Reservoir are under construction; Amazon put the combined investment at $11 billion through 2040. A third AWS campus, proposed in 2025 for 1,370 acres near the reservoir, was withdrawn in July 2025 after resident opposition.

Residents fought the third campus because it sat next to the county's only public drinking-water reservoir, and over traffic and noise. Mineral District Supervisor Duane Adams said at a June 2025 town hall that he opposed it, saying the county should see how its first two campuses performed. "I work for you. I don't work for AWS," he said. AWS withdrew the application in a July 23, 2025 letter, saying it would reevaluate after community feedback.

AWS bought the land anyway. In January 2026 it paid $72.45 million for about 1,925 acres from the Purcell family, including the tract where the third campus had been proposed, saying the purchase would "help support water infrastructure needs in the area" for a planned countywide waterline. It has not filed a new application. Adams has asked the board to remove that tract from the technology district, but the planning commission has twice pulled the public hearing without explanation, most recently in April 2026.

The county is also selling land for a new campus. In June 2025 its Industrial Development Authority sold the 697-acre Shannon Hill Regional Business Park to EdgeCore Digital Infrastructure for $42 million; EdgeCore plans a $17 billion, 3.9-million-square-foot campus drawing more than 1.1 gigawatts, and construction had begun there by April 2026. Supervisor Manning Woodward said in June 2026 that EdgeCore would generate its own power rather than draw from the grid, and would use water from the James River rather than the reservoir once a new water line is finished, expected by fall 2027.

Atlas Development is a small Carrollton, Georgia company whose president, Jonathon Ward, previously worked for the Atlanta-area contractor United Grading; it lists seven employees on LinkedIn. It has acquired land for several large Georgia data center campuses, though industry databases show no record of it completing or building one. At its biggest project, the real estate company Prologis is the actual backer, staying out of public view for months while Atlas served as the public face.

That project is Project Sail, a $17 billion campus proposed for western Coweta County. On April 7, 2026, county commissioners voted 3-2 to rezone the 830-acre tract for industrial use despite 7,820 signatures asking them to deny it. The approval clears a nine-building, 4.34-million-square-foot campus near Welcome Sargent Road and Wagers Mill Road, outside Newnan, on land the state designates a "Most Significant Groundwater Recharge Area." "Atlas Development has never built a doghouse," resident Steve Swope said. Seventeen residents, farmers and landowners have since sued the county and Atlas in Coweta County Superior Court to void the rezoning.

In Bartow County, Atlas withdrew its Project Springbank proposal near Adairsville on May 13, 2025, after the planning commission voted 6-1 to recommend denying the rezoning of 630 acres. In northern Carroll County, it pulled a data center complex depending on annexation into Temple after two weeks of opposition and the county commissioners' refusal to support the annexation. "This does not mean it's all over," the Carroll County Anti-Data Center Coalition said.

Crusoe is expanding its Stargate data center campus in Abilene, Texas, built for Oracle and OpenAI and now also serving Microsoft, to about 2.1 gigawatts of power. The site runs on its own gas power plant, and on August 5, 2026 the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality gave preliminary approval to grow that plant from 10 turbines to 49. State Rep. Stan Lambert asked for a public meeting in Abilene, and the public comment period stays open until that meeting is held.

Neighbors say they were never told. Omaira Garcia, an Air Force veteran who lives about 500 yards from the plant, said she learned of the project only after construction began in 2024. "We weren't given any time to understand what this impact was going to be on us," she told Floodlight, in reporting published by the Texas Tribune. "We're trapped here." Her neighbor Paul Daniel, 81, said, "We were never advised or anything." Crusoe received an 85 percent property tax break on the project, and some homes sit within half a mile of the plant, according to the Texas Observer.

Crusoe also helped start a 1.8 gigawatt campus called Project Jade in Laramie County, Wyoming, approved unanimously by county commissioners on January 6, 2026, but it left the project around April 2026. Its partner Tallgrass, which is building a gas plant next door to power the site, has kept developing it directly with the data center client and says it has grown to 2.7 gigawatts. The Hyndman Homesites Homeowners Association had raised concerns about wells into the aquifer, turbine emissions, noise and wastewater ponds. "You don't know until you punch a hole in it what you're dealing with," the association's president, Randy Fox, said of the groundwater.

Maharashtra's data center fight is in Thane, where Amazon Data Services India plans a campus on a 53-acre plot at Balkum, estimated at around Rs 47,000 crore. Residents campaigning as Wake Up Thanekar say it is too close to homes, schools, hospitals and the metro. In response the state is writing its first rules on where data centers can go: the Maharashtra Pollution Control Board and IIT Bombay are drafting them, due within a few months as of September.

Residents held a human chain on July 18, 2026, and later met Amazon officials, who they said did not settle their main concern. "I am not against data centre. I am against setting it up in the middle of the town and in our vicinity," said resident Anuradha Rode. Neighbors fear heat, noise from nearly 190 diesel generator sets and power cuts; resident Jatin Kothare put the site's power demand at 420 megawatts. Amazon says the site will not use water for cooling, will get power from its own extra-high-voltage substation and will meet legal noise limits.

The draft rules would set buffer zones between homes and data centers and require recycled wastewater instead of fresh city water for cooling, board chairman Siddhesh Kadam said. The state industrial agency, MIDC, is also planning water for four proposed data center clusters around Mumbai, at TTC Navi Mumbai, Taloja, Mumbai 3.0 and Khalapur, which together would need about 874 million liters a day. It proposes treated sewage for TTC and Taloja, two seawater desalination plants for the others and nearly 180 kilometers of pipelines; MIDC calls its figures preliminary.

Mexico's data center industry is centered on Querétaro, which had 12 facilities operating by February 2026 with up to 10 more planned. More than $12 billion has been invested there since 2020, including about $1.3 billion from Microsoft and $5 billion over 15 years announced by Amazon in 2024. In September 2025, President Claudia Sheinbaum's government announced CloudHQ's $4.8 billion plan for six data centers and 900 megawatts of power; CloudHQ is spending about $250 million on its own power infrastructure.

By August 2026, Sheinbaum's tone had shifted. "We do need to have data centers to advance in artificial intelligence, but Mexico does not necessarily have to be the data center of other places in the world," she said on August 18, pointing to how much electricity and water they use. Seven of Querétaro's 11 aquifers are reported as overexploited, and one data center employed only 64 people in 2025.

The campuses are concentrated in Colón, El Marqués and Pedro Escobedo. Residents of Viborillas report water rationing to three days a week, and Chichimeca and Otomí communities have marched over water use. "A standard data center consumes approximately the same electricity as a medium-sized city," said Abelardo Rodríguez Macías of the Chichimeca Otomí Assembly. Querétaro's government disputes the link between data centers and water shortages, since the state exempts projects in industrial parks from environmental impact filings.

Gauteng, around Johannesburg, holds many of South Africa's largest data centers; South Africa has about 70 percent of Africa's. Teraco's Isando campus has 70 megawatts of computing power and its Bredell campus in Ekurhuleni has 63 megawatts, Teraco says. NTT Data's Midrand facility has 12 megawatts. Vantage is building three data centers in Waterfall City planned at 120 megawatts, and Africa Data Centres runs facilities in Midrand and Samrand.

In September 2026 civil rights groups called for a halt to new data centers until their use of water, land and electricity had been investigated. The South African Human Rights Commission, which sought public input in May, said it had received more than 250 submissions. "A key issue emerging from the process is precisely the availability, consistency and transparency of information relating to matters such as electricity and water demand, land use, infrastructure requirements, environmental impacts and impacts on surrounding communities," said Dr. Eileen Carter, who leads the commission's review. Street protests have centred on Cape Town, where the Housing Assembly is fighting two data centers proposed by Equinix.

Eskom says it can meet current demand from data centers, though the country had near-daily power cuts in 2023. On water, Teraco's head of sustainability Bryce Allan said a 30-megawatt data center using closed-loop cooling "would consume the same amount of water as the average restaurant" in a year. "When we look at our domestic power requirements, it necessitates a conversation about prioritising," said Daniel Hartford of Foxglove.

Two large data center campuses are under construction in Bartow County and a third is approved. Project Bunkhouse, on the 876-acre Gaines farm on Taff Road near Stilesboro, was rezoned in June 2025 for Taurus DC SPE LLC and will be run by Digital Realty; the county says it is planned for about 1,300 megawatts of power and $18 billion. Switch is building a campus on about 126 acres outside Cartersville, and on September 3, 2026 the Cartersville City Council approved DataBank's Project Indo, a 200-megawatt campus with two 664,000-square-foot buildings at 218 Industrial Park Road.

Bartow is run by a single commissioner, Steve Taylor, and he has welcomed data centers. "I think five or six would maybe be our limit, as far as our appetite for them," he said in July 2026, adding that two or three more are in the pipeline. The county says it has given the data centers no tax abatements, and Taylor intends to use the new revenue to raise homestead exemptions for homeowners.

Not every plan went through. After the county planning commission voted 6-1 in April 2025 to recommend denial, Atlas Development withdrew Project Springbank, six buildings totaling about 2.27 million square feet on 630 acres on Barnsley Gardens Road near Adairsville. More than 2,000 people had signed a petition against it, and Barnsley Resort's president, David Friederich, called it "an existential threat" to the resort.

On July 1, 2026, Taylor adopted stricter rules for new data centers: closed-loop cooling only, noise capped at 65 decibels by day and 55 at night at the nearest homes, a 200-foot buffer from residential districts, a 50-acre minimum site, and on-site power plants capped at 300 megawatts.

Coweta County, southwest of Atlanta, approved one of the largest data center campuses in Georgia on April 7, 2026, and was sued over it within a month. Project Sail, from Atlas Development, calls for nine buildings on about 830 acres near Georgia Power's Plant Yates, using an expected 900 megawatts and 6 million gallons of water a day. Commissioners split 3-2 to approve it, and seventeen residents, farmers and landowners have since sued in Coweta County Superior Court to void the rezoning.

The lawsuit argues the land was designated for rural and agricultural use and lies in what the state calls a "Most Significant Groundwater Recharge Area," and that the developer's own fiscal study puts the tax benefit at about $20.7 million a year, not the $100 million the developer projected. Opponent Melanie Tomlinson presented 7,820 signatures against the project; supporter Al Smith said, "This is a no-brainer for the county, and I'll stake my political career on it."

Three smaller projects are also moving through the county: Microsoft's 96-megawatt Project Rita in Fayetteville, already approved; T5 Data Centers' proposed T5 Palmetto site; and Project Peach, a 700-megawatt proposal from North Coweta Investors. A fourth, Central Coweta Industrial Phase II, has been blocked. Coweta's freeze on new data center applications, in place since May 2025, has no end date.

Floyd County and its seat, Rome, in northwest Georgia, have both dealt with Atlas Development of Carrollton over data center sites, and residents have pushed back both times. In May 2025 the Floyd County Commission gave final approval to rezone 178 acres near Coosa Middle and High Schools from agricultural to heavy industrial for Project Gracie, an Atlas campus of seven server buildings; the Floyd County Board of Education sold 114 acres behind Coosa High School for it. Atlas told commissioners it could bring as much as $50 million a year in tax. Residents had campaigned for two weeks after the planning commission recommended the rezoning, over noise, light, traffic and the look of it; it made no difference to the vote.

In Rome, Atlas agreed to buy land at the former regional hospital site from the city, bordered on three sides by residential neighborhoods including Summerville Park. About 200 people packed a town hall in October 2025. One resident complained that the agenda for the development authority meeting that approved the sale had simply said "real estate" with no mention of the hospital site; officials could not say what Atlas might build there, and questions about jobs got vague answers. Mayor Craig McDaniel and City Commissioner Bill Collins told residents to run for office if they wanted their voices heard. By August 2026 the deal was off: Atlas ended its preliminary agreement to buy about 100 acres at the site, now the Battey Business Complex, and Development Authority chairman Jimmy Byars confirmed the proposal was no longer active.

Two more proposals are on the county's books. Microsoft has separately proposed a data center in Rome, called Project Firecracker, though no size has been reported for it. In unincorporated Floyd County, Atlas has proposed a second, larger campus, Project Sassy, for 504 megawatts of power, the only capacity figure reported here.

The county has since tightened its rules. On June 9, 2026 the commission approved an 80-day moratorium on data center projects, and on August 25, in front of a packed room, it adopted a data center ordinance. Data centers are now allowed only in heavy industrial zones, at least 600 feet from any existing home and behind a 300-foot setback and buffer from residential and farm land. Noise at the property line next to homes is capped at 65 decibels by day and 55 at night, private wells and direct connections to surface water or aquifers are banned, developers must submit power, water and broadband impact studies and post a financial guarantee to cover decommissioning and cleanup, and violations can cost up to $1,000 a day. Planning director Brice Wood told the commission that banning data centers "has not worked well in the states that it has been tried." The rules cover unincorporated Floyd County, not land inside Rome.

Spalding County, around Griffin an hour south of Atlanta, approved three data center campuses between July 2025 and January 2026. The largest, approved unanimously on January 22, is Wallace Jackson LLC's 190-acre, $3.9 billion campus of ten buildings along Interstate 75. Two lawsuits challenge that approval, and resident Gregory Berns objected that it was "taking precious land that people have lived here for generations to farm" for a project "that's not going to provide any jobs of substance."

By August 2026 none of the three approved projects had applied for a land disturbance permit, and a fourth, 75 South, had been withdrawn for good. Commissioner James Dutton credits the county's own rules: data centers here must use closed-loop cooling, capped at about 25,000 gallons a day. "Because our rules are so high, you'll notice that there are no data centers in Spalding County," he said, contrasting it with neighboring Butts County, which he said "is going to give away the farm."

Griffin's water is still going to data centers elsewhere. In March 2026 Dutton objected that the city had agreed to supply Henry County's Hampton with up to 5 million gallons a day for a project that would not use closed-loop cooling. "Five million times 365 days is 1.7 billion gallons of water a year!" he said.

Microsoft runs five data center campuses in West Des Moines and plans a sixth there, with construction set to start in 2026 under an agreement the City Council approved with the company. The first campus opened in 2012, and the company has invested an estimated $5 billion to $6 billion in the city. Elsewhere in the county, Edged is building a 13-megawatt data center in Ankeny, and Tract has asked Altoona to rezone about 370 acres north of Interstate 80 for a data center park.

The sixth Microsoft campus will sit on farmland across the road from David Roach's family farm near Cumming. "There's a reason that we lived out here in the country, and it wasn't to have this huge data center across the road," he said. More than 10 percent of West Des Moines' tax base is now tied to the campuses, and the city has spent over $200 million on public infrastructure to serve them. Economic development director Ryan Moffatt said the city wants to "diversify our economy" in case the buildings ever go dark.

Microsoft's buildings are cooled with water in hot weather. West Des Moines Water Works says they use 2 to 7 percent of the water it pumps each month, 2.1 percent on average from 2021 to 2025, under an agreement allowing up to 5 million gallons a day. The utility says the 2025 lawn-watering ban and its May 2026 request to cut lawn watering by half were caused by high nitrate levels in the Raccoon and Des Moines rivers, not the data centers.

In Ankeny, the Edged building is a $187 million project on 17.5 acres that Ankeny City Council approved unanimously in March 2025, with completion aimed for 2027. In Altoona, where Meta already runs a data center campus, Tract was under contract for land between Northeast 62nd and 70th Avenues; the city's economic development director, Chad Quick, said no site plan had been submitted. "There's power, there's land and we have some water," he said.

Beale Infrastructure has started grading for a $3.1 billion data center campus on about 290 acres near Edgerton Road and 103rd Street in De Soto, with up to four buildings built in phases through about 2035. In Edgerton, the City Council has approved DAMAC Digital's $860 million data center in a warehouse at 31800 W. 196th Street, and the city is in court trying to void a residents' petition that would ban such projects. As of mid-August no hearing date had been set.

In De Soto the land was already zoned for the use, so the project needed no rezoning or public hearing, the city says. The city approved property and sales tax exemptions on up to $50 billion in industrial revenue bonds in August 2025, and the first phase's site plan has conditional approval. Evergy will supply the power. Beale has also listed plans for a campus of several buildings on 300 acres near 191st Street and South Clare Road in Gardner.

Edgerton's fight is at Logistics Park Kansas City. On June 15, 2026 the council voted 3-2 against a six-month moratorium, and on July 16 it unanimously overrode the planning commission's rejection of DAMAC's plans. Residents then collected enough signatures, verified by the county election office, to force the council to adopt a ban on high-impact data centers or put it to a vote. The council did neither and sued, saying the petition gets facts wrong: Edgerton supplies neither the water, which comes from Rural Water District No. 7, nor the power, which comes from Evergy.

Resident Kim Twente, one of those named in the suit, said the council's approval was "disappointing" but "expected." In Spring Hill, Colossus Data Center Advisors dropped a 316-acre data center plan at 191st Street and Renner Road in March 2026 after residents objected.

Minnesota's largest data center plans are Google's campuses in Pine Island, about 20 minutes northwest of Rochester, and Hermantown, outside Duluth, plus Tract's 2.5 million-square-foot campus in Farmington. All three face lawsuits. Pine Island's project is on hold after a Goodhue County judge ordered developer Ryan Companies on May 22 to stop all construction and pre-construction work until the case is decided. Hermantown's still needs city council approval, and the city is redoing its environmental review, expected in September or October.

The Minnesota Center for Environmental Advocacy argues that the cities' environmental reviews did not properly study projects they knew were likely to be very large data centers. Google has promised Pine Island's schools $24 million over 20 years and Hermantown's about $70 million over 28, and the two cities offer tax breaks worth more than $100 million combined. "I think it's a bribe, honestly," said Pine Island resident Megan Post. In Hermantown, leaked recordings of city officials mocking opponents led the mayor to apologize and seek an outside investigation.

In Farmington, residents are suing over Tract's campus, which would need about 700 megawatts of power and more than double the city's water use of about 2.14 million gallons a day; a judge refused to dismiss the case in November 2025.
