In Monticello, the same advocacy group is challenging the review for a planned data center, and the city now requires it to meet a new data center ordinance before permits.

At least eight cities and counties have paused new data centers, including Eagan, Rosemount, Inver Grove Heights and Wright County. Minneapolis voted in May to pause data centers larger than 350,000 square feet, then approved a five-month moratorium June 25. "My constituents and people from across this city are so, so clear that they don't want data centers at all," said Council Member Soren Stevenson. Local boards have rejected data centers in Apple Valley, Elk River and Nobles County, and a developer dropped its plan for the former Star Tribune printing plant in Minneapolis.

The Massena Town Board voted 3-2 on September 16, 2026 against a six-month moratorium, clearing the way for North Country Colocation Services (NCCS) to keep working toward a large data center next to the former Alcoa East plant. NCCS, an affiliate of the bitcoin company NYDIG that has run a data center in Massena since 2017, says the expansion would use about 400 megawatts of power from the New York Power Authority and a closed-loop cooling system that uses little water. NCCS says the state's one-year pause does not apply because it needs no new permits from the Department of Environmental Conservation.

As first proposed, the project had three buildings totaling about 1.5 million square feet and 635 megawatts, roughly 70 percent of what the Moses-Saunders Dam produces; NCCS has since dropped one building and cut about 400,000 square feet. Supervisor Raymond Lancto and board member Kristy Baker voted for the pause. "We gotta get jobs here, so the fire department, the rescue squad, can flourish again," said Fire Chief Tom Millar. From Akwesasne, Marina Johnson Zafiris of Mohawks United in Safety and Health said: "We need substantial time. We need a moratorium."

Cheap power has drawn crypto miners and now data centers: in May 2026 the county industrial development agency counted ten proposals around Massena, though its chief executive, Patrick Kelly, said that did not mean any would go forward. On County Route 42, Petawatt Holdings has been preparing a 14-acre site with a new substation so it can sell or lease it to a data center developer. On June 1, 2026 the county legislature declined to impose its own moratorium, after its attorney said it lacked the power, and urged towns and villages to consider their own.

Much of Montgomery County's data center fight has been over one developer. Brian O'Neill's King of Prussia firm MLP Ventures filed plans for five data center sites in Upper Merion Township, on Renaissance Boulevard, Horizon Drive, Swedeland Road and River Road, totaling more than 4.5 million square feet, days before the township passed a data center ordinance setting conditional use requirements and a 1,000-foot buffer from homes. On August 13, 2026 the Board of Supervisors denied the extensions and preliminary plans for all five. "20,000 residents signed a petition opposing this development," said County Commissioner Neil Makhija. O'Neill said he would appeal; MLP had already sued the township.

In Limerick Township, on vacant land between a shopping center and the nuclear power plant, MDC 7 LLC's Project Laurel would put eight 85-foot buildings, close to 3 million square feet, on about 190 acres; officials say it would draw roughly 750 megawatts of power and use at least 750,000 gallons of water a day. Two longtime neighbors interviewed by WFMZ were relaxed about it; one said he had not really cared until "they start offering big money."

The county's three operating sites are DaSTOR's 4-megawatt Upper Merion Township facility, Flexential's 7-megawatt Collegeville data center, and TierPoint's Valley Forge site in Norristown, which has not reported its power use. A separate, smaller project in Plymouth Township is listed as proposed with no developer named yet.

On August 18, 2026 Governor Josh Shapiro signed an executive order requiring data center developers to show proof of local approvals before they can get state permits, a move that could affect O'Neill's appeal of the Upper Merion denial.

Cameron County has four data center projects proposed or under construction, one paused, and one withdrawn. Fluidstack began building the $4 billion first phase of an AI data center campus on more than 1,100 acres near Rio Hondo in September 2026, saying it would create more than 2,500 construction jobs; it had recently offered $27 million toward infrastructure and drainage in Harlingen. East of Valley International Airport, Eneus Energy is separately pursuing a $14 billion, 2,000-megawatt campus on 1,785 acres and is suing Cameron County and Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton to keep records about it sealed.

Near Rio Hondo and Santa Rosa, Soluna Holdings is developing two smaller sites, Project Ellen and Project Rosa, each on land leased from a wind farm; this year Soluna raised both projects' power, from 100 to 145 megawatts and from 187 to 242 megawatts, to serve AI computing instead of only Bitcoin mining. In Harlingen, Mayor Norma Sepulveda withdrew a September 2025 letter that had urged AEP Texas to prioritize power for a separate $14 billion campus proposed by RGV Property Group LLC, saying it "goes further than the transmission request I understood myself to be making." Harlingen has had its own moratorium on new data centers since May 2026.

In Brownsville, a proposal to put a data center in the old Southwest Key Casa Padre building, a former Walmart, set off a public outcry; Valley Interfaith's Nancy Cruz said "we cannot afford to prioritize the cooling demands of tech corporations over the basic needs of our residents." On September 1, 2026 Brownsville's commissioners voted to begin a 90-day moratorium on new data center rezonings, a process that runs from November 18, 2026 to February 16, 2027 under state law.

Ellis County, south of Dallas, is home to Google's Midlothian campus, where Google first built in 2019 and has filed for a fifth building, and to a second Google campus taking shape in the Red Oak area. The newer fight is over Red Oak, where data centers are multiplying fast: in May 2026 the city council voted 4-1 to approve Compass Datacenters' roughly 830-acre campus, the sixth in the city. According to 60 Minutes, seven campuses there are set to cover more than a quarter of Red Oak's land.

Residents came to object to noise, pollution, falling property values and how close the site would sit to homes; one organizer said it would run along her own fence line. "We're supposed to look out for the welfare of our people ... but they're not really pausing and paying attention to what their people are saying," said organizer Elda Jazmin Villegas. Dozens of residents from across the political spectrum now meet twice a month to push back.

Compass has also turned to donations. Facing what its chief executive, Chris Crosby, called "noise" over the project, the company withdrew a proposed county tax abatement before a June 23 commissioners meeting, then gave the county $15 million for a new animal shelter and $12.6 million toward a Texas State Technical College building for data center training programs. "There is no strings attached," County Judge John Wray said. Waxahachie resident Susie Hall was not persuaded: "I hate to think that we're going to be obligated to Compass because there will be something they're going to want in return."

Two of the largest data center campuses proposed in Texas are coming to Reeves County, around the West Texas town of Pecos, and each will bring its own gas plant. In June 2026 Microsoft announced a Pecos campus of about 2 gigawatts, to be built over five to seven years, with more than 6,000 construction jobs at peak. Chevron has signed a 20-year agreement to power it from a co-located natural gas plant, developed with the hedge fund Engine No. 1, that is to deliver first power in 2028 and grow to about 2.67 gigawatts. Chevron expects to make its final investment decision by the end of 2026; construction had not started when the deal was announced. Reeves County Judge Leo Hung welcomed the project, saying it "will create new opportunities for local businesses."

Water is the question any Permian town would ask, and so far the answers come from the companies. Microsoft says the campus will use closed-loop cooling that needs an initial charge of water and none after that, using non-potable water where it can. Chevron says the power plant will run on non-potable brackish groundwater and that it is working on reusing produced water from oil and gas wells; none of those volumes has been published. No resident, commissioner or water district has been quoted in published reporting on the project, and no county vote or public hearing has been reported yet.

A second campus is planned beside it: Prometheus Hyperscale and Istmo Energy intend 1.5 gigawatts of power at Pecos in a first phase and up to 2.5 gigawatts later, powered behind the meter by piped natural gas and ethane from a co-located Istmo Midstream plant, with first power through modular units slated for 2027. Also in the county, Core Scientific runs its Pecos (Cottonwood) bitcoin-mining data center, whose power use has not been reported. Next door in Pecos County, a separate county despite the similar name, commissioners approved a tax abatement on January 12, 2026 for a $5.5 billion AI data center project.

In the year to September 2025, Aligned Data Centers' West Valley site used 80 million gallons of water, while Novva's 1.5 million-square-foot campus in West Jordan used about 3 million, most of it on landscaping, according to records The Salt Lake Tribune obtained. Those are among Salt Lake County's main data centers, alongside Aligned's second site in West Jordan, Oracle's West Jordan facility and DataBank's Bluffdale campus.

The debate here has been less about whether to build than about what the buildings consume, because Utah is one of the driest states and, as Grist and The Salt Lake Tribune reported, how much water a data center uses can vary dramatically.

Records that The Salt Lake Tribune obtained from municipal water providers for October 2024 to September 2025, published in partnership with Grist, show how much cooling design matters. Novva's chief executive Wes Swenson said its closed-loop system took 55,000 gallons to fill once, and estimated evaporative cooling would need about 250 million gallons a year. Aligned's West Jordan site used 47.4 million gallons, and eBay's South Jordan data center 19.5 million. "Water is extremely cheap," Swenson said. "And cities have generally accommodated that."

The Legislature responded in 2026. HB 76, from Representative Jill Koford, requires new large data centers to report their expected water sources and use to the state before construction and their actual withdrawals every year after they open, with the figures published online. "We live in a desert," Koford said before the session.

HB 507 generally bars local governments from offering incentives to large data centers outside designated regionally significant development zones, and generally caps property tax incentives at 60 percent of the new county revenue a project brings, 80 percent at most. A 2025 law, SB 132, already requires separate accounting for the costs of serving very large loads. According to the Kem C. Gardner Policy Institute, Utah has 48 operating data centers with more than 920 megawatts of capacity, and seven under construction are expected to add about 2,600 megawatts.

Petersburg has at least four data center projects in its pipeline, and in July 2026 several of its council members said they had learned of three of them from a newspaper. Richmond BizSense reported, from city documents, that NuVu Real Estate had site plan approval in February for a three-building, 300 megawatt, $1.1 billion campus on 75 acres at 2588 County Drive by Interstate 95; Wagner Properties had approval in April for three buildings on 73 acres at 1161 Wagner Road; and Menlo Digital, whose project council rezoned in 2023, had submitted a site plan, not yet approved, for four buildings on 74 acres at 2255 Jamestown Drive. NuVu's and Wagner's projects needed no council vote: in 2024 the city made data centers a by-right use in its light and heavy industrial districts, so projects on that land skip public hearings and council approval.

"I had no clue about any of this," said Ward 4 Councilman Charlie Cuthbert, who called for data centers to need special use permits instead. Ward 1's Marlow Jones said projects "slide under the cracks that we don't know until somebody posts it like this."

The one project that did come before council is the Warrenton Group's six-building campus on about 175 acres at 2233 Halifax Road, the former CSX Collier Yard property that the city owns; council rezoned it in 2025, and the zoning was amended in early 2026 to add three parcels for access and wetland mitigation, Richmond BizSense reported. On Feb. 17, 2026 council voted unanimously to rezone 176 acres around the Collier Yard to light industrial and sell the land to the Warrenton Group for $5,000 an acre, despite more than a dozen residents who spoke against it. "We will see, hear, and smell this industrial development," one resident told council. Neighbors also objected that buffer parcels rezoned to light industrial could open the door to more development if the data center ever closes. Ward 7 Councilman Arnold Westbrook Jr., whose ward includes the site, said in a written statement that he welcomes the interest from data center developers.

Grant County, in the farm country of central Washington, draws data centers to Quincy with access to hydropower from the Columbia River. Microsoft has been building there for about twenty years and now runs its Columbia campus; Sabey and Vantage also operate data centers in Quincy, at 123 and 89 megawatts of power, along with CyrusOne's PNW1 and NTT Data's Quincy site. In nearby Moses Lake, Keel Infrastructure is building an 18-megawatt data center. Microsoft president Brad Smith said in January 2026, "we will add to the tax base that funds your local hospitals, your schools, your parks, your libraries," pointing to Quincy's high school as probably the nicest in the state. Former Quincy mayor Patty Martin, who has opposed the facilities since they first came to town, asked the other question: "What's the long-term impact for the short-term gain that we have?"

Power has become the constraint. Data centers used 37% of Grant County's power in 2025, and the public utility district, which receives about 63% of the electricity generated by the Wanapum and Priest Rapids dams, has long projected it would use its full share by 2026. In April 2025 Grant PUD said it would cap how much more power data centers could draw, because demand was outrunning its transmission lines. Its answer is a $260 million expansion to roughly double the power it can move into Quincy, including a new line from Wanapum Dam due by 2029.

That line is being fought over. Its most contested stretch crosses 112 parcels, including 34 homes; nine property owners argued the PUD had not followed the state's required negotiation and appraisal procedures. Jacque Rasmussen said the PUD's appraisal valued her property at $191,000, nearly $600,000 less than the estimate of an appraiser she hired. In August 2026 a Grant County Superior Court judge ruled the utility has the right to take the land regardless; how much owners are paid is still to be decided. Farmer Darrin Reynolds said the ruling sends a message that "we are the government and we'll steal it whenever we want."

Applied Digital's second North Dakota AI campus, Polaris Forge 2 near Harwood, is close to opening: part of its 280-megawatt data center should begin operating by the end of 2026 and the rest in early 2027, the company told The Forum in September 2026. About 1,800 workers were finishing two 907,000-square-foot buildings, which will draw power from Cass County Electric through a new substation Applied Digital is paying $112 million to build. The campus is leased to Oracle, and Applied Digital closed a $2.15 billion bond offering in March 2026 to fund construction. The North Dakota Public Service Commission unanimously approved the substation and transmission line to serve the site.

Harwood approved the $3 billion project in September 2025, weeks after it was announced, over protests at a planning and zoning meeting where members of the crowd shouted "cowards" and "shame." "This feels too fast," resident Alesha Greseth said. "I think we need to take a break and chill out." Fargo, which had voted to annex the land, dropped its annexation on Dec. 8, 2025, ending a fight between the two cities over who would collect the property taxes.

The company's first campus, Polaris Forge 1 at Ellendale, is leased to CoreWeave under 15-year leases worth $11 billion; chief executive Wes Cummins says its data centers are designed for "near-zero" water use. A third North Dakota campus is planned near Center, in Oliver County, where commissioners signed a road use agreement in July 2026 and repealed a data center moratorium after Applied Digital agreed not to discharge wastewater into the aquifer.

In Louisiana, Applied Digital is building Delta Forge 1, a $3.6 billion, 300-acre campus in Boyce, Rapides Parish, needing 300 megawatts from Cleco; site work began in January 2026 with operations expected in mid-2027. At a June 23, 2026 town hall, central Louisiana residents voiced skepticism, and records show the company has set aside 672 acres with room for two or three more buildings.

Bitdeer, a Singapore-based bitcoin miner listed on Nasdaq, is pushing into AI data centers, and in Ohio that has brought it into the same fights as the rest of the industry. On June 16, 2026 about 200 people packed Shalersville Town Hall in Portage County, with dozens more outside, for a three-and-a-half-hour meeting on Bitdeer's plan for a 15-building campus of up to 750 megawatts on about 257 acres at the Turnpike Commerce Center. Residents pressed the company on electricity, water, noise, fire risk and the environment.

Its only working Ohio site is a crypto mine at 1115 Industrial Avenue SW in Massillon, planned for 24 mining buildings, of which eight were finished when the company showed the Canton Repository around in May 2026. The site uses up to 221 megawatts, which a company representative compared to a steel mill's electricity use. Bitdeer put up a 30 to 40-foot sound wall next to the nearest homes and has pledged to keep noise at 60 decibels or less at the property line. Site manager Jon Wonsettler said all 24 buildings should be complete by the end of summer.

Bitdeer's other large project is in Texas, where it says it has access to 563 megawatts of interconnected grid capacity shared by its existing Rockdale bitcoin mine and 200 acres of adjoining land it bought in September 2026 for AI and high-performance computing, with room to grow to 742 megawatts. It also said in August 2026 that it had signed a 16-year lease with Volta for an AI data center at its Tydal campus in Norway, worth about $4.7 billion over the base term, with 42.7 megawatts due in the second half of 2027. In Portage County, nothing has been approved: Shalersville Township has a moratorium on data center development until early November while it writes rules on noise, lighting, building size, utilities and fire suppression.

Diode Ventures is a Kansas-based data center developer, a subsidiary of the engineering firm Black & Veatch, that has walked away from three US sites after local pushback while moving ahead in Canada. In Charles City County, Virginia, it withdrew its 515-acre Roxbury Technology Park proposal on August 18, 2025, eight days before a supervisors' vote, saying it had decided "to shift our focus elsewhere."

In Henderson County, Texas, it withdrew a proposal in July 2026 over the site's "close proximity to the rural residential community of Cedar Creek Lake," and Governor Greg Abbott said "Diode did the right thing by withdrawing their project." In Peculiar, Missouri, the Board of Aldermen blocked Diode's $1.5 billion Harper Road Technology Park by removing data centers from the city's light industrial zoning after residents packed meetings.

In Wheatland County, Alberta, Diode's Goldfinch data center proposal went the other way: after a July 7 public hearing and a petition against it, the county council passed the rezoning 4-3 on August 11. Councilor Glenn Koester, who voted no, said most people who had contacted him opposed it: "overwhelmingly the response has not been good for the development."

In Kuna, Idaho, Diode's proposed 620-acre Gemstone Technology Park is still in its early stages; the company says it would commit more than $40 million to local services, including $30 million over 13 years for the Kuna Rural Fire District.

Edged US wants to build Project Atlas, a data center campus of three buildings, an administration building and a warehouse totaling about 1.5 million square feet, on more than 400 acres in South Whitehall Township, Pennsylvania, next to Parkland High School; the plan is for 725 megawatts of power.

At a September 23, 2026 planning commission meeting, the company's attorney said it was not seeking approval yet and would return with a revised plan. Commissioners took the proposal under advisement and pushed their decision deadline from October 31 to December 31, 2026; no further meeting has yet been scheduled.

More than 3,000 people had signed a petition against the project by April 2026. Company executives say the nearest homes would be more than 1,000 feet from the buildings and the high school almost 1,700 feet away, that closed-loop cooling would use no water from the township's municipal system, and that the project would bring more than $8.9 billion in investment and more than $16 million a year in tax revenue.

"The only acceptable outcome is no data center," said Greg Sussman of the South Whitehall Civic Alliance, which is demanding a public hearing where residents can challenge the developer and present their own witnesses.

Edged is also building elsewhere: a campus on the former Tilford Yard rail property near downtown Atlanta; a reduced, two-building project in Council Bluffs, Iowa; and an 8-megawatt plan in Prichard, Alabama, that could be halted by a moratorium on data center permits the city council began discussing in August 2026.

Lumen Technologies runs three known data centers: College Park and Doraville, both in the Atlanta area, and one on Technology Drive in Pittsburgh. All three are established, already-operating sites built for network and colocation equipment, not the newer AI campuses driving local fights elsewhere. Lumen mostly does not build those bigger data centers; it sells the fiber that connects them to each other.

In February 2026 Lumen finished selling its home internet fiber business to AT&T for $5.75 billion in cash. It says it has since signed $13 billion of deals to link cloud companies' data centers to one another. Chief executive Kate Johnson told investors that enterprise network spending is shifting from office-to-cloud links, 36 percent of it today, toward cloud-to-AI links, now 64 percent and headed to 84 percent within three years.

São Paulo state holds almost a third of Brazil's 195 data centers, most of them in the western suburbs of the capital. The biggest project is Scala Data Centers' 600-megawatt Tamboré campus in Barueri, under construction. In Santana de Parnaíba, next door, ODATA runs a 19.4-megawatt site and Tec.to is building one planned to reach 182 megawatts of power by 2030, near a protected spring on the Tietê River. Farther out, Ascenty runs two data centers totaling 61 megawatts in Vinhedo.

Water is the local worry. In 2025 Greater São Paulo's main reservoirs fell to their lowest level since 2015, and Sabesp cut water pressure in Barueri. When Vinhedo rationed water in 2024, the city's map showed Ascenty's industrial district was spared, Agência Pública reported. "In a shortage, the priority under our water law is to quench the thirst of animals and supply people, not to generate profit for any other sector," said Ângelo Lima of the Observatório das Águas. Tec.to says its closed-circuit cooling keeps water use low.

The power grid is the other limit. In September 2025 the national grid operator ONS said most data center connection requests were in São Paulo state, and a 2025 transmission auction lot was designed to add capacity for Barueri, Santana de Parnaíba and part of the capital. Federal policy favors more building: President Lula signed the Redata tax break into law in September 2026 for operators that meet a water-use limit and buy clean power, while environmental licensing is still left to each city.

Quebec's one contested data center proposal is in Sherbrooke, where the American company Keel Infrastructure wants to build a 96-megawatt AI data center in the city's industrial district. At a public meeting organized by Sherbrooke Citoyens councilors on September 20, 2026, four city councilors came out against it. Province-wide, Hydro-Québec wants a new data center power rate of about 13 cents a kilowatt-hour, roughly double the current large-industry rate, from November 1, 2026; the Régie de l'énergie hearing is set for this fall.

About 100 people attended the Sherbrooke meeting. Two researchers from an observatory on the social impacts of AI said data centers create noise and heat islands, use a lot of water and electricity, and bring few jobs, and that the noise and climate effects of Keel's project are hard to judge because companies disclose little. "What we are doing here seems to be a step in the right direction," said professor Morgan Mouton, who urged residents to keep organizing.

Quebec has built its data center industry on cheap hydroelectric power, and the province now controls who gets it: any data center wanting 5 megawatts or more needs the energy minister's approval before Hydro-Québec can supply it. Among the biggest sites are Vantage's four-building, 86-megawatt campus in Quebec City and QScale's campus across the river in Lévis, under construction since 2021 and planned for 142 megawatts. Goldman Sachs bought QScale in May 2026. Several operators are challenging Hydro-Québec's proposed rate before the Régie.

Data center projects are spreading across Finnish towns. Earthworks are under way in Forssa for what Yle calls Finland's largest data center, which could use about 8 percent of the country's electricity if fully built. In Lahti, the utility Lahti Energia says a data center under construction for TikTok will double the city's power use, and a second data center is planned there. Google runs a large campus in Hamina and has plans in Kajaani and Muhos.

Local leaders mostly welcome the projects. In Janakkala, where a data center beside Highway 3 is in the permitting stage and about 50 residents came to a recent briefing, municipal manager Riikka Moilanen said property tax alone could reach half a million euros a year, and that power supply and prices are not the municipality's business. Fingrid, the national grid operator, estimates that data centers and electric boilers could raise Finland's electricity use by nearly 40 percent in five years if all are built.

Some residents feel left out. In Jokela, in Tuusula, many people learned of a data center only after it had been approved, and a citizens' initiative asks the municipality to explain the project and open its confidential documents; the municipality is preparing its answer. In Lapinlahti, land zoned for a solar farm became a data center project without a public hearing. Pekka Väisänen of the Järvi-Suomen puolesta association is building a network to track how towns decide on these projects and to warn the next ones.

North Holland had 67 data centers in 2025, the province says, and about 20 more are in the permit stage, which would bring the total to 83 by 2030 and 92 by 2035. Most sit in three designated clusters: Hollands Kroon, where Google and Microsoft run data centers at Middenmeer; Haarlemmermeer, including Schiphol-Rijk and Halfweg; and Amsterdam, including the Science Park and Amstel Business Park sites of Digital Realty.

The province's draft environmental vision allows new data centers only inside those clusters, under strict conditions, and only where there is enough power. "We are concerned about the large energy demand of data centers in relation to grid congestion," provincial executive Esther Rommel said in July 2026 (translated from Dutch). The province says its rules on waste heat and water use keep getting tighter, and that the industry will have to come up with its own solutions to the power shortage.

Sweden's biggest new data centers are going up in the north and in Dalarna, where power from hydro and wind is plentiful. In Långsele, in Sollefteå municipality, atNorth plans a 300-megawatt campus called SWE04 on the Hamre industrial park and signed a 200-megawatt grid connection with E.ON in May 2026. It needs an environmental permit for backup generators with 1,200 megawatts of installed capacity, and atNorth intends to apply to the Land and Environment Court in autumn 2026.

In Borlänge, EcoDataCenter is building on the site of the old Kvarnsveden paper mill, with the first data center due in early 2027 and 400 to 500 construction workers. In September 2026 it agreed to buy 52 hectares in Smedjebacken for a third Dalarna campus of up to 150 megawatts; permits are expected in early 2027. In Sandviken, Microsoft can restart two paused server halls at Tuna after the old Rörberg airport, which blocked a new power line, was ordered closed in March 2026.

The local argument is about electricity. Sollefteå Green Party politicians have written that atNorth's campus and a planned project near Ramsele would tie up about two-thirds of the municipality's wind power. Nationally, data centers account for almost 7,000 megawatts of the roughly 25,000 megawatts waiting to connect to the grid, and Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson confirmed in August 2026 that the government is working on a national data center strategy. Sweden ended its electricity tax break for data centers on July 1, 2023.

Kern County has no large data center running yet, but two are proposed and both are under review. In Inyokern, Trona-based R&L Capital wants to build a 99-megawatt AI data center on about 50 acres near Highways 395 and 178, and needs a conditional use permit from the county. In the Elk Hills oil field, California Resources Corp. has applied for a permit for the 275-megawatt Golden Valley Technology Hub, with Calgary-based Beacon Data Centers as its tenant.

The Inyokern plan is the more contested. The 238,000-square-foot building would have 40 diesel generators able to supply 99 megawatts of backup power, which is why the California Energy Commission is reviewing it; construction could start in April 2027.

R&L says its cooling would use no more than 50 acre-feet of water a year from the Indian Wells Valley basin; opponents estimate about 500, close to 8 percent of the basin's sustainable yield. The city of Ridgecrest, China Lake Naval base and the Sierra Sands school district have filed objections, and Ridgecrest asked in July for a formal role in the state review. "AI is here to stay... But not in Inyokern, and not in Ridgecrest," one resident told the Ridgecrest City Council.

Golden Valley would sit about 1.5 miles from Valley Acres and run on surplus power from CRC's gas-fired Elk Hills Power Plant. It would be cooled by a closed water loop needing about 6,000 gallons a year in top-offs, and the permit starts a two-year environmental review. Separately, the Air Force has offered more than 2,100 acres at Edwards Air Force Base for lease to private AI data centers; no company has been named.

Delaware's data center fight has been fought almost entirely in New Castle County, and the biggest project in it is, for now, dead. Starwood Digital Ventures' Project Washington would have put about 6 million square feet of data centers on roughly 580 acres north of the Delaware City Refinery, drawing 1.2 gigawatts, as much electricity as nearly a million homes by expert estimates. On February 4, 2026 Environmental Secretary Greg Patterson ruled it was barred by the state's 1971 Coastal Zone Act, pointing to its 516 backup diesel generators and 2.5 million gallons of stored fuel, which he called "entirely unprecedented." The most generators at any facility in the coastal zone until then was eight.

The state's Coastal Zone Industrial Control Board unanimously upheld the ruling in March after about 14 hours of testimony. "They're emission points, and they're emitting enough to constitute themselves, as a collective, as a major source of air pollution," board member Willie Scott said. Starwood's lawyer, Katharine Mowery, said the secretary had "distorted what Project Washington is." Starwood appealed to Superior Court, then quietly withdrew in early July, two days after the General Assembly passed new data center regulations. It says it is still looking for "a pathway forward." "I'm overjoyed," said Dustyn Thompson of Sierra Club Delaware after the board's decision. The building trades unions, the project's loudest supporters, have warned the state will lose jobs.

The county wrote its own rules in the meantime. On March 10, 2026, after months of fights that at one point featured one councilman giving another the finger, the County Council passed Councilman Dave Carter's ordinance 12-0. Data centers must now sit at least 1,000 feet from homes, or 500 feet with a noise study, use closed-loop cooling and more efficient backup generators, and set aside money to tear the buildings down if they close. "It's a good start," Carter said. As part of the compromise the rules apply only to new applications, not Project Washington or others already in the pipeline.

Two warehouse projects have since shifted towards data centers. One, near the St. Georges Bridge north of Middletown, would replace the Frightland Halloween attraction and grow to 3.2 million square feet; it also sits in the coastal zone. The other would redevelop the White Clay Center office park east of Newark; Councilman Tim Sheldon said its developers recently paused it after he brokered an informal deal with them.

Columbia County, outside Augusta, sought out data centers on purpose, and Google was named the tenant of two campuses here in July 2026. County Manager Scott Johnson described the project as 33 buildings on 3,500 acres, and land is already being cleared. Commissioners approved the White Oak Technology Park and Pumpkin Center rezonings on February 3, 2026; a third, Byrd Farms, was rejected the same day for having no named tenant.

The county's pitch is that data center tax money could eventually eliminate homestead property taxes. House Bill 439 lets the county set revenue aside for tax relief, subject to a referendum in November, and Johnson said credits could start in 2027 with bills reaching zero in 2028 at the earliest. "We understood early on that this was an initiative of our president, it was an initiative of our governor, and it was going to happen in Georgia," Johnson said. "So why not let the Columbia County residents benefit from this?"

At the rezoning hearing, Appling resident Catherine Newsome objected: "This is our home. This is our livelihood. This is our way of life. And it's just not good enough." The Pumpkin Center site's buffers were doubled to 500 feet and its berms raised to 12 feet after resident concerns about noise.

Eagle Rock Partners has tried twice to build a data center on the same 600-plus acres in Jones County, both times withdrawing before a vote. In September 2025 the developer sought to rezone land at Highway 18 and Bethlehem Church Road for the Crooked Creek Technology Park, a 1.8-million-square-foot facility; residents organized as "No Data Centers in Jones County," and Eagle Rock withdrew by email on October 20, hours before the zoning hearing. "If they choose to reapply, we will provide the same public notice," planning director Tim Pitrowski said.

The county passed a 90-day moratorium, then in January 2026 adopted an ordinance letting data centers into a conditional-use district at the Griswoldville Industrial Park, with a 200-foot setback, buffers and decommissioning rules. April Lipscomb of the Southern Environmental Law Center called the setback "utterly inadequate." "We walked into a predetermined decision tonight," said Dustin Riley, who started the opposition group. "We expect the applicant is going to be Eagle Rock again."

In February, 17 residents sued to overturn the ordinance, arguing the county gave improper notice and had been negotiating its language and timing with Eagle Rock beforehand. The county filed a motion to dismiss in March; a hearing on that motion has not been set, and the development authority's attorney said in June it could come in 2027. The authority also put a $25 million sale of the industrial park's full 956 acres to Eagle Rock on hold in March over "sticking points" in the deal.

DuPage County's western suburbs, along the I-88 corridor, have become one of the places where the Chicago data center boom has been turned back. In January 2026 the Naperville City Council voted 6-1 to reject Karis Critical's data center near Naperville and Warrenville roads. The Naples, Florida developer had already cut the plan to about 145,000 square feet, capped at 36 megawatts, and reduced its diesel generators from 24 to 16. Council member Supna Jain said neither ComEd's system nor the city's own electric utility had unlimited capacity; Ian Holzhauer said the land might serve Naperville better as housing. Mayor Scott Wehrli, who wanted to delay the vote, abstained. "All the neighbors have been exhausted by this process," said nearby resident James Butt. "I know that everyone is relieved." Karis has not given up on the city: by June 2026 it was eyeing a second, 168-acre site nearby at 150 West Warrenville Road, the former BP campus, an early-stage proposal with no capacity announced yet.

In Lisle, CloudCenters LLC proposed a 256,000-square-foot data center on the former Lockformer site at 711 Ogden Avenue, a property left contaminated with trichloroethylene that leaked into local groundwater. "A lot of people were sick, and a lot of people passed away in Lisle when Lockformer was first initially contaminated," said Mayor Mary Jo Mullen, who also noted redevelopment would offset residential property taxes. "I'm not anti-data center. I'm anti data centers right next to residential areas," said neighbor Vanessa Berry. The January hearing was cancelled when the crowd overflowed the rooms, and the developer then withdrew. The village board has since moved to remove data centers as a permitted use in its industrial district, which would effectively bar new ones without a separate zoning amendment; no one spoke against the change at its May 20 hearing.

Aurora, which lies partly in DuPage, already has data centers operating, including CyrusOne's 114-megawatt campus, and five more in development; nearby in Itasca, NTT Global Data Centers separately runs a large campus of its own. After a 180-day moratorium, Aurora's council passed new rules in March 2026 lowering noise limits, requiring sound studies and resource consumption reports, and making every new data center go to the council for approval. "We're trying to put regulations in place to help data centers that want to come here understand that we want them to be responsible neighbors," said Alison Lindburg, the city's sustainability director.

On July 29, 2026, the Department of Energy announced the Paducah American Energy Hub, a data center campus planned for the former Paducah Gaseous Diffusion Plant, a shuttered uranium enrichment site in McCracken County. Brookfield will build and run the campus, projected at more than $100 billion, on 600 acres leased from the department; NextEra Energy Resources will build a separate 2,000-megawatt energy campus of natural gas plants on another 200 acres, with 300 more set aside for batteries. Big Rivers Electric will supply wholesale power and Jackson Purchase Energy Cooperative will deliver it. No tenant has been named for the data center itself.

Gov. Andy Beshear was not at the announcement, which Energy Secretary Chris Wright attended; his spokesperson said the next day the governor "hasn't been briefed by any of the companies or agencies involved" and had questions about power, environmental impact, jobs and taxes. Bruce Wilcox of Greater Paducah Economic Development told the fiscal court on August 10 that the project already meets the standard: "To my knowledge, there are no state, local or school tax incentives offered on this project." He said the data center and gas plant would use under 5 million gallons of water a day, against the 30 million the old plant used, and that developers bear the full cost under a federal ratepayer protection pledge. The companies project 8,000 construction jobs and 600 permanent ones.

The county already has one large power user: Riot Platforms runs a 60 megawatt bitcoin mine at Industrial Park West outside Paducah, bought in 2024 with Block Mining, which it says could grow to 110 megawatts. In May 2026 Riot announced a partnership with Terrestrial Energy that could someday put a small nuclear reactor at the site, though no timeline has been set.

Frederick County has frozen new data center applications until July 1, 2027. County Executive Jessica Fitzwater extended the pause on September 14, 2026, the same day she turned down a deal from the developer of Quantum Frederick, the 2,100-acre campus north of Adamstown on the old Alcoa Eastalco aluminum smelter. The freeze does not stop work already under way there: Aligned Data Centers, Amazon Web Services and Rowan Digital Infrastructure have all broken ground, though none of their buildings was running as of June 2026.

Catellus's company Quantum Maryland had offered $110 million for schools, parks and other community benefits, plus 20% less building and 80% less drinking water, if the county promised not to change its zoning rules against the campus for eight years. After hundreds of comments, Fitzwater said residents "do not want to see any more decisions made about data centers, not until we have the next county council seated, and not until the state completes its impact study." County Council seats are on the November 3, 2026 ballot, and several residents told WYPR data centers will decide their vote.

Since December 2025 new data centers have been limited to one zone of about 2,600 acres around the campus, set by a 5-2 council vote. More than 21,000 residents signed a petition to put that map to a referendum, but in June 2026 Maryland's Supreme Court ruled it could not go on the ballot. State inspectors have found the site out of compliance or needing fixes in at least 67 inspections, and in 2024 crews drilling a fiber line released drilling fluid into streams without reporting it.

In Lyon Township, Verrus is building Project Flex, a six-building, 1.8-million-square-foot data center on 172 acres already zoned industrial; the planning commission gave it conditional approval on September 8, 2025, its first meeting on the project. In Rochester, Oakland University's board voted on June 30, 2026 to move a data center proposal from Fairmount Properties into "due diligence," on a site next to a campus parking lot. In Southfield, the City Council voted 5-2 in December 2025 to approve a 100-megawatt data center for Los Angeles-based Metrobloks near Inkster Road and I-696.

Lyon Township residents have pushed back hard. Outside reviewers found Verrus's sound study inadequate and raised fire-access and battery-storage concerns near Dolsen Elementary School, and resident Melisa Noble said a 120-kilovolt transmission line in later documents was not in the plans commissioners approved. The Oakland County Election Commission approved language on April 27, 2026 for a recall of all seven township trustees; no result on that recall has been published. The township has since paused new applications, though not Project Flex, and extended that pause six months in August.

Oakland University moved its planned site after concerns it was too close to a Native American heritage site, and the data center would include office space for the university's AI Institute. In Southfield, Council President Charles Hicks voted no, saying, "I'm just concerned there's too many unknowns, not enough fact based information to make a good decision," while Coretta Houge backed it: "We have to consider new technologies."

Amazon and Google are both building data centers on opposite sides of Interstate 70 east of New Florence, a town of about 635 people, covering about 1,900 acres of a 5,000-acre industrial site. Amazon's $10 billion Project Green, north of the highway, was approved by the County Commission in December 2025 and broke ground on April 1, 2026. Google's $15 billion Project Spade, announced in May 2026, is going up south of the highway on the former Hoette Farms tree nursery.

Both come with tax breaks. Amazon gets personal property tax exemptions of 75% to 95% from 2028 to 2052, worth $244 million to $982 million by the county's own analysis, but pays full real estate taxes; Presiding Commissioner Ryan Poston said the schools would collect $1.4 billion from Amazon over 25 years. Google gets a 70% break on servers and other equipment in return for $10 million a year for 20 years, including $500,000 a year each to High Hill, New Florence, Wellsville, Middletown and the Gasconade County school district.

Residents in the group Preserve Montgomery County sued in February to halt the Amazon project, saying the county gave improper public notice and did not disclose enough about water, power and the tax deal. On September 18, 2026, Cole County Circuit Judge Cotton Walker refused to dismiss most of the case, so it can go forward; no further hearing has been scheduled. Poston has said the sites, about 0.8 miles from town, will be "quieter than the interstate." Ameren Missouri, which will supply the power, declined to estimate how much the two will use.

Storey County is home to the Tahoe Reno Industrial Center east of Reno, a business park bigger than the city of Reno and one of the densest data center clusters in the country. Switch's Citadel Campus, one of the largest data centers in the United States, anchors the park, alongside Tract's South Valley Technology Park, PowerHouse Data Centers, EdgeCore, Novva, Vantage and Google. Nevada created its data center tax break in 2015 to bring Switch to the county, and three-quarters of the $461 million in expected breaks the state has since awarded has gone to Storey County projects.

Now the county wants the program cut back. In September 2026 it sent the Legislature a proposal to shorten the abatements, a 75 percent break on personal property tax and a reduced 2 percent sales tax rate, from 10 or 20 years to five or 10; to double the spending commitments companies must meet; to require audits at five and 10 years; to publish each data center's projected and actual power and water use; and to bar breaks for data centers on federal land. "There's benefits to them," said Will Adler, the county's lobbyist. "Modifications really are what this program needs." State Sen. Dina Neal has separately proposed ending the program and pausing new data centers statewide.

Water is the other pressure. Erik Henzl of the Desert Research Institute estimates that by 2033 the power generation serving the park's data centers could need nearly 12,450 acre-feet of water a year, and direct cooling about 9,600 more. The park's water district holds rights to more than 4 billion gallons a year, including Truckee River water. "We're making sure that customers have the water resources before they're breaking ground," said its general manager, Shari Whalen. "The plan is not to take all the water there is in the Truckee River."

New Jersey's biggest data center going up now is DataOne's campus on South Lincoln Avenue in Vineland, a 14-hall "AI factory" of up to 350 megawatts that Nebius will run for Microsoft under a $17.4 billion deal. The company expects construction to finish in late December. On September 22 the Department of Environmental Protection fined DataOne $1.07 million for installing 62 gas generators without air permits and gave it 45 days to get the permits or stop running them.

Neighbors have sued DataOne over noise since ground was broken in the spring, and in August the city halted work after crews began building a liquefied natural gas tank and fuel cells before permits were approved. "This enforcement action... sends a clear message that these facilities will not be constructed or operated with impunity in this state," said Ed Potosnak, the environmental commissioner. In Kenilworth, CoreWeave is building a data center on the former Merck campus off Galloping Hill Road after buying a building and about 27 acres for $322 million.

Towns have been banning data centers one after another. Pemberton Township was first, in February; by August 20 more than 30 towns had bans on the books, including Phillipsburg, Waterford, Logan, Millville, Bayonne, Jersey City and Howell, while Sayreville chose an 18-month moratorium. Residents stopped projects in Monroe Township, where the council removed data centers from Hexa Builders' plan on the Black Horse Pike, in Andover, in East Greenwich, where American Tower withdrew a 4-megawatt plan after a 5,800-signature petition, and in New Brunswick. Developers have sued Monroe, Andover and Montgomery over their bans.

Gov. Mikie Sherrill opposes a statewide moratorium. On July 7 she signed the Data Center Fair Share Act, which puts large data centers in their own rate class, makes them pay for their own power and grid upgrades, and requires them to cut back before households when the grid is strained. DataOne's 45-day deadline to get its generator permits runs out in early November.

Wake County has turned away the data centers proposed for it so far, and most of its towns have stopped taking new ones. The largest was the New Hill Digital Campus, a 250-megawatt data center Natelli Holdings planned off Old U.S. Highway One in Apex, near Duke Energy's Shearon Harris nuclear plant and the Western Lake water reclamation plant. The Protect Wake County Coalition fought it over noise, air pollution and its use of energy and water, and in March 2026 Natelli withdrew its annexation and rezoning applications while the town worked on data center rules, saying the project could be revisited if Apex later allows them. "This isn't the end of the conversation," the coalition said.

Apex's council then voted unanimously in April for a one-year moratorium. "It's a big win," said Michelle Hoffner O'Connor of Protect Wake County. Holly Springs approved its own one-year pause in June, and by then Wake County itself, along with neighboring Chatham and Orange counties, had each put a one-year pause on new data centers in place.

In August the fight reached Raleigh. A developer asked the City Council to annex a nearly 14-acre site at 3101 Jones Sausage Road in the southeast of the city, near the Parrish Manor neighborhood and about 1,000 feet from the back of the Chelmshire Downs subdivision, for a 100,000-square-foot data center. Council member Mitchell Silver said hundreds of emails came in over a weekend, "the vast majority" opposed, and more than 30 residents signed up to speak. Mayor Janet Cowell said Beacon Partners, which had requested the annexation, withdrew the proposal that Saturday; Raleigh itself has not adopted a moratorium of its own.

Amazon Web Services is behind two data center plans around Trenton. Prologis is building Project Mila, four buildings on 141 acres of Trenton's industrial park south of Kennel Road, with Amazon as the end user. Amazon also wants 18 buildings on about 600 acres along Wayne Madison and Hawkins roads in Madison and St. Clair townships, just south of the city. On November 3, 2026, Trenton voters decide whether to ban data centers that need more than 25 megawatts of power.

Both townships refused to let Trenton annex the 600 acres, and on September 14 the city withdrew its request, saying it may try again after the election. Madison Township's zoning is run by the county, whose six-month pause on data centers in six townships, adopted June 16, runs until December. "We have to understand what we're committing our residents to," Commissioner Don Dixon said. St. Clair adopted its own 12-month pause in May.

Trenton's Planning Commission approved the Project Mila site plan on March 30, 2026, in a meeting of about 10 minutes, because the land was already zoned industrial. "We're going to keep on fighting," said Barry Blankenship, whose residents' group sued to get the ban on the ballot; the Ohio Supreme Court ordered the city to hold the vote. Prologis says it will pay for power upgrades and that the city will collect about $120,000 a year in water, sewer and stormwater fees.

In Hamilton, Logistix Property Group's proposed data center at 1380 University Boulevard has been on hold since January 2026, when the city said it would take at least 24 months to deliver even 45 of the 240 megawatts requested. "We are not willing to sacrifice our children for economic growth," resident Jay Kidd told the council.

Pickaway County, just south of Columbus, has three data center fights under way, and in each one residents have gone to law. The furthest along is in Ashville, where EdgeConneX plans two data centers and a natural gas power plant on about 195 acres of village property. On April 6, 2026 the village council approved a term sheet with the company as an emergency measure, which took effect immediately and exempted the project from Ashville's own data center moratorium. Residents gathered signatures for a referendum; the village's fiscal officer refused to certify them, and on August 7 the Ohio Supreme Court ruled unanimously that she had to, because the council gave no specific reason for the emergency. On August 24 the county Board of Elections voted 4-0 that the resolution was legislative, putting it on the November 3 ballot for village voters. "I think it's really terrific that the Ohio Supreme Court unanimously stood up and enforced the constitutional right that citizens have to a referendum," said former Attorney General Marc Dann, who represents the opposition group Data Center Resistance.

In Commercial Point, the village rezoned about 267 acres in May 2024 exclusively for data centers, on a 4-1 vote to waive the three-reading rule with one council seat vacant. In April 2026 the developer, K-Nova II, filed a site plan naming Amazon Data Services as the end user, under the name Project Cosmos, and paid a $534,121.85 application fee. After residents pushed back, the council passed a retroactive 18-month moratorium on May 4 and offered the fee back. K-Nova refused and asked the Ohio Supreme Court to force a vote, while residents sued on the last day of the two-year limit, arguing five votes were needed to waive the readings and the zoning is void.

In Muhlenberg Township, after Pacifico Energy requested a rezoning for a data center and power plant, the trustees passed a 12-month moratorium on data center zoning certificates to applause in February 2026. Residents there worry about heated cooling water reaching Big Darby Creek, a state scenic river, and the Charles O. Trump Wildlife Area.

Tulsa County has two huge data center campuses under construction and a citywide pause on new ones. In east Tulsa, Meta revealed on April 21, 2026 that it was behind Project Anthem, a $1 billion, 340-acre data center between 11th Street and the Creek Turnpike due for completion in 2028. The city gave it an 85 percent property tax exemption through a 25-year incentive district; the remaining 15 percent is expected to raise $36 million, and Meta will pay $25 million for public infrastructure.

City staff had recommended denying the zoning, and protesters met the announcement. "Meta profits billions off destruction of our community," read a sign carried by Cheyenna Morgan of Stop Data Colonialism. Local councilor Christian Bengel, who had signed a non-disclosure agreement with Meta, was accused of "selling them out." North of the city near Owasso, Beale Infrastructure is building Project Clydesdale on 506 acres for Google, paying for a new substation and 1.5 miles of new water lines; neighbors have raised concerns about water, power, noise and property values.

In March 2026 the Tulsa City Council voted unanimously for a nine-month pause on new data center permits, cut down from the year first proposed by Councilor Laura Bellis. Anthem and Clydesdale were approved earlier and are exempt. The county's map also lists two long-operating facilities run by Hewlett-Packard/Sabre and TierPoint, an operating Compass Datacenters site, and a Google campus approved in nearby Sand Springs.

Luzerne County has Pennsylvania's best-known nuclear-powered data center and one of its most bitter fights. Next to the Susquehanna Steam Electric Station in Salem Township, Amazon bought Talen Energy's existing nuclear-powered data center campus, AWS Berwick, in March 2024 and has since won a rezoning of about 1,600 acres for 15 more buildings over the coming decade. The township gave Amazon a 10-year, 70 percent tax break, after which officials expect about $7 million a year in local taxes. Some residents said switching the land from agricultural to industrial zoning would devalue their property; others said Amazon had offered to buy them out.

In Hazle Township, residents have fought Project Hazelnut, NorthPoint Development's plan for an Amazon Web Services campus of 15 buildings and a substation on nearly 1,300 acres of the coal plateau. Gov. Josh Shapiro launched it in November 2025 as a flagship of his fast-track permitting program, promising 900 jobs; the township's supervisors denied it that same fall despite the state's forest-clearing permits. A judge rebuked NorthPoint's attempt to appeal in May 2026, and on June 8 the supervisors voted unanimously to pause all data center applications for 180 days while they rewrite their zoning, before a room of about a hundred people, some wearing "Project Hazelnot" T-shirts. NorthPoint returned on June 24 with a revised plan and a $165 million community benefits fund, including $10,000 grants to eligible households. "We have a beautiful area here. First, it was scarred by coal mines, and we don't want any more damage done," said resident Joanne Balay.

In Sugarloaf Township, developer LBT Investments has sued the township over a data center proposed on a site already approved for a warehouse, and a data center ordinance has grown out of that dispute; the company says it would use existing 230-kilovolt power lines and closed-loop cooling. "The people making the decisions don't live here," resident Andy Sanko said at a packed hearing in December 2025. "But it's people like my 85-year-old parents who will be stuck paying these bills." QTS has also proposed a project in Salem Township, though its exact site has not been made public.

South Carolina has no state rules for data centers, so its counties are writing their own. On September 21 Spartanburg County voted 5-1 for a one-year freeze on data centers larger than 65 megawatts, and Jasper County unanimously approved a one-year moratorium the same night. York, Chester, Newberry, Greenwood and Chesterfield counties have already paused new projects.

Spartanburg's freeze does not touch the Valara data center under construction on South Pine Street, and residents said the 65-megawatt limit leaves the door open to big projects. "If you let one in, you let them all in," one told the council. Residents there already stopped one project: TigerDC withdrew its application for Project Spero in February. In Colleton County, lawmakers of both parties opposed Eagle Rock Partners' proposed gigawatt campus near the ACE Basin.

The biggest projects under construction are QTS's 400-acre campus near Lake Wylie in York County, where neighbors have renewed complaints, and Meta's data center in Aiken County. Sen. Tom Davis's bill to license data centers by size, require yearly water reports and make them pay for their own power did not reach a floor vote. "I understand counties, absent the state implementing these baseline protections, simply taking the approach that they don't want data centers built until we have safeguards in place," he said.

Temple is where Bell County's data centers are. Meta opened its AI data center on Industrial Boulevard in July 2026, two buildings and more than 760,000 square feet representing more than $1.2 billion, after breaking ground in 2022 and restarting construction on a new design in 2023; it says the site has about 100 operations jobs. Rowan Digital Infrastructure is building six data centers across three projects, Project Temple, Project Stampede and Project Ranger, in and around the Synergy Southeast Industrial Park, a footprint it values at a minimum of $4.2 billion, against the $300 million campus it first proposed in 2021. Five of the six are approved or under way; the city council took up the sixth, the Lasso building, on September 17, and no report of that vote has surfaced since. Rowan has a 50 percent, 10-year abatement on city and county property taxes; the school districts get full taxes. It says it will use closed-loop, air-chilled cooling and has agreed to pay about $32 million of Temple's $71.1 million South Temple water program. It has not named a tenant.

The backlash has moved up to the county. More than 100 people packed a Commissioners Court workshop in Belton; 47 signed up to speak and nearly all opposed more data centers or asked for a moratorium. "Do better for us than the City Council did for us," said Temple resident Lynn Thomas. County Judge David Blackburn's draft resolution would stop short of a ban, calling instead for safeguards on water, power and land and for the Legislature to give counties more authority. "I don't think you elected me to break the law, although you are asking me to do that," Commissioner Russell Schneider told the crowd. In July residents pushed the court to stop giving data centers tax abatements; commissioners replied that outside city limits an abatement agreement is the only lever they have to impose noise limits, water rules or a diesel generator ban. "I don't think any data center should be given a tax abatement," said farmer Alton Fowler. "They're already ahead."

In Killeen, the Planning and Zoning Commission voted 4-1 in April 2026 against ONMINE's $30 million "computing and energy research annex" on three acres on South Fort Hood Street, overruling its staff. "I've not seen a single citizen say that it was beneficial to their community," Commissioner Scedric Ross said. The applicant withdrew before the June 2 council vote.

In Hays County, where aquifer levels have been falling for years and the governor renewed a drought disaster proclamation in February, the data center fight is about water. It came to a head in San Marcos, where Fort Worth-based Highlander SM One proposed a $1.5 billion data center on about 200 acres off Francis Harris Lane, between San Marcos and New Braunfels, next to the Hays Energy power station. Hundreds turned out; 125 people signed up for citizen comment and 57 more for the public hearing. "I ask you to envision what your future of San Marcos looks like," resident Melanie Babot told the council. "Is it one that values natural resources for people, not AI?" At 2:14 a.m. on February 18, 2026 the council voted 5-2 to deny the land use change, and the overflow room cheered.

San Marcos then went further. On June 16, after first making data centers conditional on council approval, the council voted 4-3 to prohibit them in every zoning district. Council member Lorenzo Gonzalez, who had opposed a ban in April, switched: "Ultimately, I concluded that the promised benefits remained speculative while many of the concerns raised by residents remained unresolved." Mayor Jane Hughson voted no, saying she wanted to leave the possibility open while projects still had to come before the council.

A week later, on June 23, the Hays County Commissioners Court approved Judge Ruben Becerra's resolution creating a 180-day water protection review period, during which it will not grant discretionary approvals for data centers or other high-water-use industry, and a review board to assess them. The court also petitioned Gov. Greg Abbott for a special session to give counties more power over water-hungry projects, and said it would offer data centers no tax incentives. "I am not a fan of data centers," said Commissioner Michelle Cohen. Water advocates are watching five more projects in and just outside the county, two of them in neighboring Caldwell County, that they say would draw on the Edwards Aquifer.

McLennan County has three data center proposals around Waco, each facing pushback from neighbors. The largest is Infrakey's roughly 1-gigawatt, $10 billion campus on about 520 acres in the Ross and Elm Mott area north of Lacy Lakeview, a suburb of 8,000 counting on about $50 million a year in tax revenue. Lacy Lakeview would have to annex the site and a three-mile corridor of private land, and Infrakey would need to build a sewer plant to treat up to 2 million gallons of wastewater a day for cooling; Waco, which owns the regional sewer system and the water rights, learned of the project from a newspaper.

"Without the City of Waco agreeing to it, Lacy Lakeview can't do anything out there and neither can Infrakey," said state Rep. Pat Curry, a Waco Republican. "Those guys don't know what the hell they're doing." Rural residents organized as soon as they heard, and in May 2026 Lacy Lakeview voters elected Amy Gage, who ran against the data center, as their top council vote-getter.

Ten miles east of Waco, Cipher Digital has quietly bought about 300 acres by the Sandy Creek coal plant outside Riesel for a data center of up to 500 megawatts and applied to connect to the state grid; it says it will not use Riesel's water. "We just want to be left ... alone, live our life, live in our little farms," said Josh Havens, who farms nearby. In McGregor, the city council approved Galaxy Digital's Project Merlin in June 2026, a campus north of the SpaceX site, with water capped at 3,000 gallons a day per building; its closed-door approval, along with years of water violations tied to SpaceX engine testing, has prompted a petition to recall Mayor Jim Lilley.

Fort Worth's biggest data center fight is over Black Mountain Power's $10 billion campus in the southeast, on land the company owns at Lon Stephenson Road and Forest Hill Drive, between Forest Hill, Kennedale and Everman. After council members declined to vote on revisions in May and June, the city council approved a revised 187-acre site plan 7-4 on August 25, 2026: four buildings instead of the 18 first proposed, up to 70 feet tall, with a 300-foot buffer from homes.

Sue Weston, whose historic Weston Gardens sits behind the site, told CBS News Texas she fears for the birds and her wedding business: "The cooling systems from the data centers and stuff -- the vibrations will just end up cracking all the rocks." Councilmember Chris Nettles, who represents the area, backs the project: "We don't believe that it's going to affect the garden." In southwest Fort Worth, Edged Data Centers had proposed a $1 billion, 186-acre campus at Veale Ranch and sought a 50 percent, 10-year tax break; after council members stalled the vote in February 2026, Edged rescinded its application.

The zoning commission voted 7-4 on July 8 against a draft city ordinance that would have limited data centers to industrial zones and required 250-foot setbacks from homes, calling it too thin; Commissioner Matt McCoy said, "I can appreciate the work, it's insufficient at this time." Five council members called for a citywide moratorium the next day. The council voted unanimously on August 12 to start a formal moratorium process that would not affect approved projects like Black Mountain. The next public hearing is set for November 10, 2026, with a final vote due February 16, 2027.

Chesterfield County has decided it has enough data centers. "If someone wants to do a data center moving forward, they're going to have to come before the board of supervisors," Deputy County Administrator Jesse Smith said in August 2026. "From a staff perspective, I think we would not recommend folks do that at this point. The board has indicated they don't have an appetite for these." Since the start of 2026 every data center has needed a conditional use permit, and the county counts at least 10 data center buildings already built or under construction. One of those already running is CoreWeave's 82-megawatt facility in Chester, built by Chirisa Technology Parks; PowerHouse Data Centers also has a project there, on Digital Drive, with no power figure made public yet.

Most of what is coming is Google's. It is building Project Peanut on 300-plus acres at 2700 Bermuda Hundred Road next to Meadowville Technology Park, where construction began this year; the first building is due in late 2027. Project Skye, four buildings on about 850 acres on Moseley Road, and Project Loch, three buildings on about 350 acres on Watkins Centre Parkway, were rezoned in 2025 without Google being named. Together they are a $9 billion investment that the county projects will bring $31 million to $47 million a year, with a combined maximum water use of 8.6 million gallons a day. Google's filings show Skye would permanently affect more than 20 acres of wetlands and about 8,000 feet of streams. Supervisor Jessica Schneider, who voted for Skye and Loch, blamed nondisclosure agreements for the secrecy and said the county's 24-cent computer equipment tax rate is "the lowest in the whole state"; she said she would vote for no more. University of Richmond professor Mary Finley-Brook, who lives in the county, said "it was actually happening in my own community, and I didn't know because of a nondisclosure agreement".

In February the State Corporation Commission approved Dominion Energy's seven miles of overhead 230-kilovolt lines through western Chesterfield, including 1.5 miles along the Hallsley subdivision, to serve growth including a planned Google data center; residents had asked for them to be buried. In August 2026 the supervisors deferred a vote on an ordinance to use data center tax revenue to offset a lower personal property tax rate on cars, trucks and motorcycles, saying they wanted more time to study it and hear from the public.

Cheyenne has hosted Microsoft data centers for about a decade and has become a magnet for them; Cheyenne LEADS counts 10 existing sites, five under construction and nine in advanced talks. The biggest is 8 miles south of the city in the Switchgrass Industrial Park, where county commissioners approved a 1.8-gigawatt campus designed to scale to 10 gigawatts on January 6, 2026.

Crusoe, the original developer, was asked to leave by the client; a June 30 filing revealed the client as Google, through subsidiary Jupiter Star Holdings, which now calls the project Tembo, a 716-acre campus of four data halls due by 2031. Black Hills Energy has put more than $200 million into serving the site, with power expected in early 2028.

The nearest home is a tenth of a mile away; the Hyndman Homesites neighbors asked the county to address well water, traffic, noise, light, turbine emissions and wastewater ponds, writing, "We accept the inevitability of the project and want to identify and mitigate concerns before they become problems." Project Jade plans closed-loop cooling drawing on the deep Lance Formation aquifer rather than city water, and Mayor Patrick Collins has told state lawmakers Cheyenne expects data centers to pay for all their own electric service.

IREN, the Australia-based company formerly called Iris Energy, started as a bitcoin miner and is turning its sites into AI data centers. It is still mining but winding that business down and putting its cash into renting out GPUs. Its turning point came in November 2025, when Microsoft signed a five-year, $9.7 billion contract for access to Nvidia GB300 chips, paying 20 percent up front; IREN in turn agreed to buy $5.8 billion of GPUs and equipment from Dell. Those chips go to its 750-megawatt campus in Childress, Texas, where it is building 200 MW of liquid-cooled data centers, the Horizon buildings, for Microsoft. In August 2026 Microsoft accepted Horizon 1, the first of four 50MW liquid-cooled buildings due for delivery at Childress this year, and IREN said it was targeting 480MW of gross AI cloud capacity in 2026 and 1.2GW in 2027.

Its next site is far larger. Outside Sweetwater in Fisher County, West Texas, IREN is developing two campuses totaling 2 gigawatts on 2,200 acres. It has energized the substation at the 1,700-acre Sweetwater 1, with power ramping up as data centers are built, and expects to energize the 500-acre Sweetwater 2 in 2028. In May 2026 IREN said it would use Nvidia's architecture to build out the Sweetwater campus, with about 300 construction workers already on site and more buildings to follow through 2027 and beyond.

In British Columbia, where it began, IREN runs three former bitcoin sites at Prince George, Mackenzie and Canal Flats, built partly on infrastructure left by closed pulp and lumber mills and powered by BC Hydro. The province has made its ban on new crypto mining connections permanent and, from 2026, makes AI data centers compete for a combined 300 MW over two years. "Whenever you have a situation where governments are determining allocation of resources rather than markets, I think it generally produces less efficient outcomes," said chief commercial officer Kent Draper. Kate Harland of the Canadian Climate Institute said the old first-come, first-served system gave BC Hydro "very little ability" to say no to crypto miners.

Hauts-de-France has become the center of France's plans for giant AI data centers. On May 30, 2026, SoftBank announced a first phase of up to €45 billion for 3.1 gigawatts of data centers in the region by 2031, at the port of Dunkirk (Loon-Plage), at Bouchain on a former EDF power station site, and at Bosquel in the Somme. Data4 confirmed in June a €5 billion, 700-megawatt campus on the former Usinor steelworks at Escaudain, near Valenciennes, and plans a 1-gigawatt campus on the former Cambrai-Épinoy air base.

Bosquel, a village of about 300 people, would sit beside a 46-hectare campus of up to 1 gigawatt that SoftBank will build with the French startup Sesterce. "46 hectares, that's the size of the built-up part of the village," said Camille Ego, president of the association that saw off a truck warehouse on the same fields two years ago. "We feel our village will be sacrificed in the name of digital sovereignty." The prefecture expects up to a year of impact studies and public consultation, then two years before the first phase runs.

At Escaudain, Data4 says further studies and early works will take about a year; it has not given a construction timetable. "We aim to erase the last remnants of an industrial era," said Aymeric Robin, president of the Porte du Hainaut urban community, which picked Data4 for the site.

Hyderabad is where Telangana's big data centers are going. In July 2026 Amazon Web Services began building a campus on 202 acres at Bharat Future City and 98 acres at Chandanvelly, with the first phase due within two years and about Rs 60,000 crore planned over ten years. Microsoft opened its India South Central cloud region in Hyderabad on August 6, 2026, and the state has backed a Rs 70,000 crore AI data center on 264 acres by HyperVault, a TCS subsidiary, due by June 2028.

The TCS project was challenged in the Assembly on September 11, 2026. BJP legislator Palvai Harish Babu said it would create only 7,000 direct jobs while needing round-the-clock power and large amounts of water, and called for a debate. IT Minister D Sridhar Babu agreed data centers are seen as power and water guzzlers but said the state "will ensure that power supply to domestic, irrigation and industrial sectors is not affected."

The longest local fight is at Mekaguda, a dairy village of about 1,000 people where Microsoft bought 22 acres in 2022. In July 2023 residents sued Microsoft and 35 others in the Telangana High Court, saying it fenced off about 380 meters of a communal cart-way and dumped waste into Tungakunta lake. "These big companies think they can enter small villages like ours, take our land, and destroy it," said village head Chinthalapally Pandu Ranga Reddy. Microsoft says it has the permits it needs; as of September 10, 2025, the case was still pending.

Tokyo is where Japan's data center fights have been sharpest, because operators have been building close to homes. Japanese building law has no definition of a data center, so a project classed as an "office" can go almost anywhere, which residents say is the root of the conflicts. In Hino, Mitsui Fudosan plans three buildings with a peak demand of about 250 megawatts on the former Hino Motors factory site next to streets of detached houses; it has cut the maximum height from 72 to 63.5 metres, but the old factory was under 30 metres, and a residents' group says the company has not disclosed its estimates of waste heat and noise. "Why bring a data center so close to where people live?" asked Yasuo Yamazaki, its co-chair. Residents in Koto, Akishima and Kodaira in Tokyo, and in Inzai and Saitama nearby, have joined forces and are petitioning for data centers to be defined in law.

Power is the other limit. TEPCO Power Grid had 15 gigawatts of data center transmission connection applications by the end of fiscal 2025, about a quarter of its peak demand, and its president has said it aims to halve the time it takes to connect them.

In Akishima, in western Tokyo, GLP's project covers about 590,000 square metres with eight data center buildings and three logistics warehouses. More than 220 residents petitioned against it in 2024, saying about 3,000 of the site's 4,800 trees would be felled and that the city's water comes solely from groundwater. "One company will be responsible for ruining Akishima," said Yuji Ohtake of the residents' group. In February 2026 residents protested outside city hall over how the city was drafting a new development ordinance. Governor Yuriko Koike told the metropolitan assembly on February 18 that Tokyo would publish guidelines on dialogue between data center operators and residents, the first of any prefecture.

Portugal's data center story is Sines, on the Alentejo coast, where Start Campus is building a campus of six buildings and about 1.2 gigawatts on land left by a closed coal power station, cooled with seawater. Only the first building, SIN01, has been running, since January 2025; the second, SIN02, is under development at 180 MW. Microsoft said at the Web Summit in Lisbon that it would invest $10 billion in AI data centers there with Start Campus and Nscale, which is deploying Nvidia GB300s for Microsoft at the site.
