The project brought down a government. Start Campus was one of the subjects of Operation Influencer, the corruption investigation that led Prime Minister António Costa to resign in November 2023. Wiretaps contained repeated references to efforts to get around the environmental protection of the site; the former energy secretary João Galamba was recorded suggesting that the Institute for Nature Conservation and Forests (ICNF) should redraw the boundaries of the protected area. The ICNF later confirmed after an inspection that the first building had been built on top of a temporary Mediterranean pond, a priority habitat protected under Portuguese and European law, and referred the breaches to the regional authorities. "The Portuguese State has a legal obligation to protect these habitats," biologist Rita Alcazar of the League for the Protection of Nature said.

On March 19, 2026 the government presented a National Data Center Plan to simplify licensing, with AICEP as the single point of contact and pre-serviced zones for data centers. The industry welcomed it but doubted delivery. "If a process takes two years, let it take two years. What matters is knowing how long it takes," said Start Campus's operations chief, Luís Rodrigues. In September, Environment and Energy Minister Maria da Graça Carvalho said energy-intensive industries "come ahead of data centres in our priorities" for grid connections, and that data centers would have to bid at auction and show they will not strain public water supplies. Data center requests had made up the largest share of 40 GW of grid connection applications last year; firm applications fell to about 4 GW once deposits were required.

paragraphs: Meta runs a data center campus in the North Huntsville Industrial Park, one of the largest in Alabama, and the city approved a $750 million expansion in 2021 that would bring the site to nearly 600 acres. DC BLOX also operates a smaller data center in Huntsville.

The city improved Monroe and Liberty Hill roads and added a traffic signal on Pulaski Pike for Meta, and Meta paid $2.5 million of a $2.8 million sewer extension. "They are paying their way," said Shane Davis, the city's economic development director, who estimated the second campus would add $8 million to $10 million a year for local schools once complete.

Meta's power draw is matched by a 1,000-acre solar farm the company built across the state line in Lincoln County, Tennessee. Power for both Huntsville sites comes from the Tennessee Valley Authority, whose board approved a new rate class for data centers taking effect October 1, 2026, phased in over three years, with roughly a 10 percent average bill increase and a capacity charge of about $1.5 million per megawatt for large new loads. Huntsville Utilities chief executive Wes Kelley has told the city council Huntsville will not offer incentives to recruit data centers.

Construction of Project Blue, Beale Infrastructure's data center on 290 acres of former county land near the Pima County Fairgrounds, began in April 2026, as protesters stood in front of the trucks until sheriff's deputies moved them. The Board of Supervisors voted in June 2025 to sell the land, and in December approved a side agreement 3-2 in which Beale, backed by Blue Owl, committed $15 million in community donations and "commercially reasonable efforts" to match its power use with renewable energy. Supervisors Andrés Cano and Jen Allen voted no.

Opponents thought they had won when the Tucson City Council refused to annex the site and supply city water. Beale then switched to air cooling and won a special power deal with Tucson Electric Power, approved 4-1 by the Arizona Corporation Commission. "We really believed that we had protected our community, protected the water, protected the land," said Vivek Bharathan of the No Desert Data Center Coalition. Opponents note that TEP's power is about 50 percent natural gas and 19 percent coal, which uses water at the power plants.

In Marana, the Town Council voted 6-0 in January 2026 to rezone two 300-acre parcels south of Pinal Airpark Road for a second Beale campus. Councilmember Herb Kai, whose family trust owns one parcel, recused himself. Beale projects a $5 billion investment and nearly $145 million in town tax revenue over a decade. The town clerk rejected residents' referendum petitions in February, and a Pima County judge upheld that decision in May, so there will be no public vote.

The Air Force has also offered about 300 acres at Davis-Monthan Air Force Base for lease to an AI data center; no developer has been named. Tucson adopted rules on a 6-1 vote in August 2026: any data center over 20 megawatts or 25,000 square feet now needs a special zoning district and a council vote.

The Imperial Data Center, a nearly 1-million-square-foot, 330-megawatt AI campus planned next to the Victoria Ranch neighborhood near the city of Imperial, is stopped for now. On September 9, 2026, Superior Court Judge Brooks Anderholt overturned the county's April approval of the site and ordered a full environmental review, in lawsuits brought by the city of Imperial and the Sierra Club. Developer Sebastian Rucci, of Imperial Valley Computer Manufacturing, says he will seek a new trial and, failing that, appeal.

The county has also paused all data centers on county land until mid-2027. Rucci sued over that too, and in August a second judge, Jeffrey Jones, issued a tentative ruling that the county had not shown "the current and immediate threat required" for an emergency moratorium; that ruling was not yet final. "They can't just come in and claim that they're exempt and have a right to build the biggest data center in the state without any oversight," said state Sen. Steve Padilla.

Water is the other fight. Rucci once promised the project would not "touch a single drop" of the Colorado River, but after Imperial and El Centro backed out of recycled-water talks, his company sued the Imperial Irrigation District in June for 260 million gallons of river water a year, about what 7,300 residents use. On September 15 the district, which also supplies the valley's power, adopted rules that make big users such as data centers pay for their own grid upgrades and put them first in line for power cuts during peak demand.

New London County has been the stage for most of Connecticut's hyperscale data center plans since the state passed a 2021 tax break waiving property and sales taxes for 20 years on data centers investing $200 million or more, and none of them has been built. The appeal was the Millstone nuclear power station in Waterford, the only nuclear plant in the state. The developers were two rival start-ups: GotSpace Data Partners, which proposed campuses in Groton, Bozrah, Norwich and Griswold, and NE Edge, founded in December 2021 by GotSpace's former co-owner Thomas Quinn. Bozrah rejected GotSpace's plans, partly over doubts about the company's stability, and what remains of GotSpace has filed a $30 billion lawsuit against NE Edge, the town of Groton and dozens of others that has barely moved.

Groton turned both away. In March 2022 its town council voted 5-1 against a host agreement for NE Edge's two 250,000-square-foot buildings near Interstate 95; Councilor Aundré Bumgardner said he "heard a resounding no from the public" and added "with prejudice" to the motion. After a year-long moratorium, the Planning and Zoning Commission unanimously banned data centers larger than 12,500 square feet, about the size of Pfizer's on-site facility. The landowner who had agreed to sell NE Edge 168 acres on Hazelnut Hill and Flanders roads for $5.25 million sued the town for more than $2 million.

In Waterford, NE Edge and Dominion Energy signed a host fee agreement in March 2023 for a 300-megawatt, 1.5-million-square-foot campus on the Millstone site drawing power directly from the plant, paying $231 million over 30 years in place of property taxes. Residents raised concerns about noise, traffic, fire risk and flooding at the site, and the Connecticut Siting Council refused Dominion's request to hand approval to the town. The proposal has since been dropped. The only company to use the tax break so far is Cigna, which reported $863 million of investment for five new jobs.

Athens-Clarke County said no to its first big data center proposal and then wrote rules for the rest. On October 7, 2025 the Mayor and Commission voted unanimously against rezoning 233 acres of farmland on Old Elberton Road from agricultural to industrial for a four-building, 2-million-square-foot data center filed on behalf of the landowner, FAE Clark LLC, with no end user named. The planning commission had recommended denial. "I feel like we need to lay down a moratorium and learn everything we possibly can about this technology," Commissioner Melissa Link said afterward.

The commission then imposed a moratorium on new data centers, and in March extended it to June 5 while planners drafted an ordinance; meanwhile a new data center was proposed at the Athena Studios site. Commissioner Ovita Thornton said many people, including her, had not known that a data center was already running nearby on Voyles Road, a smaller site built years earlier without needing rezoning, separate from FAE Clark's denied proposal. "There is an extreme concern throughout the community, and I think we need to make it as onerous as possible," Link said in March.

In April 2026 the commission unanimously lifted the ban and replaced it with regulations: data centers may be built only in heavy industrial zones and must use closed-loop cooling that uses less water. Commissioner Carol Myers, who moved the ordinance, proposed further rules including water and energy use reporting. Commissioner Tiffany Taylor pointed to the Pittard Road neighborhood, where residents confirmed in 2024 that their wells had been contaminated by a former industrial project: "We don't want a repeat of what happened with pollutants in communities, especially marginalized communities."

DeKalb County has banned new data center applications since July 2025, a pause extended repeatedly and now running through March 30, 2027. The county's data centers on record are a DC Blox site and Lincoln Rackhouse's 88,000-square-foot ATL1 building, which operates at 15 megawatts. Commissioners rejected a special land use permit for a third, PCC-DeKalb's three-building campus in Ellenwood, on August 13, 2026.

Ellenwood, a majority-Black community in south DeKalb, fought the PCC-DeKalb project for nearly a year. "If I sit outside too long, then my sinuses begin to act up," said Jackie Malcom, who lives less than a quarter mile from the site and organizes with the DeKalb Citizens Coalition. Resident Gina Mangham pointed to sewage overflows and water main breaks: "We already have a strained water system in DeKalb County." The county is now being sued by Shadowbox Studios, which wants to build its own data center and argues the moratorium is a ban "without any rational basis."
Inside the county, Chamblee adopted its own moratorium in July 2026, running through January 16, 2027.

Project Ruby, a proposed data center for one of the country's biggest tech companies, would sit on 865 acres of wild land in the Upatoi area of northeastern Muscogee County, bordering Harris and Talbot counties. Columbus Council voted 6-2 on June 16, 2026, to create a technology overlay zoning district, the rules any large data center must meet, but the developers still need council approval of a rezoning request they have not yet filed. As of late August, no data center had been approved.

Choose Columbus, the Development Authority's marketing arm, announced the project in February with Habitat Real Estate Partners, which owns the land, and Atlas Development, promising more than $5.18 billion in investment between 2027 and 2030, 195 jobs and property taxes rising to $68.7 million a year by 2030. Its four buildings would cover about 15 percent of the site, near high-voltage lines and a substation. The overlay sets a 500-foot buffer, noise limits of 55 to 75 decibels and on-site pretreatment of wastewater.

Residents in red shirts have protested for months, and an online petition drew 5,000 opponents. "It will bring pollution as well as raise our electrical rates and it will lower our home values," Kim Hicks told council in March. Councilors Joanne Cogle and Simi Barnes voted against the overlay; "This is a premature thing," Cogle said. At an August town hall, Councilman Walker Garrett put the low-end tax estimate at about $80 million a year and warned the project could go to a nearby county instead.

"We're seeing too many projects getting canceled," resident Ric Rivera replied. "I just don't see that promise as being believable." Resident Paul Olson has asked the Georgia Attorney General to find that the planning commission broke the open meetings law before recommending the overlay. The next decision on Project Ruby itself would be the council's vote on the developer's rezoning request, once it is filed.

Dalton and Whitfield County have hosted Core Scientific since 2018, when the joint development authority approved $42 million in bonds for what was then called a "technology facility." Two Dalton sites, now serving the AI cloud company CoreWeave, report a combined 170 megawatts and are operating. A third, larger site is under construction nearby: Dalton 4, a 250,000-square-foot building on 170 acres on Old Tilton Road, rezoned from agricultural land in March 2025, that Core Scientific had targeted to open by July 2026; that date has passed with no opening announced.

The state Environmental Protection Division is reviewing a permit for up to 80 diesel backup generators at Dalton 4, compared with eight at the older Industrial South Road site. Money keeps growing alongside it: the county court validated about $1.49 billion in Core Scientific and CoreWeave bonds in October 2025, and in June 2026 a judge was asked to validate $15.2 billion more, including $13.1 billion in equipment financing for CoreWeave Dalton II. The bonds are not taxpayer-backed, but they cut the projects' property taxes under Georgia's development authority lease structure.

Some residents want a moratorium, as neighboring Walker County and Calhoun have adopted. "With Dalton now having an AI center put in the city, we want to make sure that the next one isn't allowed," said Quentin Postell, a candidate for state House. County Administrator Bob Sivick said in July the board saw no need for one "because there's nothing in the works, and there hasn't been any problems with data centers here either in the construction or their operation."
A separate, unrelated small data center on South Thornton Avenue near downtown Dalton, on record from a commercial property listing, has no connection to the Core Scientific sites.

DeKalb's south side has become a data center district by design. Meta's DeKalb data center, first announced in 2019 under the code name Project Ventus, opened in November 2023: five buildings, 2.3 million square feet and about $1 billion of investment, capped at 200,000 gallons of water a day. "Guess who's coming to DeKalb? Facebook," former Mayor Jerry Smith recalled the city manager telling him. The city credits the tax revenue with letting School District 428 open a new $33 million elementary school without a referendum. Mayor Cohen Barnes told state legislators in April 2026 that some Northern Illinois University dormitories use more water than Meta during term, and that he wants local control rather than state-mandated community benefits.

A smaller, older proposal is still on file nearby: in 2024 Karis Acquisitions won zoning approval for a seven-building, 132-acre campus at Peace and Gurler roads, next to Meta's site, without naming an end user; the city has announced no update on it since.

In December 2025 the City Council approved a much larger neighbor: Edged, a division of Endeavour Energy, on about 560 acres of the ChicagoWest Business Center along Illinois Route 23 south of Meta, four buildings and two substations to be fully built out by 2032 and rented to hyperscale cloud companies. It will use waterless chillers, and until ComEd finishes a $197 million transmission upgrade, the Kishwaukee Area Reliability Expansion Project, it plans to run on natural gas generators. Neighbors in the South Pointe Greens subdivision objected to the noise. "I just think it's poorly placed next to a residential area," said Michelle McGill. "Our neighborhood's going to endure the noise, lights and traffic." Some speakers said the vote was rushed. "Whether spoken on the basis of fear or fact," City Manager Bill Nicklas said, "I think it's safe to say that all speakers tonight are agreed that the approval of this project would bring change."

Tazewell County has no data center proposal before it, and the county is not accepting any until it finishes writing rules for them. The one plan that got furthest, Western Hospitality Partners' campus on about 320 acres of the city-owned Lutticken Farm in Pekin, between Illinois Route 98 and Sheridan Road, is dead: Mayor Mary Burress dropped it on March 9, 2026, and the developer ended its purchase agreement on May 5.

Opposition spread fast; a Facebook group against the project grew from about 2,000 members in January to more than 6,200 by May. Burress told a packed council meeting that "it has become clear that, at this time, it's not the right project for Pekin," and the room broke into applause. In June, residents in "NO Data Center" T-shirts filled a North Pekin village meeting over the rezoning of the empty AMC theater at 1124 Edgewater Drive. Its owner, Jeff Agan, said: "It won't be a data center."

In May the County Board, with one member voting no, changed its zoning code so that any use not explicitly allowed is prohibited, and told the zoning office to refuse data center petitions until an ordinance is written. "What we don't want is to shove a data center in your backyard," said Russ Crawford, who chairs the Land Use Committee and has pointed to protecting the Mahomet Aquifer. A first draft in August would allow data centers only on industrial land outside towns, with special use permits and noise studies.

The draft still needs a public hearing before the Zoning Board of Appeals and a County Board vote. Board member Eric Stahl wants a three- or six-month moratorium in the meantime: "Everything that has been brought to us has been negative." Opponents say they are now working to stop another planned facility in Delavan.

EQT Real Estate, a Swedish investment firm that owns the data center builder EdgeConneX, wants to build the Mt. Comfort Technology Park: two-story data center buildings with four million leasable square feet on about 130 acres northwest of County Roads 500 North and 500 West, just north of Walmart's IND3 warehouse. It filed a letter of intent, to build in phases from 2027 to 2030, with the County Commissioners in August 2026, the first step under the county's new rules. The commissioners say no decision has been made.

EQT offers a one-time $22.2 million payment and $22 million a year at full buildout in place of taxes, 100 to 150 permanent jobs. It says it will pay for its own power supply and use closed-loop cooling. About 100 people came to a citizens committee session on August 18, and none of the more than 20 speakers backed the project; several asked for a moratorium. "What happens if the AI bubble bursts or the developer goes bankrupt," asked Pam Allen. Residents of Woodhaven, the nearest neighborhood, said the rules were being rushed.

In June the commissioners unanimously chose an overlay district over a moratorium. Data centers are limited to general industrial land, and a developer needs a resolution from the commissioners before a plan commission hearing, with the commissioners casting the final vote. "We have to pay the price for it, so we should make that final decision," Commissioner Gary McDaniel said. The citizens committee is due to report further rules, such as noise studies and yearly environmental reports, to the plan commission in October.
The county's first proposal, Surge Development's 775-acre site in Buck Creek Township next to Tuttle Orchards, was withdrawn in 2025 after heavy opposition.

Dallas County's data center growth, on the western edge of the Des Moines metro, is concentrated in Van Meter, where two big campuses are moving forward. COPT Defense Properties, a Maryland real estate trust that builds data center shells in Northern Virginia, bought over 300 acres in northeast Van Meter in 2024 for its first site outside Virginia, for an unnamed Fortune 100 cloud company; it says the site could hold 15 buildings, two substations and 1 gigawatt of power. Microsoft bought 377 acres next door in Van Meter's Vision Park, south of 360th Street, in January 2024, and plans at least 10 data centers there of about 227,000 square feet each.

The city rezoned the COPT land "specifically to attract a data center," said City Administrator Liz Faust, who signed a non-disclosure agreement; she said COPT's tenant would be a "heavy power user" but only a moderate water user. Van Meter expects to spend $30 million on streets, sewers and water lines for the Microsoft project, which Microsoft will recoup through tax increment financing. "I feel like everything has been moving really quickly with these guys," Faust said.

Apple has opened the first building of its long-delayed campus on Hickman Road in Waukee, announced in 2017 and originally due in 2020; the 2,000-acre site has room for up to five more buildings. State geologist Keith Schilling has said Iowa's data centers are "not necessarily" locating where groundwater is plentiful.

On June 12, 2026 the city of Ames released a letter from Lightedge Solutions proposing a data center on a 10.86-acre site. At a council listening session on June 30, 81 per cent of those attending opposed it. After a protest at the July 14 meeting, the council voted unanimously on July 28 to delay any decision by nine months while it studies the effects and gathers public input; the city attorney has confirmed the council has the authority to ban data centers in Ames entirely.

The opposition was organised largely by the revived Heart of Iowa chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America, which said it drew in residents across the political spectrum. "Certainly at the scale Lightedge was proposing, they would have been almost three times the size of the current biggest electricity demand consumer in Ames," said Aaron Lynch, its membership and outreach coordinator. "This fight is definitely not over." He added: "The council has passed a nine-month delay, but that's not a permanent decision either way." Nearby Marshalltown has passed a four-month delay on data center construction after public outcry, he said. Opponents also point to the risk to the Tedesco Environmental Corridor.

Across Iowa, more than 25 counties and at least six cities have passed some form of data center moratorium, according to Iowa Citizens for Community Improvement, while the Technology Association of Iowa argues that "in the right community, under the right circumstances, there could be an economic benefit."

Mercer County's data center fight centers on Burgin, a small city with no planning or zoning body. Panattoni Data Centers wants to build "Project Bluegrass" on about 950 acres of farmland there, and Kentucky Utilities says it is being developed in phases up to 1,300 megawatts of power, among the largest single power users proposed in the state. To make room for it, the Burgin city council voted 3-2 on July 9, 2026, at a packed special meeting where no public comment was taken and dozens were turned away, to advance an ordinance annexing more than 1,000 acres, roughly doubling the city.

Burgin canceled a planned second meeting on the ordinance, saying the first was "not legally accurate" because it had not yet had a required first reading. Harrodsburg, the county seat, which supplies Burgin's water, objected that it was not given the 14-day notice state law requires and said it had never discussed supplying water for a project this large. Records obtained by residents show school board member Ben Bradshaw, who works for utility LG&E and KU, told colleagues in June that Panattoni had applied for 1,300 megawatts and that tax revenue could reach hundreds of millions of dollars over 15 years for a district of about 500 students. "What it feels like to us is the local officials are going, 'We don't care what you think. More tax money,'" said Bethany Corea of We Are Mercer County.

On August 11 the Mercer County Fiscal Court passed a one-year moratorium on new data centers, and the county planning commission has advanced its own siting ordinance, but neither reaches land inside Burgin, which has none of its own. Panattoni says "Burgin residents should not be asked to subsidize the private infrastructure necessary to serve Project Bluegrass." Burgin's city council was scheduled to meet again on September 8, 2026; no result has been published since.

Bossier Parish is getting one of the campuses in Amazon's northwest Louisiana data center investment, announced in February 2026 as the largest single company investment in the region's history. STACK Infrastructure is developing the $6 billion Bossier site for Amazon Web Services on more than 1,000 acres off Louisiana Highway 3, north of Benton near Lone Oak Drive: a 1.3-million-square-foot campus of six buildings of about 218,000 square feet each, the first due in 2028. The legal entity behind it is TXLAAR LLC.

On March 18, 2026 the Police Jury unanimously approved the final plat after a two-hour public hearing, the first since the data center was confirmed, dominated by questions about health, water, noise, drainage and the non-disclosure agreements that kept it quiet. STACK said the campus would use about 57 million gallons of water a year, the equivalent of about 526 households, though its water agreement with Bossier City allows up to 13.5 million gallons a day. Cooling wastewater would be treated on site and discharged either to a municipal plant or to the Red River, which STACK was still working out with regulators. "We are all committed to ensuring that our ratepayers do not feel the impacts from any development from the data centers," said Amanda Nottingham of SWEPCO, which says it has the capacity without new generation; Amazon and STACK have committed to pay for new transmission. Parish Attorney Patrick Jackson said Bossier's noise ordinance, written with a Georgia Tech acoustic scientist, specifically targets low-frequency hum.

Police Jury administrator Ken Ward says the data center will pay Bossier City about $12 million a year for water, and that the upgrades Amazon is funding to a system that loses about a quarter of its treated water could cover the campus's daily needs, except in late August and September. "It's a win-win for Bossier City – they get their problem fixed and they get paid for it," he said.

Montgomery County will issue no data center permits for 18 months under a moratorium the County Council passed unanimously on July 28, 2026. The main project it stops is in Dickerson, in the county's Agricultural Reserve, where Atmosphere Data Centers wants to build on Terra Energy's land at a coal-fired power plant shut in 2020. After the vote, Atmosphere's sustainability chief, Chris Baughman, said, "It does not look like we can proceed at this moment."

The council also passed its first zoning rules for data centers, which define the biggest ones, called hyperscale, and bar them from the county for now. The pause covers projects already filed or approved but without a building permit. Council President Natali Fani-González said, "We need more information, especially from the state," meaning a state study of data center impacts due to the governor by September 1; as of mid-September it had not been completed. Darian Unger of the county Sierra Club had warned the Dickerson plan could be "an enormous electricity-price-hiking, water-stealing pollution-emitting energy hog."

An existing data center on Prosperity Drive in Silver Spring was sold on August 1, 2026, for $29 million to Sansone Group, which reportedly plans to expand its computing capacity. The council's 18-month pause replaced a six-month order County Executive Marc Elrich signed in June.

Panattoni's Project Cannoli, a roughly 1-gigawatt data center campus on already industrial-zoned land at I-94 and Haggerty Road in Van Buren Township, got preliminary site plan approval on February 11, 2026, and a substation to serve it got preliminary approval on May 14. Google and DTE Energy announced in March 2026 that Google would be the tenant, with DTE filing the power contracts as a contested case at the Public Service Commission rather than fast-tracking them as it did for the Saline Township project. More than 1,500 people have signed a petition against it.

Township Supervisor Kevin McNamara said the pushback "caused us to really pump the brakes when all of a sudden we had 200 people screaming, 'no data centers, we're all going to die,'" but also called the project potentially "life-changing" for local businesses and schools. In Allen Park, the Planning Commission voted 7-2 in June 2026 to reject Solstice Data's 26-megawatt data center near Melvindale High School, citing an incomplete sound study, and recommended a six-month moratorium.

Detroit has no data center ordinance; its City Council recommended a two-year moratorium that Mayor Mary Sheffield has not adopted, and the City Planning Commission is still drafting rules. Wayne County's other data centers are smaller: Equinix runs a colocation facility in Allen Park, and US Signal is expanding a 2-megawatt data center in Belleville. What comes next: the Public Service Commission's decision on DTE's Google contracts, and Van Buren Township's final approval of Cannoli's site plan.

Elk River's City Council unanimously rejected on July 6, 2026 the zoning change a 33-megawatt data center needed, and the project cannot go ahead without it. Elk River Capital and Swervo Development had proposed converting a vacant 62,000-square-foot former injection molding plant at 19178 Industrial Blvd. NW. The council also told city staff to draft a one-year moratorium on new data center applications; no vote on it has been published.

Weeks of packed hearings centered on noise, backup diesel generators, power, water and the site's closeness to homes, schools and parks, and the planning commission unanimously recommended denial on June 23. "I don't see anyone wanting to have a beer next to a data center cooling system," said Tim Jones, whose Aegir Brewing is next door. The city's electric utility said it had room for the load, and the developer planned a closed-loop cooling system. Mayor John Dietz said future proposals should each be reviewed as "a separate Planned Unit Development."

In Becker, home of Xcel Energy's Sherco coal plant, Amazon suspended its data center in May 2025 on a 350-acre parcel it bought in November 2024. The pause came as the Legislature debated repealing the sales tax exemption on data centers' electricity. "Amazon did tell the city that they are suspending their activities in Minnesota, which includes the property they own in Becker," City Administrator Greg Lerud said later that year.

The Franklin County Commission approved rezonings for two large data center campuses on September 15, 2026, after months of protest. Provident Data Centers plans the Gateway Digital Campus on the Eckelkamp family's Diamond Farms near Villa Ridge, next to the Shaw Nature Reserve off I-44, and a developer called Beltline plans the Meramec Valley Technology Park on the Crooked Creek farm south of Pacific along Highway O. Earlier in September the commission also voted for a three-year moratorium on new data center applications; both projects were already in the pipeline.

Opposition was loud from the start. Testimony against the Villa Ridge plan ran for four hours at a packed planning commission meeting in January, and later meetings lasted 12 hours or more. Residents picketed the Bank of Washington, whose CEO's family owns Diamond Farms. Neighbors worry about noise, power bills and their wells. "We're not going to give up until we've tried every last means that we have to say we don't want this in our backyard," said Berta Carpenter, who lives just south of the farm.

The county's new data center rules set noise standards and construction hours, keep buildings 1,000 feet from inhabited homes, and back a development agreement with fines of $20,000 a day and a $10 million escrow. Opponents say the setback was weakened because it is now measured from homes rather than property lines. Gene Elkins, who lives near Crooked Creek and depends on a well, said opponents would look for legal ways to slow the projects down.

Platte County's big project is Project Kestrel, a data center campus in the KCI corridor announced by Port KC in October 2025 as a $100 billion development by "one of the world's leading tech companies": six hyperscale data centers on 379 acres inside Hunt Midwest's KCI-29 Logistics Park. Shenandoah Computing LLC, a company associated with Google, has since bought 430 acres there, with 44 acres set aside for an Evergy substation. No construction timeline has been given, though officials have suggested work could start in 2026.

The deal gives the project a 35-year exemption from property and construction sales taxes. Port KC says it will still produce more than $110 million in new tax revenue over the bond term, against about $1,400 a year from the land today, plus about 50 jobs per phase paying above $100,000 on average. Platte County Presiding Commissioner Scott Fricker objected in November 2025, saying the tax breaks benefit one of the world's "largest and richest corporations" at residents' expense.

The county's table also lists two existing facilities in Kansas City: Lambda's AI Factory, a converted 2009-built building where Lambda plans 24 megawatts of computing power at launch with room to grow past 100 megawatts, serving a single customer under a multi-year deal, and a Nebius colocation site.

The biggest possible data center in Burlington County is on federal land. In October 2025 the Air Force offered land at Joint Base McGuire-Dix-Lakehurst, one of five bases, to private companies for AI data centers needing more than 100 megawatts of power and worth at least $500 million. It first planned to choose in January 2026; the proposal deadline later fell on May 29, 2026, and no selection for the New Jersey base has been announced.

Pemberton Township became the first New Jersey town to ban data centers when it passed Ordinance 10-2026 on February 20, 2026, to "prohibit the construction and operation of data centers." The Pinelands Alliance said the township, already worn down by the warehouse boom, chose to get ahead of developers this time rather than wait for a proposal.

Moorestown backed out of a small data center plan. It had picked New Urban LLC to build an edge data center, with solar panels over half the site, on the 25-acre former Pulverizer Services property on New Albany Road. New Urban's draft agreement dropped the data center and the solar array and asked for a tax break it had said it would not seek, so the council let the deal lapse on October 31, 2025, and plans to seek new proposals in 2026. Comcast already runs an office and data center on Centerton Road in Moorestown.

Lea County, in New Mexico's oil patch, has its first giant data center proposal and wrote rules before it arrives. In November 2025, Midland-based New Era Energy & Digital, formerly New Era Helium, signed an option on about 3,500 acres near Caprock for an AI campus it says could reach 7,000 megawatts of power, with more than 2,000 megawatts of its own gas-fired generation and a planned nuclear plant of 5,000 megawatts or more, the technology still unchosen. It starts at 250 megawatts and targets power in 2028. An option gives the company the right, not the obligation, to buy the land.

On February 26, 2026 the County Commission unanimously approved the first of what County Manager Corey Needham said could be eight or 10 data center regulations. They require closed-loop or similar cooling so drinking water is not used up; require data centers either to build their own behind-the-meter power or to negotiate with utilities so existing customers' rates do not rise; and require any industrial revenue bond or payment-in-lieu-of-taxes deal to benefit every school and hospital district in the county. "We were talking to people that already have data centers and hearing the things they wish they would have established prior to them coming in," Needham said. "The big things were regulations on water use and impacts to the power grid."

Both are tight. Usable water is scarce, and a state bill that would have forced faster rules on reusing the oilfield's produced water, 98 percent of which comes from Lea and Eddy counties, died in a House committee in February. Xcel Energy says it is some 7,500 megawatts short of regional demand, a gap that could reach 20,000 megawatts in 10 years.

Core Scientific has turned its crypto mine in Marble, a former American Thread plant of about 250,000 square feet on Palmer Lane, into an AI data center with 117 megawatts of power capacity. The county has no zoning, so the change needed only permits. It is one of three crypto mines that opened in Cherokee County from 2021, and the county has no moratorium in place.

The site plan filed in 2025 included more than 170 diesel generators, according to county commissioners and records obtained by Commissioner Ben Adams. Most of its water comes from three wells on site, with some from the Marble Community Water System, and Andrews turned down a wastewater hookup. "I wouldn't wish this on any county or entity ever," said Andrews Mayor James Reid. "It's absolutely destroyed Marble." The county collected $268,000 in taxes from the site in 2024, its last full year as a crypto mine, and is having the data center equipment appraised.

Near Murphy, Rebecca and Tom Lash have lived with a crypto mine's hum since 2021. "There was nothing in this little pasture but these electric lines," Rebecca Lash said. "And it was just nice and quiet." In January 2026 Adams asked fellow commissioners to renew the county's lapsed crypto mining moratorium and add AI data centers: "we were kind of snookered into this AI." Others feared a costly legal fight with the federal government, and Adams, who is not running again, has since asked the planning board to draft limits.

Vantage Data Centers is building a $2.1 billion campus, OH2, on about 500 acres of former farmland near State Routes 204 and 37 in Millersport, near Buckeye Lake. The company says it will have 696 megawatts of computing capacity in four data center buildings, with construction running from summer 2026 into early 2030. It will run on its own gas power plant, which still needs a state permit: the Ohio Power Siting Board must rule by November 26, 2026. Google also runs a data center on Whiley Road near Lancaster.

The power plant is the fight. Advanced Power, a Boston developer, plans 40 gas turbines, 132 diesel generators and a battery system, all serving Vantage. At a packed siting board hearing at the Millersport school, resident Lorrie Hoover said, "There is no local necessity to have a private, 1,350-megawatt fossil fuel generating station." Others said local officials ignored resistance since the project was announced in May 2025. Union members, most from the Columbus area, spoke in favor.

The state gave Vantage a 50% sales tax break through 2035, worth at least $83 million. Vantage says the campus will employ more than 50 people and use about 15,000 gallons of water a day with closed-loop cooling. Near Lancaster, Tom Bigham, who lives about 200 yards from Google's site, said in 2023 that "it could have been much worse."

An estimated 400 people, nearly a quarter of Luther, brought lawn chairs to a closed section of Main Street and chanted "let us vote" over a data center. Beltline Energy, working through BLE Landholdings, has applied for a special use permit for a campus in the town of about 1,700. The first town board meeting on it drew so many people that it had to be postponed; the next, a week later, was held outdoors. "It's like a scene from the Wild West," said resident Shannon Hopkins. "We don't want it. We're here and we're going to make a stand."

The trustees approved a moratorium on data center rezoning applications and special use permits until December 31, 2026, and extended it to applications already filed, which covers Beltline's. The ordinance cites water use, electrical demand, noise, heat, air quality and infrastructure. The Beltline permit and development agreement were on the agenda only for discussion, and no action was taken on them. Oklahoma City and Edmond have their own moratoriums while they write rules.

OG&E, the local electric utility, asked state regulators at the Corporation Commission in June 2026 to create a special rate for any customer using 75 megawatts of power or more, roughly what a small city draws. Those customers would pay for the power they say they'll use whether they use it or not, pay for their own grid connections, and pay into a fund, an estimated $25 million to $30 million a year, that could lower other customers' bills. OG&E's April contract with Google has some of the same terms, but not that fee.

Salem kept its data center talks with Verrus secret for more than a year, under a non-disclosure agreement signed in March 2025, and revealed them only in July 2026 after the company decided to proceed and details had already surfaced on social media. Verrus, a California company funded by Google, wants to build at the Mill Creek Corporate Center in southeast Salem. Its first-phase application, filed July 31, describes two buildings of about 600,000 square feet on about 100 acres; the company says it could use up to 3 million gallons of water on the hottest days and about 39 million gallons a year. The whole city uses about 25 million gallons a day.

The backlash reached the governor. After hours of angry testimony at a July 27 council meeting, Gov. Tina Kotek, who lives in Salem, ordered the state to cancel a pending sale to Verrus of 32 state-owned acres, about half the site. "Growth has to make sense for the community, for our infrastructure and for our natural resources," she said. Verrus called the move "unilateral" and said it is now looking at an adjacent 32-acre parcel. State Sen. Deb Patterson said the project had moved "under a cloak of secrecy." Verrus filed its application three days before the City Council was scheduled to consider a moratorium on August 3, 2026; no result of that meeting has been published.

Childress, a small Panhandle town, has two large data center campuses going up at the same time as its water supply is failing. IREN, a crypto miner turned AI cloud company, has a 750-megawatt campus on the south side of town. It is building 200 megawatts of AI capacity for Microsoft there, and delivered the first 50-megawatt building in August 2026. Crusoe and Lancium have announced a second campus, a 1-gigawatt AI site on 270 acres, with construction expected to start in the third quarter of 2026. A third, smaller project, Soluna Holdings' Project Fei near Childress, has grown to 240 megawatts since it was first proposed.

Childress has been under Stage 4 of its drought plan, an "emergency water shortage condition," and under a citywide boil water notice since September 8, 2026, after disinfectant levels in its supply, Greenbelt Lake, fell too low. Mayor Cary Preston and County Judge Kim Jones both declared local disasters on September 11. "We are having to buy bottled water. We can't use ice. We can't brush our teeth in the water," resident Jordan Farus said. IREN says its cooling does not consume water on an ongoing basis and has trucked in water from outside the Greenbelt system; Lancium asked Greenbelt for water and was refused. "We told them no because we don't have the water," Greenbelt general manager Bobbie Kidd said.

On August 18, 2026, Lancium offered Greenbelt water from three wells on its own property, plus a pipeline and treatment plant it would build and lease to Greenbelt free for two years. The Greenbelt board voted to move forward, but the deal still needs a formal vote and state approval.

The construction workforce has also driven up rents. In July 2026, tenants at the Madison Chase Apartments received notice their rent would double to $1,500-$2,000 a month, with some given 30 days to leave; more than 20 people protested. "When you're having 4 to 5,000 workers coming into our area, all at once, it seems like it is hard to prepare for it," Preston said, calling it a housing crisis even as sales taxes have risen sharply.

Hood County, a rural county of 62,000 people southwest of Fort Worth, has had eight data centers proposed across more than 7,600 acres, the Texas Tribune reported. The largest is Comanche Circle, a 2,100-acre campus near Tolar from Sailfish Investors, which commissioners approved without conditions on June 9, 2026, after twice rejecting a moratorium. Two smaller sites in Granbury are further along: MARA Holdings' Bitcoin mine is running, and Amazon's Project Spectrum, conditionally approved in January, has since been withdrawn.

Residents asked commissioners to pause new development for six months to study water, energy and wildlife impacts; the court said no twice in February 2026, both times 3-2, after the county attorney revealed a letter from state Sen. Paul Bettencourt warning that counties have no authority to impose moratoriums. "You've got to wonder what kind of backroom stuff was going on," said Commissioner Dave Eagle. The court instead asked Attorney General Ken Paxton for an opinion; County Attorney Matt Mills said by June it might not come until after the November election.

The county has also been sued twice by developers: once after it rejected a data center's concept plan for lacking information on its water source, and once after it tabled a vote on another. Comanche Circle won conditional approval in January, and its founder Ryan Hughes threatened to sue if the county did not grant unconditional approval; commissioners did so 3-1 on June 9. "Ryan Hughes is telling this court to pound sand," said Brian Crawford, whose family's garden sits about 600 yards from where the campus would stand.

The county's operating site, MARA's Bitcoin mine in Granbury, has its own long-running noise fight. In November 2025 nearby residents tried to incorporate their community as the city of Mitchell Bend so they could pass a noise ordinance; voters rejected the measure 62% to 38%. "We are going to move forward and we will continue to do what we can to not let industry take over Hood County," said resident Danny Lakey, who lives half a mile from the mine. MARA called the incorporation bid a "sham."

Unincorporated Clayton County has banned new data center applications since September 2025, a pause the county board has extended twice, now running through December 2026. The ban followed two approvals: TA Realty's 180-megawatt data center in Ellenwood, approved in October 2024, and a Digital Realty campus in Forest Park on the former Fort Gillem site. Clayton County also already has one operating data center, Intero Systems in Atlanta.

In June 2025 the county's Development Authority, known as Invest Clayton, gave TA Realty's $959 million project a 10-year property tax break; the authority would not say what it was worth, but county records point to more than $36 million. Eight residents had spoken against the project in 2024 over water use, noise and traffic. "Data centers are such a massive growth industry that there is no reason why state and local governments should provide incentives to this industry," said Kasia Tarczynska of the watchdog group Good Jobs First. The authority's chairman, C. Harrison Braddy, called the deal "a win-win."

The county's ban does not reach its cities. In Lovejoy, Stillwater Development filed in December 2025 to rezone land for a data center campus of up to 1.25 gigawatts, across the road from two schools. After residents and county commissioners objected at meetings through the summer, Lovejoy withdrew the plan in August 2026; the mayor said the developer would pursue housing there instead.

Two large data center campuses are approved in Monroe County and a third was turned down. The city of Forsyth approved Trammell Crow's Forsyth Technology Campus, about 12 million square feet on some 1,600 acres west of I-75, by a 5-1 vote on February 2, 2026, and Google owns about 950 acres at I-75 and Rumble Road that the county rezoned for a data center in November 2024. County commissioners are also rewriting their data center rules.

In August 2025 commissioners voted unanimously against rezoning about 900 wooded acres at Bolingbroke for a $5.8 billion data center, after hundreds of residents in red "Say no to rezoning" shirts packed the meeting. "Data centers bring in a lot of money," Chairman Alan Gibbs said. "I don't want to fundamentally change how we do things in this county over money." The landowners, Otis Ingram, Holly Doss and Haley Newnam, have sued the county over the denial.

Google paid about $42 million for the Rumble Road land in September 2025 but has given no timeline. In November the county attorney advised against signing a non-disclosure agreement Google had asked for, and commissioners voted unanimously not to sign it. In Forsyth, landowner Tye Hanna said the Trammell Crow campus would bring about $200 million a year in taxes. "We are moving too fast on a project with consequences that will last forever," resident Josh Pruitt told the council.

On March 3, 2026, commissioners put off new county standards, which would move data centers to light-industrial zoning with a 500-foot buffer, to rework the rules on generators and buffers. "That's not far enough away," homeowner Ida Head said. "Five miles might be adequate, but not 500 feet." A revised amendment was drafted for the April 2026 meeting; no result of that vote has been published.

Southern Ada County's data center story runs through Kuna, a small city on farmland south of Boise. Two large campuses have been approved there on former farms. Meta's came first. The Idaho Statesman reported that the company switched on its $1.2 billion, 750,000-square-foot Kuna data center in September 2026, its first in Idaho. The second is Diode Ventures' Gemstone Technology Park, a 620-acre campus near Locust Grove and Barker roads. It passed the Kuna City Council 3-2 in April 2025, with Mayor Joe Stear breaking the tie. Council President Chris Bruce was the loudest no. "We did build an industrial section for stuff like this, if you look at where Meta is at, that's why we put everything out there," he said. "I have no idea why we would even think about putting it right there." Stear answered: "My biggest concern is if not this, what?" He said he did not favor the idea of apartments on the property instead.

The Gemstone deal promised $12 million to Kuna Police and $32 million to the Kuna Rural Fire District, but only $500,000 to the Kuna School District. School trustee Hillary Lowe told the council: "our assistant superintendent showed them actually close to $20 million in needs from the school and we were offered $500,000." Neighbors then went to court. In August 2025, farmer Layne Thornton and two entities behind Toledo Dairy petitioned for judicial review of the approval. Council member Greg McPherson had voted while employed by Thornton, whose land borders the site for more than a mile, and they argued he should have recused himself. The city replied that Thornton had shown no direct economic interest that could be imputed to his employee. By April 2026 BoiseDev reported the project on hold because of the lawsuit.

Water is the local worry, and the city's answer is that the farms used more. Meta's property carries water rights for nearly 3.7 million gallons a day. The company signed over roughly 2.5 million gallons a day of those rights to the city, and the project is expected to peak at just under 2 million gallons a day in July and August. The Diode property's three water rights total 1.63 million gallons a day, and a transfer from irrigation to industrial use was pending. Kuna Public Works Director Adam Wenger said the data centers would use considerably less than farming. "Given that, do I consider groundwater an unlimited resource? No. There would be water issues here in some number of years, regardless of what that use is. Are we expediting that by pivoting that land to a data center? I don't think so, but it's to be determined." He said southern Ada County is probably "at a saturation point." Boise State engineering professor Sondra Miller was less sanguine: "If you're taking that water to cool data centers, what are you taking away from everything else?"

The biggest proposal now sits on federal land. In September 2026 the Bureau of Land Management confirmed that Rhea Data, a subsidiary of Las Vegas-based Arevia Power, had applied to build a 4-million-square-foot data center complex near Blacks Creek Reservoir on Kuna-Mora Road. The site would cover some 3,750 acres, a 3,200-acre campus plus 550 acres of transmission, and would include a natural gas power plant. The BLM said it first received the application in August 2025 and is still asking how the plant would be cooled and how much water it would need. Idaho Power said the project is "still preliminary" and not in its load forecast. Lisa Young of the Sierra Club's Idaho Chapter called it "unacceptable": "An additional data center with its own gas plant would wreck our local air quality and climate." BLM field manager Jarod Blades said he plans to publish a notice of intent, which opens public comment, before the end of 2026. "This is an application the BLM is required by law to evaluate, it's not a BLM proposal," he said.

Two hyperscale data centers are under construction in the Big Cedar Industrial area at the southwest edge of the Cedar Rapids area: Google's campus is in Cedar Rapids itself, and QTS's neighboring campus is in the adjacent city of Fairfax. In December 2025 the city council unanimously approved a revised QTS agreement, and no one spoke at the public comment period. The revision caps the campus at seven phases, each a building of at least 300,000 square feet representing a $250 million investment. QTS will pay $300,000 per phase into a community betterment fund. In July 2026 Mayor Tiffany O'Donnell defended both projects against residents' claims of kickbacks. She said the city is giving the companies a 15-year tax break and will still collect about $25 million a year in property taxes during it, rising to about $55 million afterwards. "We need those projects here whether we want to admit that or not," she said. She said water modeling by Black & Veatch, using worst-case drought conditions from the 1980s, found the city could sustain the projects. Asked about secrecy, she said: "Never signed an NDA, a nondisclosure agreement." KCRG had obtained two nondisclosure agreements the city signed, one with Google and one with QTS, and reported that the copies were signed by the city manager and the utilities business manager. "No kickbacks, no lined pockets," O'Donnell said.

Google's next campus was planned for rural land outside Palo, beside the Duane Arnold Energy Center, Iowa's only nuclear plant. Google signed a 25-year agreement in October 2025 to buy most of the plant's power once it restarts. That plan prompted the Linn County Board of Supervisors to spend about seven months writing what Inside Climate News called one of the most comprehensive local data center ordinances in the country, adopted on February 18, 2026. It created an exclusive data center zoning district, 1,000-foot setbacks from residential zoning, and noise and light limits. It also required a water study and a water-use agreement with the county, and a community betterment fund. "Why has Linn County, Iowa, become a dumping ground for soon-to-be obsolete technology that spoils our landscape and robs us of our resources?" asked Dorothy Landt of Palo at the first reading. Supervisor Brandy Meisheid's answer to developers was: "If it's too high a price for them to pay, they don't have to come."

Google did not come. On February 26, the same day county staff told it the board would accept its economic terms, Google said it would instead seek annexation of the site into Palo. Board chair Kirsten Running-Marquardt said Google had told her it planned to need 12 million gallons of water a day from the Cedar River. "Google has decided to bypass the protections that we put in place in our ordinance," she said. Palo wrote its own rules: its ordinance defers water regulation to the Iowa Department of Natural Resources, drops the county's mandatory water-use agreement, and lets the company redact information it deems confidential. The council passed it 4-1 on July 20, 2026, with Doug Hanover voting no. "We have one shot at this in one ordinance, and it needs to be solid," resident Shelly Jacobus told the council. Council member Eric Van Kerckhove argued: "Right now, we have an opportunity to be in the lead. Opportunities like this do not come along often for small communities like Palo, and they do not come twice." Mayor Bryan Busch said Google, not the city, would have to request annexation, and that nothing was set in stone.

By then Linn County had begun an 18-month moratorium that pauses all applications in its data center zone. At the same time, it directed staff to consider allowing data centers as an accessory use to a nuclear plant. Planning director Charlie Nichols said: "It's hard to say it's not project-specific because there is only one nuclear plant in Iowa." Elsewhere in the county, developers approached Fairfax and county leaders about a three-square-mile area near Morgan Creek. Residents formed Save Morgan Valley. "If they build 2,000 acres of data centers, I won't be here still," said homeowner Jon Lee. Fairfax Mayor Jo Ann Beer said construction traffic had already become her residents' first complaint. On July 14, 2026, the Fairfax City Council passed a moratorium 3-1 with no expiration date. Its sponsor, Dan Wozniak, said of how long it would last: "That might be tomorrow, it might be 10 years from now."

Dickey County's data center is Applied Digital's Polaris Forge 1 campus at 9685 87th Ave. SE, just west of Ellendale. It started in 2023 as a cryptocurrency mining site and is being expanded into an AI campus built for 400 megawatts of power, all leased to CoreWeave under a 15-year deal worth about $11 billion. The first 50 megawatts opened to CoreWeave in October 2025, and more buildings are still being finished.

Ellendale annexed the campus in 2025, so its property taxes go to the city instead of the township. Mayor Don Flaherty, who is also the county's tax director, said the growth answers rural decline: "This is not an Ellendale problem, it's a national problem." Not everyone agreed. At a packed city meeting in August 2025, residents in No Eminent Domain shirts said, "We want to let our elected representatives know we've had no representation or say in any of this." The campus paid about $4.3 million in property tax for 2026, the company says.

Farmers in the county have also fought JETx, a high-voltage power line on 150-foot towers running 92 miles from near Jamestown to a substation west of Ellendale. State regulators granted its route permit in June 2026, saying most landowner worries, including that the line could serve data centers, were outside their authority. "We just never had a fair shake at any of this," said Lucas Wald of Edgeley. In July 2026 the North Dakota Supreme Court ruled unanimously that the townships and landowners had no standing to challenge the line's 2024 approval.

Dauphin County has two data center proposals. HCI DP Land Acquisition wants to build two data centers, of 401,800 and 195,000 square feet, plus a substation, on almost 250 acres of a former quarry off Wagner Street in South Hanover Township, and has also asked to rezone 496 acres of nearby land that is not currently zoned for industrial use. Separately, the Dallas-based Provident Realty has agreed to buy Dauphin County's money-losing Dauphin Highlands Golf Course, which sits in Swatara Township and Steelton, for $45.6 million to build a data center there; the sale is not expected to close until December 31, 2027.

South Hanover Township supervisors voted unanimously on July 1, 2026, to advertise a data center ordinance, after more than 100 people packed the meeting and some in the crowd shouted "No!" The draft would make every data center a conditional use, keep buildings 400 feet from homes, cap heights at 55 feet, and require water and noise studies. "Good zoning is proactive, not reactive," said Supervisor Kevin Busher. "We have a responsibility to put rules in place before decisions are made."

Neighboring Hummelstown borough has sided against HCI, saying it will help South Hanover fight the company's rezoning request before the township's zoning hearing board. The residents' group Protect South Hanover says HCI has asked to postpone both of its hearings indefinitely, so no date has been set for either one.

Montour County, Pennsylvania's smallest county by area, turned down Talen Energy's request to rezone land near its Montour Steam Electric Station in Anthony Township, outside Washingtonville, for what Talen acknowledged "could include data centers." Residents linked the request to Talen's 2024 sale of a nearby power plant campus to Amazon Web Services for $650 million, and organized as Concerned Citizens of Montour County, gathering 3,000 signatures against it. In February 2026 the three county commissioners unanimously denied rezoning more than 800 acres. "No evidence was provided demonstrating that the benefits outweigh documented and foreseeable public harms," said commission chair Rebecca Dressler.

Residents said Talen offered to buy land at six to seven times market value, and hundreds turned out to hearings in red "Say No!" shirts. Farmer Mike Leighow, who works land his grandfather bought in 1901, said, "If we can't get water, we can't survive." Talen said afterward it remained "committed to pursuing a path forward in Montour County," and a Food & Water Watch organizer said landowners in surrounding communities were being approached about alternative sites.

The county has since written its own data center rules. At the end of April 2026 the commissioners unanimously approved planning commission amendments to the county's land-use ordinance capping data center heights at 45 feet, plus 15 feet for equipment, and doubling the setback from homes and other sensitive sites from 500 to 1,000 feet. Planning Commission chair Greg Molter said the amended ordinance still needed a 30-day public notice, a hearing and a final vote by the commissioners; no final vote has been reported since.

Two data center campuses tied to Talen Energy's power plants are proposed in neighboring townships in Northampton County's Slate Belt. The larger, the Lower Mount Bethel Tech Center from Peron Development, J.G. Petrucci Company and Talen, sits next to Talen's Martins Creek and Lower Mount Bethel power plants; developers describe a 1.2-gigawatt, more-than-$5 billion project. After resident pushback the team filed a revised plan in August 2026 that drops about 350 farmed acres and now seeks to rezone about 239 acres, including farmland and quarry land, saying closed-loop cooling would use neither groundwater nor Delaware River water. Lower Mount Bethel's supervisors have adopted their own data center ordinance.

At a town hall, of about three dozen speakers WFMZ counted none in support. "We do not want to be Bethlehem. We do not want to be Forks Township," said resident Marge Holmes. Developer John Callahan, a former Bethlehem mayor, told residents electricity bills "will not go up," and the team estimated $7 million to $8 million a year in township tax revenue against current revenue of $550,000.

Next door in Upper Mount Bethel Township, Slate Belt Holdings, a partnership of Talen and River Pointe Logistics, bought about 754 acres for a planned 23-building campus with a possible 2 gigawatts of power. After the developer offered $50 million in donations in exchange for a by-right zoning change, supervisors instead voted 3-1 for their own ordinance making data centers a conditional use, requiring disclosure of total power demand and cutting the height limit to 45 feet. On August 24, 2026 the board voted 3-2 to keep negotiating rather than abandon talks, while directing its solicitor to fight the developer's legal challenge to the township's zoning. "Can we keep them out? I don't know," board chair John Bermingham said. "Can we regulate them? Yes, and that's where we're at."
The county's only operating site, TierPoint's Bethlehem data center, has not disclosed its power use.

Austin has no large-scale AI data center inside city limits yet, and on August 27, 2026 the City Council voted unanimously to make sure none arrives without its say. The resolution orders staff to write land-use, site-development and business rules, and until those rules exist, any large-scale project needs council approval. Austin Energy counts 10 smaller data centers in the city, each drawing 1 to 20 megawatts; the land code has no rules above the state's 75-megawatt large-load threshold.

Several council members want a full ban. "We won't wait for a crisis to happen here, which is why today we are pursuing a full ban on large-scale data centers in Austin," said Council Member Vanessa Fuentes. Council Member Ryan Alter said it would take "a very high bar" for him to approve a local data center. Mayor Kirk Watson asked for "legal, durable and enforceable rules," while resident Brad Massingill warned a blanket ban risks "one lawsuit to strip that away."

The county's biggest computing site sits outside the city's reach, at Tesla's Gigafactory Texas in unincorporated Travis County. Tesla is building Cortex, a cluster InsideEVs described in 2024 as more than 100,000 Nvidia GPUs training its self-driving software and Optimus robots, apparently needing 500 megawatts in future. The Austin American-Statesman reported 16,500 employees on a site that could grow to 3,500 acres, with a new building for Tesla's Terafab chip project under construction; Tesla did not respond to the paper.
Elsewhere in the county, Skybox Datacenters operates a 30-megawatt building in Pflugerville, the Austin Chronicle reported.

Water is where Tesla and the data center debate meet. Austin's Water Forward Task Force heard in June 2026 that Tesla had climbed from the utility's fifth-largest customer to its third in two years, with the five largest customers using about 4.5 billion gallons in 2025. In July, the council asked the city manager to study stricter conservation rules for high-water-use industries, including large data centers; those recommendations are due in December 2026.

Stream Data Centers has spent 2026 fighting for its largest proposal: a $19.46 billion, 2.2 million square foot campus at the Science, Technology and Advanced Manufacturing Park in the Town of Alabama, Genesee County, New York, on land less than a mile from the Tonawanda Seneca Nation. "We told them we don't want them as a neighbor," said Grandell Logan, a spokesperson for the Nation. In July 2026 Governor Kathy Hochul ordered a one-year moratorium on state data center permits, and the Nation, the Sierra Club and a town resident sued to void the 2012 zoning agreement that created the park.

At a Town of Alabama Planning Board hearing that ran past midnight, about 73 people spoke, most against the project; building trades members spoke in favor. Stream has asked the county's economic development agency for $1.46 billion in state and local sales tax breaks. "Without the incentives, the project would not come here," said Mark Masse, the agency's chief executive. The state Department of Environmental Conservation has also demanded an updated wetland study before it will weigh in on stormwater permits.

In South Carolina, Stream abandoned a separate project in Marion County in June 2026, citing utility timing; residents had learned its terms only after the county council approved it in January, because members had signed non-disclosure agreements. In Texas, Stream agreed in July 2026 to pay up to $76.5 million for a cancelled hydrogen site near Graham, planning an 890-acre, roughly $10 billion campus there while it negotiates a tax abatement with the city and Young County.

Sabey Data Centers, owned by the Seattle real estate firm Sabey and National Real Estate Advisors, runs eight sites in Washington, New York, Texas, Virginia and Indiana. Its biggest project is a $4.3 billion, two-building campus on 130 acres at 6400 Kentucky Avenue in Decatur Township, on Indianapolis' southwest side. The city's Metropolitan Development Commission approved it in March 2026 and added more than $240 million in tax breaks on September 16, 2026; Sabey expects to finish by 2031.

Sabey asked only for zoning variances, not a full rezoning, so the district's city-county councilor could not call the case to the full council. "This was deliberate to deprive us of our rights," said Pat Andrews, who chairs the land use committee of the Decatur Township Civic Council. "It does not belong in the middle of these residences." Seven Decatur Township residents are suing to block the project, and Indianapolis has since passed a moratorium on new data center projects that runs through December 31, 2027.

Elsewhere, Sabey started vertical construction in July 2026 on a 120 megawatt campus in Umatilla, Oregon, planned in two buildings. In Butte, Montana, it walked away from a 606 acre land deal in May 2026 after finding an existing tenant, REC Silicon, held first right to buy it. In Quincy, Washington, where Sabey and other companies now use 37% of the local utility's power, new construction has slowed as the grid nears its limit.

County Offaly's data center prospect runs through Bord na Móna, the semi-state company founded in 1946 to develop Ireland's peatlands. In April 2024 Bord na Móna named Amazon Web Services as the first business to join its Eco Energy Park, subject to regulatory and planning consent. The park is a plan launched in 2021 to turn about 3,000 hectares of its land in Offaly, Westmeath and Meath into a business park where large energy users sit beside wind, solar and gas generation. The deal would create a pathway for AWS to develop data centres in the Midlands, according to the two companies, which did not give a number of buildings, a size or a timetable. AWS also signed a 105-megawatt power purchase agreement for Bord na Móna's Derrinlough wind farm, 21 turbines on two Boora bogs in west Offaly, and pledged up to 800 megawatts of new renewable projects in Ireland. "We can co-locate these large companies with our renewable energy assets to offer a sustainable pathway to grid capacity that is backed up with Flexible Technology power as required," said Bord na Móna chief executive Tom Donnellan.

The county had already been making its own case. In July 2023 Offaly County Council heard that a commissioned report had found Rhode, in north Offaly, suitable for a data centre. "One of our positives in Offaly," said Director of Services Sharon Kennedy, "is we have an excellent connection to the electric grid." Councillor Noel Cribbin said reports by EirGrid and Siemens pointed to north Offaly's renewable output from Edenderry Power, six wind farms and solar farms, and that big energy users should "be located where the green energy is being developed."

Friends of the Earth objected to the arrangement itself. "It is concerning to see an Irish semi-state body, Bord na Móna, put forward energy plans purely to generate power for data centres," said David Rossiter, its fossil free campaigner. The group argued that Derrinlough's output would be consumed by new Amazon demand instead of displacing fossil fuel, so that "we will effectively be running to stand still."
/data-centers/ireland/county-offaly/.unconfirmed: No planning application for an AWS data centre in Offaly was found in three searches, and nothing newer than May 2024 on the Eco Energy Park deal was read; the page does not say whether one has been lodged. A search engine summary claimed An Bord Pleanála had granted permission after appeals; no article supporting that was found and it is not used. The Offaly Independent places the park's main development near the M6 at Rochfortbridge in Westmeath, so whether the AWS buildings would sit in Offaly itself is not stated. The Rhode report's authors and the 2023 proposal's developer were not named in the source.

paragraphs: Israel's Center District holds much of the country's data center building. In Modi'in, Mega Or runs a data center where the AI cloud company Nebius leased 8 megawatts of power in May 2025, and in December Mega Or signed a 19-megawatt lease across Modi'in and Masmiyya with a customer CalcalisTech reported is Google, for delivery in the third quarter of 2026. In Netanya, NED and the Levinstein Group are building a 50-megawatt underground campus for 1.3 billion shekels. Amazon Web Services runs cloud data centers at Tnuvot and in Shoham.

Real estate money is pouring in. Ofer Yanai, controlling shareholder of Nofar Energy, bought land in Shoham for 361 million shekels for a data center. "This is picking gold off the floor," he told Calcalist, saying a small 50-megawatt center like Shoham's could leave its builder "with $850 million in your pocket." Kardan Israel holds stakes in server farms in Kfar Saba and Shoham, the Yochananoff supermarket family has bought land in Yavne for a campus, and Rami Levy's group is studying sites in Netanya.

For now, no large new project can get a grid connection. In July 2026 Israel's Electricity Authority froze applications from data centers of 8 megawatts or more for 140 days, until early December, after the grid operator Noga received 19,000 megawatts of requests in two months. During the freeze, regulators are writing rules for which projects get power. The Society for the Protection of Nature in Israel had called the government's February decision to treat data centers as national infrastructure "a dangerous gamble on Israel's energy security."

Nakuru County's data center story is Olkaria, the geothermal field near Lake Naivasha run by the state generator KenGen. In May 2024, during President William Ruto's state visit to Washington, Microsoft and the UAE AI firm G42 signed a letter of intent with Kenya for a $1 billion package. At its centre was a geothermal-powered data center campus at Olkaria of 100 megawatts at first, rising to as much as 1 gigawatt, meant to host Microsoft's first East African Azure cloud region within two years. "This represents the single largest and broadest digital investment in Kenya's history," said Microsoft president Brad Smith. A smaller local project was already under way: EcoCloud broke ground in 2023 on its 'Project Eagle' data center at KenGen's Green Energy Park in Olkaria.

The big campus stalled over power. "To switch on that one data center, we would need to shut off power for half the country. That's when I knew there was a problem," Ruto said in Nairobi, Data Center Dynamics reported on 7 May 2026, citing Business Insider Africa. DCD put Kenya's total supply at about 3 gigawatts. The Citizen reported he had made the same point to Kenyans in Doha in November 2025. Officials said a concept note to the National Treasury never won clearance, and by August 2025 the May 2026 launch date was already lost. Bloomberg, as cited by DCD, reported a different account: Microsoft and G42 had asked the government to commit to leasing a set amount of capacity every year, and talks broke down when it could not. The government's technology envoy, Philip Thigo, disputed that it had stalled: "His point has not been that the project was suspended, but Kenya must confront the scale of energy required to support next-generation digital infrastructure."

Around the lake, residents are asking about water. The companies promised "state-of-the-art water conservation technology" but published no water figure. KenGen told Al Jazeera the project remains at the design stage. "Currently, we are relying on water vendors to get water, our animals are walking for kilometres, and we fear things could get worse as demand for water rises," said Musa Olorkedienye, who lives near Olkaria. Silas Wanjala of the Lake Naivasha Riparian Association recalled that "This lake in 2010 nearly dried up due to over-abstraction, and this could be repeated due to high demand for water by these investors in Olkaria." Absolom Mukhuusi of the Naivasha Professional Association welcomed the investment but said: "our biggest fear is what happens to our water bodies and communities as water is diverted to Olkaria for the heavy users."
/data-centers/kenya/nakuru-county/.unconfirmed: Two searches, below the three-search minimum. Ruto's words differ between occasions: the 'shut off power for half the country' wording is from Business Insider Africa via DCD, while the Citizen quotes a partly Swahili version from Doha ('For us to do the data centre, we have to shut down half the country'). Kenya's capacity figure varies by source (2,300 MW in Ruto's Doha remarks, about 3 GW per DCD, 3,192 MW grid-connected per Tech-ish citing EPRA), so the page uses DCD's round figure. Business Insider Africa and Bloomberg were not read directly. None of the sources states the county, so Olkaria is placed by its location near Lake Naivasha.

paragraphs: Two large data centers are planned in Flevoland. In Lelystad, Equinix is investing €1.5 billion in a 150-megawatt data center on the Flevokust Haven business park, allowed under a 2021 zoning change, so the city can no longer stop it. In Almere, the Dutch company Ocom, through EvoSwitch, plans a €61 million campus on the Sallandsekant business park beside the Hoge Vaart canal, still awaiting permits from the province, water board and city. The province's council is due to adopt new rules on where data centers may go at the end of 2026.

Lelystad's council was misinformed about Equinix. A notice to councilors put its power use at 3,000 to 5,000 households; the real figure is about 200,000, Omroep Flevoland reported, more than the whole city uses. Equinix said it would draw spare power straight from the neighboring Maxima power station, but owner Engie said it had not been asked: "The neighbor is speaking a bit out of turn" (translated from Dutch). The city now says it was explicitly agreed in 2021 that the site must not become a hyperscale center.

The Almere campus would use about 272,000 megawatt-hours a year, like more than 80,000 households, and take about 225 million liters a year from the Hoge Vaart for cooling, about 80% of which evaporates. It would keep almost a million liters of diesel underground for 28 backup generators. EvoSwitch says it will start at 10% of capacity and reach full use only after five to ten years; a second building is planned for 2028.
