The province's draft plan would allow new data centers only on existing business parks linked to energy hubs, and only where they do not hold up house building. Zeewolde, where Meta dropped a giant campus in 2022, is fighting again: the Amsterdam region's maps drew a possible data center cluster on its land. "As far as we are concerned, the MRA's plans are objectionable," alderman Helmut Hermans said.

Page, a small city near Glen Canyon Dam, has agreed to sell 500 acres across State Route 89 from Horseshoe Bend to Huntley LLC, which intends to seek permits for a 1-gigawatt data center campus, about 1,000 megawatts of power. The City Council voted 5-2 in October 2025 to sell the land for $14,000 an acre, $7 million in all. The sale closes only after an 18-to-24-month feasibility study, and the city can buy the land back at the same price if the conditions are not met.

Opponents gathered more than 400 signatures for a referendum on the sale, but in December 2025 the city rejected the petition because some signature sheets had missing or wrong serial numbers or lacked a copy of the ordinance. A recall effort against several council members, including Councilwoman Debi Roundtree and Mayor Steve Kidman, was also launched. "This is my home," said Teyana Begay, 19, one of the opponents. Councilwoman Amanda Hammond, who voted no, said the acreage, water use and power source were still open: "all of that is unknown."

The site borders the LeChee Chapter of the Navajo Nation, about five miles south of the city, and the chapter passed a resolution opposing the sale. "Water is precious to us," said chapter president Irene Whitekiller. Arup, the engineering firm working on the proposal, told the council that air-cooled chillers would mean "we're not pulling water from the municipality in order to cool the closed loop."

In Flagstaff, the county seat, no data center has been proposed, but the City Council is weighing two zoning changes: one would require a conditional use permit for large data centers, the other would ban them. In May 2026 the council postponed the vote a second time so staff could do more public outreach, and no new date has been set.

Humain, the state-backed AI company, is building a data center in Dammam with an initial 100 megawatts of power. It broke ground in August 2025 on this site and a sister site in Riyadh, and said both would go live in the second quarter of 2026; no opening has been announced. Chief executive Tareq Amin said the timing depended on receiving Nvidia chips from the US, subject to "the governance and the protocols and the approval of the US government."

Humain says it has secured 211 plots of land across Saudi Arabia toward about 6 gigawatts of data centers over the next decade, but would not say where. Heat is a local cost: nearly all of Saudi Arabia's data centers sit in areas hotter than the 18 to 27°C range recommended for efficient operation, a Rest of World and Climate Central analysis found, which means more power spent on cooling.

Lowndes County has paused data center applications for 60 days, from August 25 to about October 24, 2026, while it writes rules for them. The fight is over 719 acres on Coleman Road in north Valdosta, next to the Foxborough neighborhood, owned by Pope Langdale, who has said he is talking with Atlanta developer DC Blox. No data center application has been filed for the land.

Commissioners rezoned the land to light manufacturing unanimously on July 8, 2025, after a 4-3 planning commission vote; the minutes describe "a large warehouse type campus." At a July 2026 information session, officials said no data center was planned and that Langdale's land allegedly would not be one, but a county presentation said DC Blox was in talks with a "private land owner." Langdale has signed a non-disclosure agreement with DC Blox.

Lowndes Citizens Against Data Centers has held town halls, put up billboards and spoken at nearly every commission meeting. Tetiana Babcock, whose land adjoins the site, said loggers in March 2026 "cleared over the fence line, dragging the fence onto our property," breaking a 200-foot buffer condition. Retired Valdosta State geographer Michael Noll warns the site sits on limestone prone to sinkholes above the aquifer.

The draft ordinance discussed in July would require closed-loop cooling using water from outside the county's aquifer, send wastewater out of the county and bar variances. County Manager Paige Dukes said the draft will be made public before commissioners vote. Resident Joel Dion called the pause "a step in the right direction," but said most of the crowd "were hoping more for a full moratorium and a full ban."

Upson County has no data center, and its fight is over whether it is trying to get one. On September 8, 2026 commissioners voted 4-0 to rezone 222.6 acres near The Rock, bought by the Thomaston-Upson Industrial Development Authority, for the county's third industrial park, on Race Track Road beside the airport. Twelve residents spoke against it, most on the suspicion that the land is meant for a data center, citing noise, power and water use and the county's comprehensive plan. "Is it a fact? Are you trying to get a data center in here?" one asked commissioners. "We're exactly what they're trying to exploit… a county full of poor people with lots of land." The authority's Slade Gulledge said the site needed industrial zoning to be marketed through the state, and that for now it would be leased for cattle and hay. Vice chair Chris Biggs told the room: "There are no back doors."

The suspicion has a history. In July 2025 the commission unanimously adopted an ordinance letting technology businesses seek an overlay district on agricultural-residential land, pushed by the then county manager and by Gulledge, who said: "At the [T-U IDA], we're in the opportunity business." A month later the Upson Beacon found a 1,443-acre tract at 795 Windsweep Farm Road marketed as a data center "Megasite", advertising 115 kV and 230 kV lines, a gas pipeline and three power plants nearby. Commissioner Biggs asked then where the water from Thomaston would go once used, and how a volunteer fire department in Rock Hill would cope.

Now the county is writing rules. By August the planning commission had recommended more than 20 conditions for data centers in industrial districts, including a 500-foot setback from any home, a 50-foot natural buffer, a 100-foot stream buffer, an environmental impact study covering air, water, energy, noise and traffic, a letter from the utility confirming service, public water and sewer with no private wells, screened HVAC, an emergency response plan, and a decommissioning bond set by an independent engineer. Commissioner James Ellington worried about the message: "If 100 people show up, out of 28,000 residents, and say 'I don't want it,' it becomes a political issue." At a September 8 work session Commissioner Ben Watson proposed also requiring a development plan approved by the board, and the county attorney, Heath English, said it should list "everything we can think of" to put prospects on notice. Ellington's remark there, "I guess first off, we got to get one," became the evening's flashpoint when resident Rusty Blackston repeated it at the public hearing; Ellington said it was taken out of context: "We don't have one and may never have one." That evening the board unanimously approved the zoning text amendments.

The board is also short a member. Chairman Dan Brue resigned at the end of August, and the four remaining commissioners will serve until a special election in March 2027, and Blackston argued in challenging the rezoning that the development authority's board is left without the county chair who normally sits on it. What would go on the new industrial park, whether any data center developer has approached the county, and whether the Windsweep Farm megasite was ever sold have not been made public.
/data-centers/united-states/georgia/upso.unconfirmed: Rewritten by lane p from the HOLDS list (held by lane t for having nothing after August 2025). All sources are the Upson Beacon; no other outlet covering Upson was found. paragraphs: Google is exploring a data center on about 900 acres of farmland that the town of Salix, south of Sioux City, annexed in April 2026. MidAmerican Energy, which took options on the land, named Google as the prospective customer on August 3, and no rezoning or development application had been filed. The county's own one-year moratorium covers unincorporated areas, and its zoning commission holds a town hall on data center rules in Salix on November 9.

Salix, a town of about 300 people, is split. On August 20 the City Council voted 3-2 against a one-year pause, after an earlier meeting was cancelled over what Mayor Kevin Nelson called "death and terroristic type things" posted online. "It's too big of a decision for us five people," said council member Gene Monk, who backed the pause. Council member Denise Burkhart voted no: "We need to open conversations with Google to see what they want to bring here." A petition against the project passed 540 signatures.

The annexation is in court. Landowners say four of the five annexed parcels did not touch the city limits and that neighbors were not properly notified, and Woodbury County is also challenging it. Google's Trent Fellers wrote to residents that the company had "finalized an agreement with MidAmerican Energy Company that enables us to explore a potential data center development in Salix."

The Board of Supervisors voted 5-0 for the county moratorium on June 23, 2026, and is writing an ordinance through town halls. At one in Moville, Winnebago Tribal Council member Keely Bassette Purcell warned, "Harm our fish, harm our water," while resident Tom Morgan asked, "How much business are we running away from Woodbury County?"

Madison County, in the Metro East across the Mississippi from St. Louis, has been courted by one developer, Cloverleaf Infrastructure, for three data centers at once. County Board Chairman Chris Slusser said in January 2026 the developer wanted "three, and it's kind of an all-or-nothing deal." Troy and Granite City were two of the three communities publicly discussed; emails later showed Cloverleaf had also been talking to Edwardsville. After a December 2025 tour of Google's Papillion, Nebraska campus, Slusser said he went from "80-90% in favor" to "100% in favor."

Troy pushed back hardest. Cloverleaf presented a 500-megawatt site near I-55, and hundreds of people packed Triad High School for the developer's meeting in February 2026. "We're not an industrial town. We're a small rural town. There is nowhere you can put this here that it won't impact somebody," said Derrick Ramert of Troy Residents for Responsible Growth. The city passed a six-month moratorium in March; by June its draft rules would ban hyperscale campuses outright, capping any data center at 30 megawatts with 1,000-foot setbacks from homes and schools and a decommissioning bond worth 150 percent of construction cost.

Elsewhere the talks were quieter than officials let on. In February, Edwardsville told residents it had received "no formal proposal," but emails obtained by the Illinois Answers Project showed city and county officials had discussed land surveys and site selection with Cloverleaf for almost a year. Granite City's plan commission postponed a zoning change that would allow data centers; Mayor Mike Parkinson said, "We want to hold them accountable for air and water quality issues." Godfrey passed a six-month moratorium in January 2026, and Collinsville's planning commission a one-year moratorium at the end of 2025.

Meade County turned down its only data center proposal. In late September 2025, a filing asked to rezone about 135 acres of farmland near Ekron, at Joe Prather Highway and Garrett Road, from agricultural and residential to light industrial for an "IT infrastructure facility" that would run around the clock with up to 100 employees across shifts. Landowner Tommy Hobbs said the buyer's plans involved artificial intelligence, but neither he nor local officials would name the company. The Planning and Zoning Commission voted against recommending the rezoning, and the Fiscal Court voted it down in October 2025.

Neighbors objected at once. "If a place like this gets built and the value of the property plummets, and the water quality is diminished, and everything else like that ... we're gonna have to give up somewhere else and try again," said Lucas Kudrna, who lives on nearby Buck Knobs Road. Samantha Campbell, whose home borders the site, worried it would be "sucking the county dry." A Change.org petition gathered more than 2,800 signatures.
In January 2026 the county fiscal court adopted a one-year moratorium on new data center permits, running through January 2027, which now covers any future proposal in the unincorporated county.

No new data center has been proposed in Boston, and City Councilor Miniard Culpepper wants to keep it that way. At the council's September 16, 2026 meeting he filed a zoning change that would ban new data centers anywhere in the city, including ones for artificial intelligence, cryptocurrency and cloud computing. It needs the Boston Zoning Commission's approval before it can take effect.

"Boston's density, scarcity of developable land and existing demands on our infrastructure make large-scale data centers incompatible with the direction we should be taking as a city," Culpepper told the council. Existing data centers could keep running but not expand. Among them is Markley Group's building in Downtown Crossing, open since 1998, which runs on 30 megawatts of power, about enough for 30,000 households. Businesses, phone companies and research labs could still run the servers they need.

The proposal follows an order Gov. Maura Healey signed on September 8 requiring any data center using more than 25 megawatts to win a community benefits agreement from its host city before state permits can go ahead. "Unless a community says yes to a data center, we're saying no," Healey said.

Cass County's data center is already built, and its neighbors say they can hear it. Hyperscale Data's facility, run by its subsidiary Alliance Cloud Services, opened at the Business Center of Southwest Michigan in Dowagiac in 2022 as a digital asset mining site. It sits across the street from homes. "It's almost like having a vacuum cleaner running all the time," said Mitchell Gourley. Ami File, who has lived opposite it for 17 years, said: "Once it started we're like, 'Oh my gosh we have to listen to this for how long?' Well four years later and it's still there." Neighbors told WWMT sound levels in front of the site reach 60 to 70 decibels. Some have sued the company, alleging it "emitted and continues to emit, unreasonable and excessive noise onto Plaintiffs' property," and blaming its cooling fans and the lack of barriers. John Valdes said that when city officials came to listen, their answer was that he "should buy some headphones."

The company wants to grow. It announced in 2025 that it intended to expand the site from 30 to 340 megawatts, and in March 2026 an agreement to buy about 48.5 more acres for cloud computing. City Manager Kevin Anderson said the city learned of it from the press release. The company does not use the city's electric utility, and no development proposal had been filed. Dowagiac amended its noise ordinance in March 2026 with separate day and night limits for businesses near homes, and began looking at its zoning, sewer and water rules. Mayor Patrick Bakeman called the company's expansion announcements "vague" and said it had "neither applied for nor received any approvals necessary to facilitate" them.

In January 2026 the Cass County Board of Commissioners unanimously passed a resolution urging its municipalities to adopt a clear regulatory framework. It calls for public disclosure of how a data center's electricity will meet clean energy goals, its daily water use, and a plan so residents are not left with the bill if a project fails. "We're not against data centers and we're not pro-data centers," said Commission Chair Jeremiah Jones. "We just want transparency and what's best for the community." He said the county has "zero power" over the Dowagiac project, and that it is the only data center development he knew of. Penn Township, one of the county's 15 townships, went further, extending its own data center moratorium to a full year on May 21, 2026 after residents said even that did not include the zoning rules they wanted. Residents have since been organizing to get the rest of Cass County's townships to coordinate their zoning and demand developer investment in roads and emergency services before any new proposal arrives.

Kalkaska County's data center rose and fell in the autumn of 2025. Matt Rine, a Traverse City geologist whose company Rocklocker is a subsidiary of the oil and gas firm Reefworks, proposed a gigawatt-scale campus on 1,440 acres of state land near Island Lake and South River roads. It would have had its own natural gas power plant with carbon capture and storage. Rine called Kalkaska a "bullseye": "Basically it has all the ingredients that you need for a data center project to be co-located with a power plant," he said. "You need high voltage electrical lines, need gas transmission lines, you need public support." He estimated more than $40 million a year in tax revenue. Local officials were keen. The county commission, Kalkaska Township board and others sent letters of support. "The proposed data center project presents a rare opportunity for Kalkaska County to expand its tax base, create quality jobs, and fund long-overdue improvements in our community," said Township Supervisor John Arnold. Rine himself said: "It would be a different Kalkaska in 10 years, that's for sure."

The land was the problem. More than half the county is owned by the Department of Natural Resources, and in July 2025 the department rejected Rine's request to buy the site. "We have heard strong opposition from conservation stakeholders to any conversion of state-managed public lands for this use," it wrote, "and to date have received no letters of support from legislators for this proposed use of state-managed public lands." Residents started a "Say No to the Data Center" website and petition. Heather Smith of The Watershed Center Grand Traverse Bay warned that some data centers "withdraw large amounts of groundwater for data center cooling needs that may stress aquifers." In November, state Sen. Michele Hoitenga said she had "received assurances that public lands will not be sold for the data center's development." Within days Rine withdrew, saying it "became clear through these discussions that pursuing a data center development on public lands is not feasible or appropriate at this time, and Rocklocker will no longer be pursuing this project."

A Citizen Portal item reports a county MOU with Rocklocker for an exploratory study; it is not used. Garfield and East Bay townships' zoning work, reported by The Ticker in the same coverage, is in Grand Traverse County and is left out.
