paragraphs: Google wants to build a data center campus on a 200-acre site in Hermantown, a city of about 10,000 next to Duluth, and the project still needs City Council approval. In August 2026 Google cut the plan from four buildings to three, totaling 1.66 million square feet. The council is expected to take up the project's revised environmental review this fall; no meeting date has been announced.

For more than a year the project went by the code name "Project Loon." Several Hermantown and St. Louis County officials signed non-disclosure agreements with the developer, Mortenson, and the city said only that a "Fortune 50" company wanted a $650 million data center. The council approved the rezoning on October 20, 2025, at a meeting of nearly 300 people that ran until almost midnight. Google named itself on March 3, 2026. "Google is a heartless corporation run by heartless people," said Jeffrey Donahue of Stop the Hermantown Data Center.

That group and the Minnesota Center for Environmental Advocacy sued, arguing the city's environmental review called the project "light industrial development". The city has since redone the review to say it is a data center. In an August 25 letter the state Department of Natural Resources said it "does not formally object" but listed "information gaps" and a "lack of defined mitigation," including for nearby wetlands and trout streams. In May the council tabled a vote on a property tax break for Google that could reach $80 million.

The county has no say over the Hermantown site, but about 250 people came to an April 14 hearing on a county zoning rewrite that would have treated data centers as an industrial use. The board took data centers out of the rewrite and started a separate process to define them and set standards. "It's kind of polarizing, and we need to get all the proper information," Commissioner Mike Jugovich said.

Rankin County's data center is AVAIO Digital's Taurus campus in Brandon, at the East Metropolitan Center Business and Industrial Park. Gov. Tate Reeves announced it in August 2025 as a $6 billion investment, the third largest in state history after Amazon Web Services in Madison County and Compass Datacenters in Meridian. The Connecticut developer promises at least 60 direct jobs and expects construction to be complete in the first half of 2027. Entergy Mississippi will supply power. The Mississippi Development Authority approved the project for the state's data center tax exemption and had earlier helped develop the park with a site development grant, and Rankin County and the city are also assisting. "This project will not only transform Rankin County and the Metro Jackson region, it will transform our economic landscape and lead to even more high-tech leaders choosing Mississippi," Reeves said. Brandon Mayor Butch Lee called it "a monumental day for the city of Brandon."

Some residents want guarantees first. A petition to the Rankin County Board of Supervisors, which gathered nearly 1,000 signatures, asks for written confirmation that the campus "will not result in any increase in utility bills or cause air or water pollution" and, failing that, urges the county to "immediately stop the planned construction." "I'm even more concerned about the secrecy surrounding this process," said resident Bailey Henry. "If this is such a great development for Mississippi, then why have Mississippians been kept in the dark on this?" The governor's office defended the state's data center push. "Our state reviews data center projects on a case-by-case basis to ensure Mississippi has the resources needed to sustain them," said Reeves's deputy chief of staff, Cory Custer. The supervisors did not respond to SuperTalk Mississippi's questions. Construction is under way.
/data-centers/united-states/mississippi/.unconfirmed: Mississippi Today's petition story (September 2025) returned no article text to the extraction, so it is not a source. The fee-in-lieu agreement, the 329-acre figure, and Entergy's 'Fair Share Plus' pledge appeared only in search summaries or company releases, and are not used. The SuperTalk petition story is undated in the text read, so the petition's timing is given only as before construction was complete. The two SuperTalk stories spell the chief executive 'McComiskey' and MBJ spells him 'McComisky'; neither spelling is needed on the page.

paragraphs: Amazon Web Services has begun building a $3 billion data center campus south of Vicksburg along U.S. Highway 61, with its main entrance off Old Cain Ridge Road. AWS named the site in April 2026 and said construction mobilization was under way, with up to 1,250 workers on site at the peak. Amazon has promised at least 200 full-time jobs at the campus and about 300 more in the county.

The state authorized $44 million in incentives, and Warren County supervisors approved a $20 million state loan for roads and other work tied to the project. AWS agreed to make the county's loan payments if they come due before the data center produces tax revenue. Asked about water, AWS's Roger Wehner said the company expects to use water for cooling about 9 percent of the year: "So it's probably 30 days out of the year ... Probably somewhere around August."

Entergy Mississippi is building the Vicksburg Advanced Power Station, a gas plant replacing the Baxter Wilson plant, which closed in 2022 and cost Vicksburg and Warren County an estimated $3.2 million a year in taxes. "We were only going to build one new power plant for the next five or six years," said Entergy's Ed Gardner. "Now we're building three new gas plants." AWS says it pays the full cost of its energy use and related infrastructure.

Union County's data center is going up in Kenilworth, on the 103-acre former Merck campus, now the Northeast Science and Technology Center, which borough officials said had been vacant since 2023. The borough council approved the sale of land there to CoreWeave in 2025, and the planning board approved the redevelopment, called the Galloping Hill Technology Campus, in May 2025. Mayor Linda Karlovitch told News 12 construction should be finished by the end of 2027. Residents learned of it late. "I wasn't notified at all," said Kenilworth resident William Daughtry. "I know it might be too late to stop it," said Diane Moxley of Garwood at a May 2026 protest outside borough hall. "But I'm hoping if we get the numbers out from Kenilworth and the surrounding communities, maybe we can get the municipal government to listen to us." Borough leaders told the crowd the window to stop the project had long passed.

At a planning board meeting that month, resident Danielle Palmie described what had been approved: "a 280,000 square foot building converted to a 24/7 industrial energy use, 250 megawatts of electrical load, 50,000 square foot exterior chiller yard, 31 diesel generators on concrete pads." "What is an AI data center in the face of a drought?" asked Imani Nam Burton. The board unanimously tabled the borough's 2026 master plan to review the concerns. "For the public, we heard you. You think we didn't? We heard," said its chairman, Rich Picerno. In June officials defended the deal. "We have a vacant industrial park that doesn't benefit the town being vacant," said Council President William Mauro. "They have their own electric grid, they are not tapping into our electric grid at all," the mayor said. "And they're not using water." She said the council still had to approve a redevelopment agreement with CoreWeave, and negotiations were continuing. "We are being asked to trust the process that has provided very little transparency and very few concrete answers," said Victor Gomez of Union Township.

Linden went the other way. In September 2026 Mayor Derek Armstead and the City Council moved to introduce an ordinance banning AI data centers in every zoning district. "After a comprehensive review of the potential environmental, infrastructure, and quality-of-life impacts, we concluded that this type of development is not right for our city," Armstead said. By late August at least 69 New Jersey municipalities had banned data centers, according to the Pinelands Alliance, as cited by the New Jersey Globe.
/data-centers/united-states/new-jersey/u.unconfirmed: Two searches. The mayor's name is spelled 'Karlovitch' by Patch and 'Korlavitch' by News 12; Patch's spelling is used. The resident is 'Victor Gomez' in one Patch story and 'Victor Gomes' in the other; the June story's spelling is used. Whether Linden adopted the ban after its 15 September introduction was not found. Union County Life's Linden item is a Google Alerts rewrite and was not used. The 250 MW and 31-generator figures are a resident's description of the approved plan, attributed to her, and were not confirmed from planning documents.

paragraphs: Meta's campus in Los Lunas began in 2016 as a single $250 million building beside Interstate 25, south of Albuquerque. It now has seven operating buildings and three more under development on a parcel of roughly 750 acres. The Santa Fe New Mexican reported it has brought Los Lunas an extra $145 million in gross receipts tax and helped grow the village from about 17,300 people in 2020 to close to 20,000 in 2024. "I don't think that anyone could have expected a company this big," said Victoria Archuleta, the village's senior economic developer. Meta has financed its build-outs with industrial revenue bonds from the village: about $30 billion for the first buildings in 2016 and a little more than $40 billion in 2021, the Valencia County News-Bulletin reported.

In December 2024 the village council unanimously approved an intent resolution for a third series of bonds, up to six series of up to $7.5 billion each, for Meta's affiliate Greater Kudu LLC. They would fund two more buildings, around $800 million, which the village said would be Meta's first dedicated to AI and machine learning, adding about 30 full-time jobs. "I'm excited about the concept of the high-tech around here," said council member James Runyon. The New Mexican later reported that the council had approved the bonds. The equipment bonds bring an abatement, a reduction, of gross receipts and compensating tax, the village's bond attorney, Jill Sweeney, explained.

The costs are in water and power. According to Meta's own 2024 sustainability report, as cited by the New Mexican, the campus used about 75 million gallons of water and more than a million megawatt-hours of electricity in 2023, while much of Valencia County was in extreme drought. Meta says it has helped add 885 megawatts of renewable energy and 100 megawatts of battery storage in New Mexico. A PNM substation, equipment that steps power down for local use, came online in November 2024 to serve it and the neighboring business park. "It does take a lot of power and resources to actually operate a data center," Archuleta said, adding that "at the end of the day, if our utility can't deliver, then nothing can come here."

Broome County's data center sits in the village of Endicott, the birthplace of IBM. Global AI runs a data center across two buildings there, including 1701 North Street, which IBM originally built; a nearby Bloom Energy fuel-cell system supplies it with an added 9.36 megawatts of power. The company claims it holds the largest cluster of Nvidia GB300 processors in New York, Data Center Dynamics reported. Both founders came out of IBM: co-founder John E. Kelly III created IBM's Watson and spent nearly 40 years at the company.

The county's biggest development fight is not over a data center. The Broome County Industrial Development Agency plans a technology park of more than 500 acres off Airport Road in the towns of Union and Maine, modeled on Onondaga County's White Pine park that drew Micron. The agency says it will support 7,000 jobs. "We look at this as a generational investment for Broome County," said its director, Stacey Duncan. Neighbors say they do not know what would be built there. "We still don't know who is planning to build over here. Are we going to have to worry about our water supplies, our wells?" said John Feehan. "If we had wanted to live in the city, we would have lived in the city," said Diane Sattler. "We moved out here for a reason."

At a packed Maine town board meeting, resident Bob Utter said: "There's been no transparency from the IDA ... This project is a ghost." The Town of Maine sued the agency, accusing it of buying property before environmental reviews were finished; according to the agency, a State Supreme Court judge rejected the suit. The public comment period on the draft environmental impact statement ended in May 2026, and the county is now preparing a final statement, Spectrum News reported.

Google has run a data center at 708 Lynhaven Drive in Lenoir since 2007, and in March 2026 it pledged $1 billion over two years to expand it, mostly to meet demand from AI and cloud services. A separate plan, "Project Cardinal," would add a $600 million expansion on about 60 acres next door, at 914 Virginia Street and 919 Fairview Drive. The city and county approved tax breaks for it in 2024; Google has five years to make the investment and said it has no confirmed timeline.

The Project Cardinal deal returns 50 percent of real property taxes and 85 percent of personal property taxes over 20 years, in exchange for 30 new full-time jobs. The city will supply extra water, with Google paying $6.8 million toward it, and closed part of Virginia Street for the company's security. With the March pledge, Google added a $2 million fund to help county residents make homes and schools more energy efficient.

What Google uses and employs here is partly secret. Under the 2024 agreement with the county and city, the number of workers is a "trade secret" and its energy, water and sewer use is confidential; the company has said 400 people work there. Google paid about $5.2 million in property taxes last year, nearly 10 percent of the county's total, in a county the state ranks among its most economically distressed.

Chatham County tried to stop data centers and lost the first round in court. On 11 February 2026, after a public hearing, the county commissioners approved a 12-month moratorium on development approvals for data centers, data processing facilities and cryptocurrency mining in unincorporated areas, lasting until 11 February 2027 or until new zoning rules are adopted. It applies even to web hosting and genome sequencing, WRAL reported. The developer it caught was Eco TIP West, which plans a 750-megawatt data center campus at Triangle Innovation Point West near Moncure, on land in the Moncure Megasite rezoned for heavy industry in 2018. Its manager is Kirk Bradley, chair of Sanford's Lee-Moore Capital and a member of the University of North Carolina Board of Governors.

Eco TIP sued on 23 April, saying it had spent more than $11 million and that in October 2025 the county had issued a zoning permit confirming a data center was a use "permitted by right" once water and sewer were in. It called the moratorium the product of "closed-door" discussions, and its lawyers called it "a legal trainwreck that should have never been approved, and never been applied, to take away Eco TIP's property rights in its project." In September 2026 Superior Court Judge John Morris ruled for the developer, finding "that there is no genuine issue as to any material fact and that Plaintiff is entitled to a judgment in its favor as a matter of law," and ordered the county to pay damages. The project can proceed; the moratorium still covers everything else. At least 30 North Carolina local governments have passed data center moratoria, NC Newsline noted, and it is unclear how the ruling will affect them.
/data-centers/united-states/north-caroli.unconfirmed: Two searches. The county's own moratorium release refused (403), so the public-hearing detail rests on the lawsuit and news reports. The amount of damages was not reported in the texts read. Whether the county will appeal was not found. The Carolina Journal account of the ruling was not read. Chatham County, Georgia's separate moratorium (WSAV, The Current) surfaced in searches and was excluded.

paragraphs: Durham County is not new to data centers. The county tax office counts 14, all but one built before 2000, most in Research Triangle Park; the largest is Dell's, at about 293,000 square feet, and CyrusOne runs a 242,000-square-foot facility near the park, the INDY reported. Planning Director Sara Young told commissioners some had never been recorded as data centers, since it isn't a use category in the ordinance. The city of Durham moved first, passing a 60-day moratorium in May 2026 that has since been extended and now runs to May 2027.

On August 24, 2026, county commissioners voted 4-1 for a nine-month moratorium to match, with exemptions for data centers under 100,000 square feet that use closed-loop cooling and no diesel backup generators. Commissioner Nida Allam cast the lone no vote, opposing those exemptions: "For me, in my perspective, a delay for a company of nine months is monetary. But the impact on folks' health and wellbeing, and financial stability, is going to last a lifetime." Her amendment requiring builders to disclose water use and fuel passed. Neuse Riverkeeper Samantha Krop warned, "Closed loop does not mean zero waste," and Commissioner Larissa Williamson said the county had "no enforcement powers over the electrical usage."

Richmond County is getting what North Carolina officials call the largest economic development project in state history: a $10 billion Amazon data center near Hamlet, now under construction. It will have 21 buildings of 200,000 square feet each and need about 1 gigawatt of power. Inside Climate News pieced together how it arrived: on March 19, 2025, county officials drafted a confidential purchase agreement with "Project Blue Marlin" for a 646-acre county-owned forest and a disused chicken farm, then rezoned the farm to heavy industrial two weeks later. An agreement dated April 3 granted a 50 percent property tax break on buildings and 65 percent on machinery over 20 years, for $1 billion of investment and 50 jobs; the public hearings drew no speakers, and no document disclosed that the land would become a data center.

Neighbors say nobody told them. "I don't recall any public hearing," said Lee Quick, who lives across the road. "No one informed me that it was coming." More than 200 people came to the state's July 2026 hearing on air permits for Amazon's generators and for 57 more diesel units Duke Energy will run as "bridge power" for a year until the transmission line is built. "It is shameful to sign away public trust while residents are left to ask basic questions about our energy, wells, water, wildlife and our health," said Shaun Ingram of the Richmond County Coalition for Justice and Black Empowerment. The state approved both permits, 645 generators in all. Amazon says the generators are for emergencies and testing only.

No new data center is proposed in Grand Forks County, County Administrator Tom Ford said in September 2026. The county already has two cryptocurrency mining sites in the city of Grand Forks. Core Scientific runs a 100-megawatt bitcoin mine in two beige warehouses at 5601 11th Ave. S., on the city's western edge south of the DeMers Avenue Amtrak station. Sundog Mining, a local startup, runs a shipping container of mining rigs at a Minnkota Power substation in the industrial park.

Core Scientific opened its site in November 2021, filed for bankruptcy 13 months later when crypto prices fell, and came out of it in January 2024. The Grand Forks Herald reported in 2024 that the site was valued at more than $7 million and will pay more than $100,000 a year in property tax once a five-year exemption ends in 2027. The city also earns a franchise fee on electricity: about $390,000 from Nodak Electric Cooperative in 2020, before the miners came, and $772,000 in 2023.

City leaders want AI data centers next. "We really hope ... that we can become that hub for really smart AI data centers," City Administrator Todd Feland said, and the city says it is talking with Minnkota, Nodak and Xcel Energy so residents do not pay higher rates. The county is writing its own rules first. "We want to develop or create a development policy for data centers, just like we do for wind turbines, just like we do for solar panel farms," Ford said. Commissioners saw a model ordinance in June covering permits, buffers and wastewater; no vote on it has been scheduled.

Stutsman County's one data center is Applied Digital's cryptocurrency hosting site about 7 miles north of Jamestown. No new data center is proposed in the county. On February 3, 2026, the County Commission unanimously adopted rules that keep any new data center at least 2 miles from any building and 3 miles from an existing data center.

The people living near the Applied Digital site shaped those rules. The first draft set a 1-mile setback, but when the county surveyed residents within 2 miles of the site, they reported problems with sound and light from it. "I thought, you see in those responses, it was very, very appropriate to put into the ordinance a 2-mile setback," said Tyler Perleberg, the county's zoning administrator, adding that some residents wanted it farther. The rules also require screening and security fencing, and may require road repair agreements during construction.

The county is also on the route of JETx, a high-voltage power line on 150-foot towers running 92 miles from a substation near Jamestown to one west of Ellendale, where Applied Digital is building an AI campus. State regulators granted the route permit in June 2026. Landowners had raised setbacks, eminent domain and "the potential for the line to be used for data centers." "We just never had a fair shake at any of this," said Lucas Wald of Edgeley. In July 2026 the North Dakota Supreme Court ruled that the townships and landowners who challenged the line's 2024 approval had no standing to do so.

Aligned Data Centers is building the first of four data center buildings at 2509 Hayes Avenue in Perkins Township, just south of Sandusky, on the site of a former auto parts plant. The company paid $52 million for the 129 acres in 2023, is spending more than $200 million on the first phase and planned to finish the first building this year. A second, larger proposal in Oxford Township, AVAIO Digital's Project Andromeda, has been tabled.

Perkins Township welcomed Aligned. Its trustees, the school board and the career center agreed to return 70% of the new property taxes to the project for 30 years and share the other 30%, and Aligned paid the township $325,000 up front. The first building is expected to create 18 permanent jobs by February 2027. "From my lens, as an educator, this has been a godsend," said Perkins Schools Superintendent Lonny Rivera.

Oxford Township was different. AVAIO proposed a 250-megawatt, four-building campus on 146 rural acres near the EHOVE Career Center. Hundreds came to the developers' meeting, many shouting objections, and yard signs went up along the roads. The township trustees then tabled the project, saying it was "not in the best interest" of the community. The developer plans to revisit it after the November 3, 2026, election.

Lawrence County's data center arrived without a public hearing. In December 2025 Strata Expanse, a company from The Woodlands, Texas, held a ribbon-cutting for an AI data center at 1476 County Road 1A near Hanging Rock, in Hamilton Township, with RAVEL and Supermicro as tenants and collaborators. The Lawrence County Economic Development Corporation sold it the land. Hamilton Township has no zoning, and because Strata Expanse asked for no tax breaks, there was no public comment period, the corporation's executive director, Bill Dingus, said. The company says it will generate its own power from solar and hydrogen, cool with geothermal instead of water, and create 200 to 300 jobs. Dingus said he had not seen its power numbers but had seen its business plan.

Ironton has no say over the site, but its council held a special meeting on January 8, 2026. "It basically is probably a moot discussion because you know there's just no places in Ironton where a data center could ever go," Dingus said. Councilman Jacob Hock said the meeting "raised more concerns than it resolved," adding that Dingus "seems to be pretty ill-informed about data centers and their potential impact on the community." "I don't believe that 16 jobs are worth the possibility," said Councilman Chris Haney. A petition, "Stop the AI data centers in Lawrence County, Ohio," drew more than 5,000 signatures, and Ironton adopted a moratorium on new data centers on February 12, 2026.

At a May 2026 meeting the county commissioners debated whether to take over zoning from the townships. "I think it is unchartered waters that the county would enter into countywide zoning," said Commissioner DeAnna Holliday; Commissioner Colton Copley called the idea an overstep unless the trustees asked for it.

Hood River County's one data center proposal ended in a recall. On February 3, 2023 the Port of Cascade Locks signed a memorandum of understanding with Roundhouse Digital Infrastructure, a startup few had heard of, that could have led to a 25-year lease on Flex 6, a vacant port building on the Columbia River, plus 10 adjacent acres for a second building. The port commission approved it 4-1. Roundhouse aimed to invest $40 million in the first building and $60 million in the second, targeting "niche government and energy industry" clients. The port needed a tenant: it owed nearly $6 million on Flex 6 and was paying more than $50,000 a month on the loans after its previous tenant left in 2022.

Columbia Insight then looked into Roundhouse's chief executive, Stephen D. King, and found more than $1 million owed to former partners from an earlier Hood River venture that was never built. "The state of Oregon looked into it and found that there was no issue," King said, adding that he meant to repay those he owed out of the data center. "If the whole entire city said they wanted the data center, by God, I would back them," said Hood River dentist Jerald Kyle House, who had helped develop the plan with King. "But things aren't adding up with Roundhouse."

Power was the other fear. The city supplies about 4.5 megawatts to homes and businesses, up to 7 in winter; King's figures put the two buildings at about 10 to 11. The Bonneville Power Administration confirmed it would charge the city a higher rate partly because of the data center. "The whole thing is a gamble," said Mayor Cathy Fallon. "I don't want Cascade Locks holding the bag." Residents organized: in May 2023 two critics of the proposal defeated two incumbent port commissioners, and on June 13 voters recalled two port commissioners, including the port president, two to one. On July 20 the port and Roundhouse jointly announced they were discontinuing the project, saying "the level of community support required for its successful implementation was not achieved."

Bradford County's largest data center plan comes with its own gas-fired power plant. KDI Wyalusing Power, an affiliate of New Fortress Energy working under its Klondike Digital Infrastructure division, is developing a large data center on a 335-acre property along Route 6 in Wyalusing Township, about 20 miles from Towanda. The plan calls for eight natural gas turbines making up to 218 megawatts of power for the data center; state regulators approved it on October 9, 2025. The turbines will not connect to the regional power grid, and the data center's future operator is not yet named.

The county now has its own rules. On July 9, 2026, the three commissioners unanimously added data center standards to the county's land-use ordinance - the rules that govern how big buildings and lots can be. New projects must keep a 200-foot buffer next to homes, put up 8-foot security fencing around substations, and post a bond worth at least 125% of the cost to tear the site down if it closes. No formal application has been filed yet, but county planning director Duane Naugle named two possible areas: about 200 acres in Wysox Township and up to 400 acres in Asylum Township.

Asylum Township resident Sue Corie said consultants were asking owners to sign listing agreements and proposing "to take the whole interior of Echo Beach Road." Smaller landowners who don't want to sell, she said, are "afraid of what the impact is going to be if they remain." Commissioner Daryl Miller said data centers are "no different" from other industrial development, and that he opposes tax breaks for them. A separate cryptocurrency mine proposal in Wysox Township, from Soltier LLC, was withdrawn on June 22, 2026.

Bucks County's biggest data center project is planned for the old U.S. Steel site in Falls Township. Amazon Web Services announced in June 2025 that its data center campus, at 1 Ben Fairless Drive in the Keystone Trade Center that NorthPoint Development is redeveloping, is part of a $20 billion investment across Pennsylvania. It is the only Bucks County project in the governor's fast-track permitting program, and Governor Josh Shapiro visited the site in August 2025. The 1-million-square-foot campus is under construction and connected to the electricity grid.

State Representative Jim Prokopiak defended the site choice: "It's better to have some here where it has less of a negative impact on a community than someplace else [such as] next to a residential neighborhood." Ginny Marcille-Kerslake of Food and Water Watch said such projects are "primarily creating short-term construction jobs." Shapiro's office estimates the $20 billion of Amazon projects statewide will bring 1,250 permanent jobs.

Upper Bucks has its first application. West Rockhill Township's supervisors adopted a data center ordinance on April 15, 2026, after residents called earlier drafts "rushed." The final version sets a 400-foot setback from homes, a 35-foot height limit, a 35-acre minimum lot, and requires closed-loop cooling, which recycles water instead of releasing it as vapor. In July 2026, a sketch plan arrived for a data center at 215 Cathill Road seeking a special exception from the township's Zoning Hearing Board. "We don't yet have a land development application," said township solicitor David Keightly.

Centre County has no data center proposal, and its townships are writing rules before one arrives. College Township was the first in the Centre Region to act. Its council made data centers a conditional use, where they had been permitted like any industrial development, giving it about 120 days to review a proposal and room to attach conditions such as buffers against light and noise and energy and water standards, StateCollege.com and WJAC reported. "It's also not a solicitation of these types of facilities. We're prepared should one end up on our doorstep," said Assistant Township Manager Mike Bloom. The change was aimed at state Senate Bill 939, which Bloom said could "hamstring local municipalities" by cutting the review period to 30 days and barring special conditions.

Not everyone agreed. At a February 2026 Centre Regional Planning Commission meeting, Patton Township Supervisor Bill Burnett called the plan "a very bad idea." "You have a lot more issues and a lot more problems with data centers coming into an area, and it doesn't support the number of jobs that people think it does," he said. College Township Councilman Eric Bernier replied that Burnett had "completely misunderstood" it: "Without this action, we got nothing." The county planning director, Ray Stolinas, said the county was urging townships to keep data centers in industrial zones and away from homes, because of noise and vibration. By June 2026 Snow Shoe Township had sent the county a zoning amendment, and Ferguson, Rush and Half Moon townships were looking at theirs, he said.
/data-centers/united-states/pennsylvania.unconfirmed: Three searches. No data center proposal in Centre County was found. The date of College Township's council vote is not in the StateCollege.com text read (it says only 'Thursday'); it came after the 5 February 2026 regional planning meeting and before WJAC's 3 June 2026 report. Whether Snow Shoe's amendment or the other townships' changes were adopted was not found.

paragraphs: Cherokee County's data center deal was sealed before residents got a chance to weigh in. In June 2025 the County Council finalized tax incentives for Cielo Digital Infrastructure, a Texas company owned by Arroyo Investors, which pledged $2.1 billion for a campus of four buildings, about 400,000 square feet each, plus a substation, on Ford Road east of Gaffney. Cielo says the site could hold up to 300 megawatts of power and expects to open by the end of 2028 with 30 jobs. Ken Moon, executive director of the county's development board, would not disclose the size or length of the tax breaks, saying "the paperwork has not been finalized."

Cielo describes itself only as a site finder. "We identify and negotiate sites ready for data center development," its website says. It would not tell the Gazette whether it plans to keep the site or build for other companies; it earlier sold a Culpeper County, Virginia, campus to Edgecore. Ken Moon told WSPA the project is "a storage facility for data," not an energy-intensive AI center, and that the county is requiring Cielo to "bring their own power" using closed-loop cooling systems.

Residents have pushed back since January 2026. "This is not opposition to growth," said Allison Tracy. "It is a request for transparency in responsible decision-making." "The idea that we need a data center in Cherokee County to be on the forefront of progress and growth is nonsense," said Courtney Smith. Gaffney adopted new zoning rules for data centers on January 6, 2026, and resident Denise Maista has asked the council to appoint district liaisons to keep residents informed.

Brazoria County's only operating data center is small, and its neighbors say they can feel it. Giga Energy's 17-megawatt, air-cooled site on 6 acres just outside the city of Brazoria began operating in March 2026, next to about 10 families, The Facts reported. "Since it started, it hasn't shut off, and the noise is constant, 24/7, and is very annoying," said Wesley Burnett, who lives a couple of hundred feet from its fence. The site sits in Brazoria's extraterritorial jurisdiction, where the city has no say. Giga told Houston Public Media the site is owned by a Fort Worth investment group, that it had commissioned a sound study and would build sound walls this fall, and that the site "is fully compliant with all local laws and regulations."

Much bigger projects are coming. Nightpeak Energy of Oakland plans the Old Ocean data centers on a 158-acre site off FM 524 near Sweeny, powered by its own 310-megawatt gas plant, Bulldog Power; The Facts put the investment at $3 billion. In March 2026 commissioners voted 5-0 against the reinvestment zone its four 100% tax abatements needed; the campus could begin energizing as soon as 2027. "I would bet you money they do this project, and we can't do a damn thing about it," said County Judge Matt Sebesta.

CleanSpark announced in January that it would develop a 447-acre data center site near Angleton, with a 300-megawatt load expandable to 600. On June 9 the court unanimously passed a resolution opposing any data center that does not safeguard the grid, water, farmland and public infrastructure, and asking the Legislature for setbacks and local authority. Sebesta called it "not worth the paper it is printed on" unless residents went to Austin: "They don't need tax abatements. We're not going to give them tax abatements. They're still gonna come." Alvin's council passed its own resolution opposing data centers in city limits.

Brazos County's data center is a four-year-late building on Texas A&M's RELLIS Campus. The county approved a tax abatement with RELLIS Campus Data and Research Center LLC in April 2022 for a project on a 25-acre tract of A&M System land. Construction was meant to finish in fall 2022, but Winter Storm Uri set it back, ground was broken only in 2024, and in November 2025 the developer filed for Chapter 11 after a financial partner reportedly withdrew. ThisWay Global, Inc. took the nearly finished building out of bankruptcy.

Bryan's council approved a replacement abatement unanimously on June 26, 2026, giving the new owner a September deadline to begin construction; no report has said whether construction started by that deadline. The new terms are smaller: the agreement puts the project's value at about $298 million and requires at least five full-time jobs with a $518,000 payroll, against the $700 million and at least 100 jobs the city was told of in April 2025. On August 18, 2026, county commissioners voted 4-0 to transfer their own agreement, which taxes the project at 50% for 10 years and in full for 30 more. "Should [ThisWay Global] fail, the county is not left really on the hook for any of this," said Commissioner Chuck Konderla.

College Station said no to a bigger one. On September 11, 2025, its council voted unanimously, shortly before midnight, against selling about 200 acres in the Midtown Business Park to Priority Power Management for $30 million; more than 75 people had registered to speak and a petition had 5,047 signatures. Site plans called the scheme Project Aggie and sketched a possible 600-megawatt campus. "It's been a 'no' for 11 months, and I'm still a hard no today," said Councilmember Bob Yancy.

Grimes County has one data center project on record: Cipher Digital's Milsing site, which the company lists in its pipeline at 500 megawatts of power with a completion target of 2030 or later. No formal application for it has been filed with the county. Rumors that a separate company, Geronimo Power, held a contract on about 800 acres for a possible data center drew resident pushback starting in March 2026, KBTX reported.

Bedias residents packed county meetings over water. "Water is a precious, precious resource," said resident Jodi Pistler, and Karen Shiver of Bedias said she was "most concerned about our water." County Judge Joe Fauth said in May that no proposals were on file: "rumors are just that. They're rumors." He added that the county has little power over a landowner's sale: "when you live in the county, the restrictions that the court has put on landowners are very few."

The county's tax fight over a different project set the tone. On June 3, 2026 it created a 21,000-acre reinvestment zone and approved a 35-year, 100 percent tax abatement for the SpaceX-linked Terafab chip plant at the Gibbons Creek Reservoir, with $20 million a year in payments to the county, The Eagle reported. In July, Fauth brought a resolution backing "responsible data center and associated technologies development" and opposing high-volume water cooling in dry areas, but the court tabled it for more public comment. "We're not going out and soliciting these companies," Fauth said. "They've all come to us." Resident Bobbie Jo Swaffer told the court, "One thing is undeniable. Public trust was damaged."

Leon County, a rural county of about 17,000 people, faces two large data center proposals. The first is Belltown Power's Kahla Project, a 1,500-megawatt data center on private property in Marquez, KBTX reported in December 2025. "They said it was going to be a $15 billion project," County Judge Byron Ryder said at a January 2026 town hall attended by nearly 200 residents, adding that Belltown hoped to build half in 2026 and half in 2027. He was frank about the county's power: "We can make it difficult for them, and we probably will make it difficult for them, but we really can't make, we can't keep them from coming if they want to come." Ryder said the county would not give the project a tax abatement, and officials said they would form a 391 sub-regional planning commission to bring agencies together. "We'll make a stand until they run bulldozers through the pastures," said resident Daniel McCoslin.

The second is a data center proposed by Crusoe Technologies. On July 13, 2026, after more than 20 residents signed up to speak about the planned data centers, water use and tax abatements, the commissioners court voted to reject Crusoe's application for a tax abatement and designation of a reinvestment zone "as submitted", the court's minutes show. At the same meeting the court voted 4-1 to approve new tax abatement guidelines and criteria drafted by Commissioner Kyle Workman, subject to the county attorney's review. It formally adopted the guidelines, criteria and resolution on July 27 after a public hearing.

Lubbock County has one data center under construction and one rejected so far. TeraWulf is building a 168-megawatt data center in Abernathy for artificial-intelligence company Fluidstack. In January 2026, Lubbock's planning commission voted against rezoning 936 acres off Northeast Loop 289 for a separate project by Texas Solar Works, which withdrew before it reached the city council. Since then the county has moved toward new rules for any future large data center.

Residents in north and east Lubbock opposed the Texas Solar Works rezoning, saying they already lived with heavy industry. "Gas turbines, pollution, noise. No, absolutely not," said Fabian Mata. In July, a local station reported that the Lubbock Economic Development Alliance had approved a deal with CORVA for "Project Infrared," a 50,000-square-foot inference data center in East Lubbock that LEDA's John Osborne said was "not a done deal" until it secured a grid connection through Lubbock Power and Light. A petition with nearly 2,500 signatures sought an 18-month moratorium, and at a July council meeting some residents threatened recalls: "You can vote with us today, the people that voted and put you in place, or you can watch us do a recall," said Phyllis Gant.

In August, county commissioners passed a non-binding resolution, 4-1, asking large projects to disclose water and power use; County Judge Curtis Parrish voted no, saying it should target data centers specifically. In September, the planning commission delayed proposed rules on a 500-foot setback, water limits and a power study, and the city council voted 5-2 to start the process for a 90-day moratorium on large data centers while staff draft permanent rules.

Iron County approved its first big data center just after pausing all new ones. On June 4, 2026, the county Planning Commission unanimously granted a conditional use permit to Pronghorn Development LLC for the Antelope Data Center, on about 640 acres along Antelope Springs Road west of Cedar City: up to five buildings and an on-site natural gas plant of up to 1.5 gigawatts, built over 8 to 10 years, St. George News reported. KSL put its built-out value at an estimated $30 billion.

About 350 people came to a March hearing, many worried about water in the fully allocated Escalante Valley basin; the developer's documents projected a closed-loop system with a one-time fill of about 2.6 million gallons and about 3.13 acre-feet a year after that. The permit carries 62 conditions. "This thing has more conditions of approval than probably everything that's ever gone through this commission combined," said commissioner Dennis Gray. Zoning administrator Terry Palmer said officials had little choice: "as long as they can satisfy our ordinance, then yes, the Planning Commission has limited discretion." After the vote, attendees held up paper plates reading "appeal."

In late May the county commission barred processing of new or incomplete data center, data center power plant and solar applications for 180 days, but Antelope's application had already been deemed complete and is vested under the old rules, county planner Brett Hamilton said. A second project, BrightNight's Red Butte Energy and Data Center Campus, is planned on private land about 7 miles northeast of Newcastle to grow from 300 megawatts to as much as 1.5 gigawatts with gas, solar and battery storage on a footprint of about 2,600 acres.

"Ultimately, we've got to find a customer that wants to build their facilities here," said BrightNight's Erik Ellis. Residents raised concerns at its May open house in Cedar City, which The Salt Lake Tribune headlined as facing "overwhelming opposition from locals." In September the county was drafting a new ordinance for data centers, gas plants, solar and battery storage.

In 2024 Campbell County made data centers a by-right use on heavy industrial land, "to better market some properties that we had," Concord supervisor Matt Cline said. In October 2025 the Board of Supervisors voted 5-2 against Mesh Capital LLC's request to lift a proffer on about 57 acres at U.S. 460 and Cabin Field Road in the Concord District, where it had planned three buildings of about 450,000 square feet, Data Center Dynamics reported. Mesh then submitted a scaled-down plan that the zoning administrator found in general compliance with the existing proffered site plan, needing no rezoning. "A lot of folks thought that we defeated data centers. That was really not the case," said Ashby Smith, who lives beside the property and petitioned the board to review the decision. The applicant's end user is unknown, and Mesh did not answer WSET.

On December 2, 2025 the board voted 5-2 for an emergency ordinance ending by-right data centers, after residents said they feared other developers would flock to the county. On January 6, 2026 it voted 4-3 to extend the emergency rules for 120 days rather than make them permanent. At a Lynchburg summit that month, Vince Barnett, data center industry leader at the Virginia Economic Development Partnership, said operators seek by-right zoning "to mitigate risk." On May 5, 2026 the board voted unanimously to make data centers special-use-permit only. "I move that we make data centers special use permit only," said Cline. The Cabin Field Road project and a second one on Mt. Athos Road, where talks had stalled since concept plans in February 2024, were proposed before the change and remain grandfathered.

Tucker County learned of its data center from a legal notice. In March 2025 resident Pamela Moe spotted a small notice in the Parsons Advocate: Fundamental Data, a Virginia-based company, had applied to the Department of Environmental Protection for an air permit for its "Ridgeline Facility," an off-grid natural gas power plant between the mountain towns of Thomas and Davis, West Virginia Watch reported. Company representatives later told The Wall Street Journal it could be "among the largest data center campuses in the world," spanning 10,000 acres across Tucker and Grant counties. The application, heavily redacted, described gas turbines with heat recovery steam generators and three 10-million-gallon diesel tanks, 66 feet tall, for backup. It was filed the same day House Bill 2014 was introduced; that law lets high impact data centers override local zoning ordinances. "Honestly, I feel like if this happens, it will destroy this place," said Nikki Forrester, who lives near Davis and is among the residents who formed Tucker United.

The DEP approved the permit in August 2025, classing the plant as a minor source. "There's no other power plant of the equivalent size that has been approved as a minor source of the contaminants," Forrester said. In 2026 the Department of Commerce said it had found no Tucker County property owned by Fundamental Data, and the county assessor's map listed the permitted parcels under Western Pocahontas Properties. The company, which said its plans were still "conceptual," then produced a heavily redacted July 2024 agreement to buy 291 acres, which the DEP in August accepted as proof of site control. "Private is not the same thing as secret," said company representative Casey Chapman. In September the Intermediate Court of Appeals dismissed two appeals by Tucker United and conservation groups on jurisdiction, without ruling on the merits. "We are disappointed that, after all this time, no court has heard the merits," said Olivia Miller of the West Virginia Highlands Conservancy.
/data-centers/united-states/west-virgini.unconfirmed: Three searches. The plant's capacity (785 MW in a search summary) was not confirmed in text read raw and is not given. WBOY refused both of its stories. The Wall Street Journal story was not read; the 10,000-acre figure is as West Virginia Watch reported it. Speaker Roger Hanshaw's representation of the developer, raised by Miller, was not independently confirmed. The appeal's next step before the state Supreme Court was not found.

paragraphs: Upper Austria is getting Google's first data center in Austria, on farmland at Kronstorf in the Linz-Land district. Google bought the site in 2008 and left it undeveloped for 18 years; of the roughly 70 hectares it acquired, about 20 were later given back, SOLID reported. Ground was broken on 23 April 2026 with Governor Thomas Stelzer present, and the first phase, of up to 150 megawatts, is due to open in 2027 with about 100 permanent jobs. In July Google filed plans for further phases covering the whole 50-hectare site, up to 500 megawatts in all according to the company. If fully built, it could use as much electricity each year as up to 900,000 households, the grid operator Austrian Power Grid estimated; the province has about 676,000, ORF reported. Profil reported that Google holds a grid access commitment for up to 3.5 terawatt-hours a year, about a quarter of Upper Austria's use. Cooling will draw groundwater from wells near the Enns, and the water permit lets Google discharge up to 5.8 million litres a day of warmed water into the river at up to 30°C.

Every party on Kronstorf's council voted for the project, but resistance grew once the expansion was public. More than 200 people demonstrated at the site on 17 July, ORF reported, and later about 20 activists climbed a building on the site to demand a halt to construction. Data centers are not covered by Austria's environmental impact assessment law, so the project has had no single review. "Projects of this size should be subjected to an environmental impact assessment before any approval," said the province's Green environment councillor, Stefan Kaineder. Harald Müllner of the Kronstorf citizens' initiative said: "Austria cannot simply conjure up the electricity." Economy councillor Markus Achleitner called Google's arrival "a clear international vote of confidence in our province." A provincial law in force since 1 April 2026 requires data centers above one megawatt to use their waste heat where technically and economically possible; Google says talks with possible users are under way.
/data-centers/austria/upper-austria/.unconfirmed: Three searches. Quotes are translated from German. An IT vendor blog's figures of 400 MW for the first phase and 1 GW in all conflict with Google's 150 MW and 500 MW as reported by ORF and SOLID and are not used. The investment amount is only 'in the billions' as reported, and is not confirmed by Google. The date of the activists' protest is not in ORF's text; it came after the expansion permit filings at the end of July. Microsoft's three Austrian data centers are in Lower Austria, not Upper Austria.

paragraphs: Buenos Aires province's largest data center plan is at Bahía Blanca. Pampa Energía has agreed to supply 30 MW for the first stage of a data center in the city's free trade zone, and Pablo Amarelle, general manager of the zone's concessionaire, said it had begun building an IT park and expected final investment agreements by late 2026, Reuters reported. The park covers 54 hectares and is described as the first data center project in an Argentine free trade zone. Bahía Blanca competes for such projects with Patagonia: in Neuquén, Pampa is studying a data center of up to 500 MW beside its Loma de la Lata plant, and Sur Energy, OpenAI's partner in Stargate Argentina, has said it is working with Neuquén to find a site. Pampa's commercial director for electricity, Ruben Turienzo, said investors first want smaller pilots of 20 MW to 40 MW before expanding, and that the electrical infrastructure for 500 MW would cost almost $900 million. No published report describes local opposition to data centers in the province.

The province is bidding from a small base. Argentina had 13 operating data centers above 1 megawatt in May 2026, with 32 MW in total, 71% of it in the City of Buenos Aires and 29% in the province, according to the internet chamber CABASE as reported by BNamericas. Most are between 1 and 6.5 MW, serving colocation, cloud and interconnection. "There is a historic opportunity," said CABASE president Ariel Graizer, who said about 14 hyperscalers were weighing Argentina.
/data-centers/argentina/buenos-aires-pro.unconfirmed: Three searches. The Reuters story was read through a syndicated copy. The IT park's 54-hectare size and free-zone details come from a Cushman & Wakefield article that interviews the developer and the power supplier, a promotional source; only those facts are taken from it. No customer for the Bahía Blanca park has been named. Operating data centers in the province, such as EdgeConneX's in Pilar, are known from listing pages and were not described in news read. Claro's new data center is in the City of Buenos Aires, not the province.

paragraphs: The Valparaíso Region's main data center is Scala Data Centers' campus at Curauma, about 56 miles from Santiago, and Scala is expanding it. Its first building, SSCLCR01, opened in August 2023: a $65 million, 5-megawatt data center built in 10 months and fully leased to one large unnamed cloud customer. Scala says the campus could grow to about 30 megawatts, and the property firm Colliers listed the Curauma expansion among projects under construction in Chile in 2026.

Scala says the building is air-cooled and uses no water, a point that matters in a country where data center water use is contested. The company picked Curauma partly for Google's Humboldt undersea cable, which the regional coastal-use commission has approved to land at Santo Domingo, in the region, and link it to Sydney, Australia. The cable is due to be laid in the last quarter of 2026 and to start carrying traffic from 2028. Most of Chile's data centers, and its data center disputes, are in the Santiago region.

The biggest data center proposed in Region Zealand is on Lolland, where the developer Stender Innovation wants to build a campus of up to 1,000 megawatts of power on about 114 hectares east of Rødby. A majority of Lolland's council voted for it, though several members opposed it, and the public comment period on the municipality's first planning paper closes September 29, 2026. Next, the municipality drafts a plan change and a local plan, which go out for eight weeks of public comment before a final vote.

About 100 people came to a public meeting in Rødby on September 15. "I think it seems exciting and interesting," said Anders Ploug, a landowner next to the site. Stender expects 390 to 450 permanent jobs, which Karina Tyron Sahler of Nakskov doubts: "I think it's very drastic. It's a huge intervention, and it will matter for all of Lolland. Good farmland is destroyed."

In Faxe municipality, an application proposes a data center on about 203 hectares of Bregentved estate land between the southern motorway and the Køge–Haslev railway, with about 120 jobs in its first phase. "It is a big project, which we must assess thoroughly," Mayor Mikkel Dam said.

Microsoft already runs two of the three sites of its Denmark East cloud region here, in Køge and Roskilde; the third is in Høje-Taastrup. Microsoft says the sites use no water for cooling and plans to send waste heat from Køge to local district heating.

Suez Governorate's data center plans sit in the Sokhna Industrial Zone of the Suez Canal Economic Zone (SCZone). The main one is the Kemet Data Center, named after the ancient name for Egypt. In September 2024 Intro Technology, part of the Egyptian conglomerate Intro Group, signed a memorandum of understanding with Oman Data Park, a joint venture of the Omani telco Omantel, for a $450 million, partly solar-powered data center on 80,000 square metres, to be built in two phases, Data Center Dynamics reported. In November 2024 SCZone signed a land usufruct agreement giving Intro a plot in Sokhna, according to a cabinet statement reported by Enterprise. Intro told Prime Minister Moustafa Madbouly the project would grow to four phases of 20 MW each, raising its cost to $1 billion, and Madbouly said it should be complete by the end of 2030. Sterling and Wilson Data Center is to be the engineering, procurement and construction contractor.

The project is aimed at exporting cloud services to the Middle East and Africa. Egypt's data centers have historically been concentrated in Cairo, DCD noted, and Cairo, Alexandria and SCZone are now emerging as focal points for hyperscale and colocation facilities under the government's Digital Egypt strategy, Arab Finance reported. "A single data center can consume as much power as an entire industrial zone," said Ahmed Yehia Hegazy of the National Telecommunications Regulatory Authority, adding that cooling "is achieved primarily through water." In April 2026 SCZone reported $20 million of new industrial and technology investment in Ain Sokhna, none of it described as a data center.
/data-centers/egypt/suez-governorate/.unconfirmed: Three searches. No report of construction starting at Kemet was found; the latest reporting read is from November 2024. A proposed hyperscale data center and AI zone with HEKA Insights and a US developer alliance, reported by Amwal Al Ghad, has no stated location and is not included. Ahram Online refused its story.

paragraphs: Google plans a data center at Otanmäki in Kajaani, part of the €13 billion it announced in September 2026 for sites in Kajaani, Vaala, Muhos and Hamina. Kajaani's council has approved a 1,870-hectare master plan for Otanmäki–Humpinsuo that includes land owned by Google's Finnish company, Tuike Finland; the next step is a detailed plan for about 392 hectares east of Otanmäki. Google says permits can be sought once the environmental impact assessment is finished.

A week after the announcement, the Finnish Association for Nature Conservation accused Google of suspected illegal clear-cutting at Otanmäki and Muhos. "Either this is gross incompetence by Google's Finnish project company, Tuike Finland Oy, or gross disregard for Finnish law, or at worst both," said its chair, Hanna Halmeenpää. Google says the trees were felled fully in line with the Forest Act. The state Permit and Supervision Authority has asked Kajaani, Muhos and Tuike Finland for explanations; "all the inquiries are unfinished," said its unit head, Sari Myllyoja.

Two other projects are already being built. The trading firm XTX Markets is building a 22.5-megawatt data center about 5 kilometers from the town center, due in 2026, and plans four more on the same site, an investment it says could top €1 billion; it says it will give its waste heat away free. At Renforsin Ranta, a former paper machine hall is becoming the home of the LUMI-AI supercomputer; it was topped out on September 3 and is due to open at the end of 2027.

Bordeaux's plan for a giant AI data center has lost its site. BXIA, backed by the developer Nouvelles Fonctions Urbaines and the fund manager Osae Partners, proposed a €3 billion campus of five data centers and a supercomputer, 250 megawatts of computer power with a grid connection of up to 380 megawatts, on about 19 hectares of parking lots at the Parc des Expositions in Bordeaux-Lac. On September 10, 2026, the new mayor and metropolitan president, Thomas Cazenave, said: "I do not want these mega data centers on the parking lots of the Parc des Expositions."

Cazenave has not ruled BXIA out. He says several already-developed sites have been identified and talks with the backers continue; no new site has been made public. The metropolitan council had voted on January 30, 2026, under the previous mayor, to open negotiations on the Bordeaux-Lac site.

At Gauriaguet, near Libourne, the developer Altarea is designing a campus of logistics buildings and an AI data center on about 40 hectares, with permission for a 400-megawatt grid connection; so far only a building permit application has been filed. "The town needs financial means," said Mayor Alain Montagon, who expects about 300 jobs. Valérie Guinaudie, who chairs the Grand Cubzaguais community of towns, noted the town had water supply trouble in a late-May heat wave: "If a big water user arrives, will it be able to share this resource?"
In Pessac, a month-long public inquiry was held on a data center of more than 8,000 square meters. Equinix already runs a data center in Bordeaux, BX1.

Odisha's biggest data center proposal is the Adani Group's: a 1-gigawatt AI data center worth Rs 1 trillion, for which it has asked the state for about 250 acres, with Cuttack named as the tentative site. State officials told Business Standard on August 3, 2026, that the proposal was "under detailed evaluation" for its land, power, water and connectivity needs. Once its incentives are settled, it goes to the high-level clearance authority headed by the chief minister.

Bhubaneswar has the rest. On July 24, 2026, HCLTech signed an agreement with the state and the AI startup Sarvam for its first AI data center, in a planned Odisha Sovereign AI Park, with a planned outlay of Rs 14,257 crore that includes state money. The Reserve Bank of India's Rs 169 crore data center at Info Valley is nearing completion, the state is building a Rs 266.48 crore State Data Centre 2.0, and Adani holds a separate agreement for an Rs 800 crore data center. Zoho is building a Rs 306 crore center in Khordha.

The worry is power and water. Odisha had about 9,118 megawatts of installed power capacity in November 2025, and a 1-gigawatt campus running around the clock would use roughly a fifth of the state's yearly electricity, a columnist wrote in The Statesman. "The Mahanadi is already a contested river, and the state's agriculture depends on the same basins," he wrote. "MoUs are announcements; megawatts, aquifers and trained engineers are constraints."

Nairobi holds 15 of Kenya's 19 data centers and more than 80% of the country's data center power, Capacity reported, and several operators are expanding. Digital Realty runs two buildings, NBO1 and NBO2, at Langata South Road and LRC Road; the second opened in September 2026 and added 6.4 megawatts of power, Business Daily reported. iXAfrica, whose NBOX1 campus is designed for 22.5 megawatts, has financing for a 20-megawatt expansion and has agreed to buy 11 acres for a second Nairobi campus.

Africa Data Centres, part of Cassava Technologies, is building a second Nairobi facility of up to 20 megawatts and is securing land for a third, more than $200 million in all. Airtel broke ground in early August 2026 on its Nxtra data center at Tatu City, planned at 44 megawatts in two phases, with completion set for July 2027. In January 2026 iXAfrica was chosen to host Oracle's first public cloud region in Kenya.

Power is the limit. Kenya's grid totals about 3,000 megawatts and already struggles at peak times, Dawan reported. Explaining why the Microsoft and G42 project at Olkaria, in Nakuru County, was paused, President William Ruto said in Nairobi: "To switch on that one data centre, we would need to shut off power for half the country."

Mombasa has two small data centers running and one large proposal. Digital Realty operates MBA1 and MBA2; the larger, MBA2, is on Kongoni Road off Beach Road. The big plan is Hercules, a $1.5 billion (Sh194 billion) AI data center proposed by the Greek company Amaco Energy Group, which is still seeking government approval and has named Dongo Kundu and Kilindini, near the port, as possible sites.

Amaco says Hercules would not draw on Kenya's power grid. In September it announced a deal to put GE Vernova gas turbines on a floating power barge fueled by liquefied natural gas, which would power and cool the center. The company has not said how much power the center would use, when it would be built or who its customers would be. Its chief executive, Theodore Theodoropoulos, met ICT Cabinet Secretary William Kabogo in August, Business Daily reported.

The coast matters because it is where Kenya's internet comes ashore: more than 95% of the country's international traffic runs through Mombasa, Dawan reported. Dawan warned that a foreign-owned site making its own power could become "a rich digital enclave on Kenyan soil" unless Kenya insists on local ownership, training and data rules. Hercules still needs a confirmed site, financing and government approval before any building starts.

The State of Mexico's best-known data center sits in the industrial corridor north of Mexico City. Scala Data Centers built its first Mexican site, SMEXTP01, in Tepotzotlán: an $80 million, 5-megawatt building of about 13,200 square meters (142,130 square feet), signed to a large cloud client before it opened and scheduled to start running at the end of 2023.

Space and power are getting tight. The Cuautitlán-Tultitlán-Tepotzotlán corridor had only 4.2% of its industrial space free in mid-2026 and almost no large plots left, pushing new building north toward Huehuetoca and Zumpango, the property platform Spot2.mx reported. For data centers, it said, "the decision criterion is no longer the available square meter, but megawatts" (translated from Spanish), and Toluca is gaining ground because of its high-voltage lines while the grid in the core of the metro area is saturated.

Østfold has three large data center plans, none yet approved. In Våler, Google has applied for 480 megawatts of grid power for a possible data center at Gylderåsen, but says it has not decided to build. In Sarpsborg, DC Sarpsborg, a company in which the municipality holds a large stake, plans a very large data center on about 2,152 decares (530 acres) of mostly forest at Hasle. In Halden, the paper company Norske Skog and Green Mountain signed a letter of intent to explore a data center at the Saugbrugs mill, which is being rezoned.

"We have not made any investment decision yet. We have not decided whether we will build a data center there; it depends on whether we get access to power," said Sondre Ronander of Google Norway (translated from Norwegian). In Sarpsborg, Red Party group leader Jan Petter Bastøe said: "We are very critical of this." Mayor Magnus Arnesen said the skepticism rests on a one-sided picture of data centers, and zoning work has begun.

Red Party MPs Remi Sølvberg and Sofie Marhaug want a halt to new data centers until Norway has a licensing system. "Now data centers make up 50 percent of the queue at Statnett," Marhaug said on a visit to the Våler forest where Google may build.

Oman is selling itself as a smaller, neutral alternative to the Gulf's AI giants, built on its subsea cables. The country hosts one of the Middle East's highest concentrations of international cable landings, and Salalah in the south is becoming a hub: Equinix and the state-controlled telco Omantel opened the carrier-neutral SN1 data center there, Equinix's second in Oman after MC1 in Muscat, with direct fibre between the two. "By next year, we plan to land multiple subsea cables in Salalah," said Omantel's chief executive, Talal Al Mamari. Omantel, majority owned by the Oman Investment Authority, has since announced a further Salalah data center, and Meta's Daraja cable from Kenya is to land there too. Other operators include Ooredoo, Oman Data Park and Cloud Acropolis.

Royal Decree 50/2026 created an Artificial Intelligence Special Zone in Muscat, on about 104,000 square metres near the Civil Aviation Authority headquarters by Muscat International Airport, targeting AI, semiconductors, robotics and data centers with tax incentives and full foreign ownership, the Oman Observer and Computer Weekly reported. The special zones authority's board is to appoint the entity that will develop and run the zone, and a roadmap for it is being prepared. On May 18, 2026, five companies from Oman, the UAE and Italy signed an agreement for a 150 MW "green" hyperscale AI data center, Data Center Dynamics reported, and the state-backed clean energy firm O-Green says it is targeting more than 200 MW of AI-ready data center capacity across Oman, Spain and other markets by 2028, tied to a planned 2.7 GW solar, wind and battery project at Duqm and Mahout. Not everyone is convinced. Muscat did not make the top 100 of Counterpoint's 2025 AI cities index, and analyst Ahmad Shehab said the strategy is "unlikely to turn Oman into a regional hub under the current parameters."
